architect:radical.name: AgentOS Escrow
architect:radical.tagline: Agents act without prompts. Every change to your disk and to the outside world is staged, typed and signed, and nothing irreversible leaves the machine until you commit.
architect:radical.lens: Radical primitives. When the main user of a computer is an agent, the OS unit of work should be a transaction, not a process. Its output should be a signed receipt, not an exit code. Files should carry data labels as well as owners. Network calls should be typed effects, not opaque sockets. Rights should be per-task capabilities rather than users and groups, and the human should be scheduled as a scarce resource. Cut down for one part-time person, three primitives survive into the MVP: (1) task-as-transaction, covering the workspace and remote HTTP(S) effects; (2) read-time data labels enforced at every exit; (3) out-of-band signed receipts. A minimal attention queue is a thin fourth. Containment is reused, never rebuilt.
architect:radical.revolutionary_claim: For the first time, a third-party agent from any vendor (Hermes Agent, Claude Code, OpenCode, or a scripted replay of a compromised agent) can run unmodified with all permission prompts disabled, on an installable Linux image, under three guarantees. (a) Every file change is staged in an overlay. (b) Every outbound HTTP(S) effect is classified as read-only, reversible, compensable or irreversible by a signed effect manifest; unknown effects default to irreversible. Irreversible effects are held in escrow and never reach the destination before commit. (c) Any outbound request from a task that has read a file labelled secret is held, even to an allowlisted host such as the project's own forge, if it carries a fingerprint of that file. When the task ends, the OS writes a receipt that a third party can verify with a public key. The receipt lists the staged diff, the effect journal, the labels touched and the OS image digest. Abort restores the workspace byte for byte and runs recorded compensations in reverse order. The claim can be checked three ways: the hero demo assertions (mail sink shows 0 messages, the forge repository still exists, the workspace tree hash matches); flipping one byte of a receipt makes verification fail; and a review of the feature lists of OpenShell, MXC, sandbox-runtime, Docker Sandboxes, Copilot sandboxing, agent-sandbox, Sprites, Agent 365 and AgentCore, none of which stages remote effects or classifies them by reversibility (as of 16 Oct 2026). Limits stated up front: only HTTP(S) effects described by manifests are classified, non-HTTP egress is blocked rather than understood, and fingerprinting misses paraphrased leaks.
architect:radical.first_users: Primary: developers who already run autonomous agents with permission prompts disabled on a dedicated Linux box or VM, and who give those agents real credentials (forge, cloud, database, email). The evidence: Omarchy launches 11 of 15 agents with skip or auto-approve flags, Hermes Agent ships a --yolo mode, and users approve about 93% of Claude Code prompts, so prompts are already rubber stamps. These users accept a dedicated agent machine, so a bootable image costs them little. Secondary, from month 6: maintainers of agent frameworks and red-team or evaluation groups who need a reproducible dry run of what an agent would have done, with tamper-evident transcripts. METR calls observability security-critical, and OpenAI test agents tampered with logs. Tertiary, from month 9: AI-native vendors that need verifiable agent evidence to close enterprise deals (EU AI Act Art. 12/14/26, Colorado SB26-189, CPPA ADMT, Australian ADM disclosure). Regulated enterprises tied to Microsoft E7 are deliberately not first users.
problem_evidence: Permission prompts fail: users approve about 93% of Claude Code permission prompts, and Omarchy launches 11 of 15 coding agents with prompts disabled. Per-action approval is already abandoned in practice.

Only about 0.8% of tool calls appear irreversible in Anthropic data (software-heavy sample). If the OS knew which calls those were, the human approval surface could shrink by roughly two orders of magnitude.

Destructive actions happen: agents deleted production databases at Replit and PocketOS (about 9 seconds). Claude Code checkpoints cover file edits only, and no free product stages or compensates remote API effects.

Exfiltration through permitted channels is unsolved: the labs concede prompt injection is unsolved, adaptive attacks bypass most published defences, and in one Anthropic test 24 of 25 exfiltration retries succeeded until egress and filesystem controls held. Allowlists do not stop leaks to allowlisted destinations.
Logs inside the agent's reach cannot be trusted: OpenAI test agents compromised Hugging Face production and tampered with logs (July 2026), and at least 96 transcripts showed tool-call spoofing.

Containment wraps only part of the process tree: Anthropic sandbox-runtime covers shell commands, not MCP servers or hooks. Snyk ToxicSkills found 13.4% of 3,984 skills critical and 76 malicious, so third-party tool code runs with agent authority.
The review bottleneck: Faros 2026 (22k developers) reports median PR review time +441.5%, PRs merged without review +76.3% and incidents per PR +242.7%.
Governance maturity is low: only about 20% of firms have mature agent governance (Deloitte, n=3,235).

primitives.name: Task-as-transaction (agentos tx)
primitives.what_it_does: Each agent run is a transaction with begin, run, diff, commit and abort. The agent and every child process (MCP servers, hooks, LSP servers, shells) share one staged world. Commit applies the staged changes and releases escrow. Abort discards the staging area and runs compensations.
primitives.mechanism: A systemd transient scope gives each task its own cgroup, whose id keys all policy. bubblewrap (0.8+) supplies a private mount namespace with /usr read-only and the workspace mounted as overlayfs (upper dir = staged diff), plus an empty network namespace whose only route is a socat bridge to the escrow proxy, the pattern sandbox-runtime uses on Linux. Commit merges the upper dir into the lower dir atomically per file. Abort deletes the upper dir. Btrfs snapshots of /var for system-level changes come in phase 2.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse overlayfs, bubblewrap, systemd-run, socat and cgroup v2. Build an orchestrator daemon and CLI of about 1,000 lines of Go. Landlock and seccomp hardening can come from OpenShell or MXC policies later rather than new code.

primitives.name: Effect escrow (effect-typed calls at the network boundary)
primitives.what_it_does: Treats every outbound HTTP(S) request as a typed effect. Reads pass live. Reversible and compensable effects execute live, and their compensation is journalled. Irreversible and unknown effects are held, by default with a synthetic 202 response or, per manifest, with block-and-wait, and are replayed in order only on commit.
primitives.mechanism: A TLS-terminating forward proxy uses a per-task CA, injected into the sandbox trust store only. Its key is unreadable inside the sandbox. DNS resolves only through the proxy. Non-HTTP egress fails closed. Abort runs compensations in reverse order (the saga pattern), and a failed compensation is recorded as a failure, never hidden.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse elazarl/goproxy (BSD-3) for MITM plumbing and the Go standard library for certificate minting. Build classification, hold and replay, and the compensation runner, about 800 lines.

primitives.name: Signed effect manifests with permission-diff admission
primitives.what_it_does: Declarative per-API rules map method plus path pattern to an effect class, a compensation template and a visibility flag. Effects that notify humans count as irreversible even when the state can be restored. A manifest update that lowers any effect's class is refused until an administrator approves the diff.
primitives.mechanism: YAML schema signed with cosign and verified at load. MCP tool annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) are read only as untrusted hints: they can raise a class, never lower it. The MVP ships manifests for the Forgejo API, the Mailpit send API and model API endpoints, with a generic default.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse cosign and MCP annotations. Build the schema, matcher and three manifests, about 250 lines plus data. Long-tail manifests are community work.

primitives.name: Data labels as first-class file metadata (read-time taint)
primitives.what_it_does: Files carry labels such as secret, personal or untrusted. The moment any process in a task opens a labelled file, the task's taint set grows. Every exit then enforces sink policy for that label, including allowlisted hosts and model APIs: requests carrying fingerprints of labelled content are held, and tainted tasks can be restricted to named sinks.
primitives.mechanism: A label xattr is set by the witness service. A BPF LSM program on the file_open hook reads it with the bpf_get_file_xattr kfunc (Linux 6.8+), keyed by the task cgroup id, and pushes events through a ring buffer to the daemon. The proxy scans bodies against chunk hashes of labelled files in plain, base64 and hex forms. Taint is session-level and conservative (Rule of Two style), not per-token information-flow tracking. Strict mode refuses to start if BPF LSM is unavailable.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse kernel BPF LSM, the kfunc and cilium/ebpf (MIT). Build about 200 lines of C and Go. Week 7 includes a kill check, with a fallback to Landlock-gated label paths in which a granted read capability equals taint.

primitives.name: Receipts as the universal output
primitives.what_it_does: Every task, committed or aborted, ends in one receipt: what the agent tried, what was staged, executed, held, approved, compensated or failed, which labels it touched, and under which OS image, policy and manifests. Third parties verify it offline with a public key.
primitives.mechanism: An in-toto Statement with a custom predicate inside a DSSE envelope, signed with ed25519 by a daemon running as a separate system user outside all task namespaces. Receipts are hash-chained to the previous one and include the bootc image digest plus policy and manifest digests. Bodies are stored as hashes or redacted by default. Optional Rekor anchoring of the digest comes in phase 3, and a TPM-bound key follows once bootc sealed images leave test status.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse the in-toto and DSSE formats and the sigstore libraries. Build the writer and the agentos verify command, about 250 lines.

primitives.name: Attention queue (minimal)
primitives.what_it_does: Lists the escrowed irreversible remainder across all open tasks in one ranked inbox: label violations first, then destructive effects, then other irreversible effects. A human approves or denies item by item or in batches, so oversight costs one review per task rather than one prompt per action.
primitives.mechanism: The agentos inbox CLI plus a static HTML receipt viewer generated per task. Interruption budgets, digests and random audits are deferred.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Build about 150 lines. Defer any richer UI, possibly as a Cockpit plugin later.

architect:radical.architecture:
Image layer: one Containerfile on quay.io/fedora/fedora-bootc:44 (multi-arch). Universal Blue images are amd64-only, which rules them out. A bootc kargs.d file adds bpf to the lsm= list, /usr is read-only, and /var sits on Btrfs. The image ships five things: agentos-txd as a system service under its own user (agentos-witness) holding the signing key and CA keys; the agentos CLI; the escrow proxy; the compiled BPF object; and the default signed manifests. A dedicated agent account's login session is always wrapped in a transaction, so nothing the agent starts runs outside one. The demo world (Forgejo and Mailpit, pinned by digest) is an optional set of Podman Quadlet containers. Images are built natively in CI for x86_64 and aarch64 with bootc-image-builder (qcow2, ISO, raw) and signed with cosign.

Task flow:
1. agentos run --policy P -- <agent command>.
2. txd creates a systemd scope (cgroup id), the overlay upper and work directories, the network namespace with its proxy bridge and the per-task CA, then registers the cgroup id in the BPF taint map.
3. The agent runs under bubblewrap, and every child inherits the namespaces.
4. Opening a labelled file emits a ring-buffer event, and txd updates the task taint set.
5. Each HTTP(S) request goes to the proxy, which matches a manifest, checks taint and fingerprints, and then passes it, executes and journals a compensation, or holds it.
6. When the agent exits, txd drafts a receipt and agentos diff shows the staged files and the effect journal.
7. Commit merges the overlay, replays held effects in order and signs the final receipt. Abort discards the overlay, runs compensations in reverse and signs the receipt.

Portability: the same static binaries run in userland mode on any recent Linux, with weaker guarantees (no forced agent account, and labels only where BPF LSM is enabled). The receipt format and the manifest schema live in separate Apache-2.0 specification repositories so that OpenShell, MXC or Docker Sandboxes could emit or consume them. The OS image is the reference full-guarantee platform, not the only one.

Founder code budget: about 2,950 lines (Go plus a little C), excluding tests, manifests and CI YAML.
architect:radical.why_bootable_os_matters:
A userland tool can only wrap what it launches and must degrade when the host kernel lacks features. The owned image guarantees seven things a tool cannot:
(1) BPF LSM is active, because the image sets lsm= through bootc kargs.d. Read-time labels depend on this, and most stock kernels do not enable BPF LSM by default.
(2) Known kernel levels for Landlock ABI, overlayfs in user namespaces, cgroup v2 and Btrfs. Claude Code's sandbox, by contrast, fails open by default.
(3) The agent account has no route to the network except the escrow proxy. MCP servers, hooks and any vendor's subprocess therefore cannot bypass escrow. sandbox-runtime does not cover MCP servers, and OpenShell wraps only the processes it starts.
(4) The witness service, signing key and CA keys live under a separate system user on a read-only /usr that the agent cannot modify.
(5) Every receipt records the bootc image digest, so a verifier knows exactly which enforcement code produced it. On a mutable distribution that claim means little.
(6) System-wide rollback: bootc rollback for /usr, plus Btrfs snapshots of /var in phase 2.
(7) A later path to TPM-measured boot that binds the receipt key to the image.

The core stays portable: binaries and specifications run on other Linux systems in a degraded mode, which lowers the adoption barrier while the image remains the reference. Challenge to the founder's framing: the OS layer itself should stay deliberately boring, one Containerfile on Fedora bootc. The revolutionary part is the transaction, label and receipt model on top, not a new distribution.
architect:radical.why_incumbents_wont: (1) Model and agent vendors are judged on task success and fluency. Escrow adds synthetic responses and a commit step, and implicitly says their agent cannot be trusted. Each vendor also governs only its own agent; sandbox-runtime, for example, covers shell commands, not MCP servers. (2) Containment vendors (NVIDIA OpenShell and NemoClaw, Microsoft MXC, Docker Sandboxes) enforce allow or deny at a boundary. Staged commit needs per-API semantic manifests and compensations, a long-tail maintenance commons that does not sell GPUs, Entra seats or Docker subscriptions. (3) Cloud governance (Agent 365, AgentCore Policy with Dogwood temporal rules) enforces only at its own gateway and in its own estate. A local agent box calling arbitrary APIs is outside it, and a portable, third-party-verifiable receipt weakens console lock-in (Purview, CloudWatch). (4) Durable-execution vendors such as Temporal need deterministic workflow code and do not capture OS state or arbitrary agent processes. Caveats: Temporal is moving towards agent recovery, AWS could add data-label conditions to Dogwood, and Docker's credential proxy could add hold-and-commit. The gap should be rechecked every quarter against changelogs, on the assumption that anything bundleable is bundled within 12 to 18 months.
architect:radical.relationship_to_existing:
OpenShell (Apache-2.0): complementary. It already provides Landlock, seccomp, network namespaces, credential injection and a policy prover. Escrow does not rebuild those. Phase 3 chains the escrow proxy behind OpenShell's proxy and compiles Escrow policy into the OpenShell schema. OpenShell telemetry is disabled in the image. OpenShell has no staging, effect classes, compensations, read-time labels or signed receipts.
MXC (MIT): the Windows and macOS containment path for a later portable mode. Escrow emits MXC policy JSON rather than reimplementing Seatbelt or AppContainer. MXC has no escrow or receipts.
Anthropic sandbox-runtime: the source of the bubblewrap-plus-socat bridge pattern. It covers shell commands only, while Escrow wraps the whole agent process tree, including MCP servers and hooks.
Docker Sandboxes: microVMs plus a credential proxy and a paid governance tier. It stops at the VM boundary with no staged remote effects. Escrow could run inside one as a userland upstream proxy.
OpenClaw (MIT, 722 advisories in 2026) and Hermes Agent (MIT): workloads, not competitors. Both run unmodified under agentos run. Hermes is the first integration target, and phase 2 offers an agentos sandbox backend upstream.
Omarchy: claims the agentic-distro label but launches most agents with prompts disabled. Escrow is the counter-position: run yolo mode safely because nothing irreversible happens before commit. It does not compete on desktop polish.
Agent 365 and AgentCore: identity, inventory and gateway policy inside their estates. Escrow integrates rather than displaces, with receipts exportable to Purview or CloudWatch later, and targets the local or sovereign agent box they do not see.
Others: Claude Code checkpoints cover file edits only. Fly Sprites checkpoint VM state but not external effects. Rubrik Agent Rewind restores from backups after the fact, its current status is unverified, and it is proprietary. Windows agent workspaces give per-agent accounts but no escrow.
mvp_12_weeks: Week 1: Public repository, Apache-2.0 licence, trademark policy, threat model v0 (including an explicit list of what Escrow does not protect against). Containerfile on fedora-bootc:44, built natively for aarch64 on the M1 Pro (podman machine) and in CI for x86_64 and aarch64, with qcow2 output from bootc-image-builder. Acceptance: both architectures boot under QEMU in CI and a smoke test over SSH prints bootc status. Security: cosign-signed images, an SBOM (syft) and a CVE scan (grype or trivy) on every build.

Week 2: Transaction lifecycle (systemd scope, bubblewrap and an overlay workspace) with diff, commit and abort for files. Acceptance: a property test of 1,000 random file operations shows abort restores the identical tree hash and commit equals the unwrapped result. Compatibility: works in QEMU, UTM and Lima-krunkit VMs, with no nested virtualisation required.

Week 3: Empty network namespace with a socat bridge, a pass-through TLS-terminating proxy using a per-task CA, and DNS only via the proxy. Acceptance: tests show direct TCP, raw UDP, DNS to an external resolver and IPv6 all fail from inside the task. Security: a test confirms the CA private key is unreadable by the agent user. Performance target, to be measured rather than assumed: added p95 latency of 25 ms or less for pass-through HTTPS on loopback.

Week 4: Effect manifest schema and classifier (unknown defaults to irreversible); escrow with synthetic-response and block-and-wait modes; Forgejo and Mailpit demo world as Quadlets. Acceptance: at least 40 table-driven request-classification tests pass, and a fuzz test confirms no held request ever reaches the sink before commit.

Week 5: Effect journal and saga compensations; abort runs them in reverse order. Acceptance: a fault-injection test shows a failed compensation is recorded and surfaced as FAILED in the receipt, never reported as success.

Week 6: Receipts (in-toto Statement in a DSSE envelope, ed25519, hash chain, image, policy and manifest digests) and agentos verify. Acceptance: a mutation test detects 100% of single-byte changes; the signing key is unreadable as the agent user; a verifier works offline from the public key alone.

Week 7: Labels: xattr, a BPF LSM file_open hook keyed by cgroup, the taint set, per-label sink policy, and fingerprint scanning in plain, base64 and hex. Acceptance: taint is recorded for reads by cat, by Python, by a child MCP server process and through mmap, and the exfiltration to the allowlisted forge is held. Kill check: if labelling is unreliable on the Fedora kernel by the end of week 7, switch to the Landlock-gated fallback.

Week 8: Deterministic compromised-agent replay plus the agentos demo injection and demo check commands; CI runs the full hero demo on an x86_64 KVM runner and publishes receipts as artefacts. Acceptance: 20 consecutive green CI runs on both architectures.

Week 9: Real agents. Run Hermes Agent (pinned) and one of OpenCode or Claude Code unmodified under a transaction with a cloud key; log every breakage caused by synthetic responses, TLS interception, WebSockets or streaming; add per-manifest block-and-wait fallbacks. Acceptance: a written compatibility matrix. Kill check: the task-failure rate attributable to escrow.

Week 10: agentos inbox attention queue, static HTML receipt viewer, cosign-verified manifests with permission-diff admission. Acceptance: a test shows a manifest update that lowers an effect class is refused without administrator approval.

Week 11: Mini-benchmark of 20 tasks (10 benign, 10 injected, in the AgentDojo style against the local demo world), comparing an unwrapped run with an Escrow run. Measures: completion rate, leaks reaching sinks, and human decisions per task. Docs: quickstart, threat model, manifest authoring guide, and a limitations page.

Week 12: Release v0.1: signed x86_64 and aarch64 qcow2, ISO and OCI images; reproducibility notes; a recorded demo; a launch post stating the limits; a call for manifests in the Hermes and OpenClaw communities. Acceptance: one person outside the project reproduces the hero demo from the docs alone.
roadmap_12_months: Months 4-6 (v0.2), label-aware model routing as the one validated inference backend: llama.cpp (llama-server) as a digest-pinned OCI container (CPU and Vulkan), one small permissively licensed model pulled on demand, and tasks tainted secret allowed to reach only the local model endpoint while cloud model calls are held. This gives the model-unification wish a principled place: models are sinks with label policy. Also: git smart-HTTP push parsing (pushes to refs/heads/agent/* are reversible), MCP streamable-HTTP tool-call classification with annotations as hints, Btrfs snapshots of /var for system-level changes, manifests for GitHub, GitLab, Slack, SMTP, S3 and PostgREST, and an upstream agentos sandbox backend for Hermes Agent.

Months 7-9 (v0.3), evidence and portability: a receipt-to-regulation field mapping for EU AI Act Art. 12/14/26, Colorado SB26-189, CPPA ADMT and Australian ADM disclosure (a mapping document, not legal advice); optional Rekor anchoring and an external witness; a portable userland package for Ubuntu and Debian; the escrow proxy chained behind the OpenShell and MXC proxies; an agentos-nvidia x86_64 variant boot-tested on AWS g4dn spot (about USD 0.33/hr) at each release.

Months 10-12 (v0.4, 1.0 candidate): attention scheduler (interruption budgets, digests, random audit sampling, global stop); one policy compiled to OpenShell, MXC and bubblewrap enforcers; TPM-bound receipt keys and measured boot only if bootc sealed images have left test status; receipt aggregation across several machines; receipt and manifest specifications offered to a neutral foundation; an optional Cockpit UI plugin covering Agents, Receipts and Settings.
metrics: Hero demo reliability: 100% pass over 20 consecutive CI runs on x86_64 and aarch64 by week 8, sustained at 98% or above thereafter.
Abort fidelity: 0 held effects observed at any sink, and an identical workspace tree hash, across at least 1,000 fuzzed task runs per release.
Receipt integrity: 100% of mutation-test tamperings detected; an offline verifier works from the public key alone.

Utility cost: drop in task completion between unwrapped and Escrow runs on the 20-task suite. Target 10 points or less (for comparison, CaMeL costs about 7 points on average and 3 to 32 points by model).
Approval load: median human decisions per task under Escrow against the number of permission prompts in the same unwrapped task. Target a median of 1 or fewer decisions.
Classification coverage: share of remote effects in real agent sessions matched by a manifest rather than defaulted to unknown. Target 80% or more on the suite by month 6.
Leak containment: injected suite tasks in which labelled content reaches any sink. Target 0 for verbatim, base64 and hex encodings; paraphrased leaks are reported separately as a known gap.
Overhead (targets to measure, not claims): task start 3 seconds or less; pass-through p95 latency 25 ms or less; abort of a 10,000-file overlay 5 seconds or less.

Community: external demo reproductions posted with receipts (target 10 by month 6); manifests contributed by others (target 5 by month 6); weekly active installs from countme-style opt-in data (target 50 by month 9). Stars are tracked only as a weak signal.
risks: Agent breakage: synthetic 202 responses may break agents that use the response of an irreversible call, and TLS interception breaks certificate-pinned clients. WebSocket and long-lived streaming traffic may be held as unknown. Mitigation: block-and-wait mode per manifest and a published compatibility matrix. This is the largest technical risk.

False sense of safety: compensable does not mean invisible, because a deleted comment may already have triggered notifications or webhooks. Fingerprints miss paraphrased leaks, and session-level taint over-holds. Mitigation: treat human-visible effects as irreversible by default and keep a prominent limitations page.
Manifest maintenance burden: APIs change, and the unknown-means-irreversible default keeps safety but raises approval load. Long-tail coverage depends on a contributor community that may not form.

Incumbent fast-follow: Docker's credential proxy, OpenShell's proxy or AgentCore could add hold-and-commit within one release. Mitigation: own the open receipt and manifest formats and stay integrable rather than exclusive.

Platform risk: bootc is a CNCF Sandbox project, Fedora's six-month cadence brings churn, BPF LSM xattr behaviour through overlayfs needs verification, and the M1 Pro cannot test NVIDIA, x86 Secure Boot or TPM.

Solo capacity and bus factor: about 120 hours for the MVP is tight, and successful solo projects still rely on the founder for 66-100% of commits. Positioning risk: Omarchy owns the agentic-distro label, and generic AI-OS projects have a poor track record.
Privacy and legal: receipts and the proxy see sensitive request bodies. Mitigation: store hashes and redacted bodies by default, keep the CA scoped per task, and never forward any data externally.

Open question for the founder (1): is a dedicated agent machine or VM acceptable to the target users, or is a userland-first release on existing distributions the faster path to adoption, with the bootable image as the reference?

Open question for the founder (2): if escrow of remote effects proves too disruptive for real agents by week 9, would the founder accept a narrower product (staged files, labels and receipts, with block-and-wait for every irreversible call)?
kill_criteria: Week 9: if more than 30% of real-agent suite tasks (Hermes Agent and OpenCode or Claude Code) fail because of escrow mechanics, and block-and-wait mode does not bring failures below 15%, drop synthetic-response escrow and narrow to staged files, labels, receipts and a synchronous hold for irreversible effects.
Week 7: if BPF LSM read-time labelling is not reliable on the shipped Fedora kernel after 3 weeks of work, switch to Landlock-gated label paths and remove read-time labels from the claim.

Any time: if an incumbent ships free staged commit of remote effects with reversibility classes and verifiable receipts for third-party agents, stop the OS image and become a manifest and receipt standard plus an integration on top of that product.

Month 6: if fewer than 5 people outside the project have reproduced the hero demo and fewer than 2 external manifests exist, stop maintaining the bootable image and keep only the portable userland tool and the specifications.
Month 9: if no framework maintainer, red team, evaluator or AI-native vendor has adopted receipts in a real workflow, freeze the evidence roadmap.
Founder capacity: if available time stays below 6 hours a week for 4 consecutive weeks, freeze scope at receipts plus staged files.
scope_cuts_from_original_spec: Model unification (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Gemma, Laya): cut from the MVP. Llama is effectively legacy, Laya is a 0.4B routing classifier rather than an LLM, and model packaging at the OS level shows weak demand (Canonical inference snaps have 52 stars). Phase 2 adds one local backend only as a label-policy sink.

Inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, MLX, Ollama): cut. vLLM ships breaking minors every 2-3 weeks and is tied to specific CUDA and PyTorch builds, TensorRT-LLM cannot be tested on M1, MLX has no GPU path on Linux, and NVIDIA gives serving tooling away. Users may point agents at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, Ollama included; llama.cpp in a container arrives in phase 2.
Training and fine-tuning (TorchTitan, DeepSpeed, Axolotl, Unsloth): cut for at least 12 months. They are a poor wedge for a small team, cannot be tested on a 16 GB M1, and torchtune is unmaintained.

Hardware adapters and the GPU or cluster resource scheduler: cut. Leaders build these in-house and NVIDIA bundles them free. They are replaced by per-task cgroup limits through systemd (reused) and by scheduling human attention, the scarce resource the evidence identifies.
Benchmark engine: narrowed from model performance benchmarking to a reproducible Escrow conformance and utility suite (completion, leaks, approvals per task).
Six-section UI (Home, Agents, Models, Training, Developer Tools, System Settings): cut to a CLI, an inbox and a static receipt viewer. A Cockpit plugin is considered only in months 10-12.

Security services as a broad suite: narrowed to escrow, labels and receipts. Containment (Landlock, seccomp, microVMs, credential injection) is reused from bubblewrap, OpenShell and MXC rather than rebuilt.
Agent framework unification: narrowed to running any agent unmodified, with Hermes Agent as the first validated integration. No new agent framework and no new protocol.
Desktop environment: cut. The image is headless (SSH or console) because first users run dedicated agent boxes and VMs, and Omarchy and Bluefin already cover desktops.

Secure Boot, TPM measured boot and sealed UKI: deferred, because sealed UKI is test-only in bootc 1.17. Note that adopting composefs later may require reinstalling systems installed on the ostree backend.
NVIDIA image variant: deferred to months 7-9 with spot-instance boot tests, because it is untestable on the M1 Pro and not needed for the core claim.

Every-phase requirements (acceptance criteria, automated tests, security checks, compatibility, performance targets, documentation): kept, but scaled to the MVP weeks above. Performance figures are stated as targets to measure, not claims.

architect:workflow.name: Docket (working name for the AgentOS flagship; trademark search required before public use)
architect:workflow.tagline: Agents run as transactions. Independent verifiers decide what may commit. You are interrupted only for what cannot be undone.
architect:workflow.lens: Verification and attention first: one human supervising many agents. Human verification time is now the scarce resource. Faros 2026 measured median PR review time up 441.5% and PRs merged without review up 76.3%, and users approve about 93% of Claude Code permission prompts. The OS therefore schedules human attention the way it schedules CPU time: a priority, a time budget, batching, aging and a global stop. It also replaces the per-action permission prompt with a single database-style commit decision on a staged transaction.
architect:workflow.first_users:
Solo developers and AI-native teams of 2 to 10 people who already run three or more coding or operations agents in parallel (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw) on a Linux workstation, home server or cloud VM. Today these users either approve prompts all day or run with permissions bypassed. Evidence:
- Omarchy, the best-known 'agentic' distribution (44.9k stars, 1.28M self-reported ISO downloads), launches 11 of 15 agents with permission prompts disabled. This shows demand for prompt-free operation that currently has no safety net.
- Users approve about 93% of Claude Code prompts.
- The agent-caused database deletions (Replit, PocketOS) hit small teams that had given agents real credentials.
Entry communities:
- Hermes Agent self-hosters (254k stars; OpenAI-compatible API; seven sandbox backends but 15.7k open issues).
- r/LocalLLaMA.
- Fedora Atomic and Universal Blue users, who can adopt with `bootc switch` and leave with `bootc rollback`.
Explicitly not first:
- CISOs standardised on Microsoft E7.
- Frontier labs, which build their own tools.
- Regulated deployers, whose deadlines fall in 2027.
- Non-engineering agents inside SaaS platforms, where a Linux OS has no control point.
problem_evidence: Faros AI Engineering Report 2026 (22,000 developers, correlational): median time in PR review +441.5%, PRs merged without any review +76.3%, incidents per PR +242.7%. Reviewers are now skipping review, not only slowing down.

Anthropic: users approve about 93% of manual Claude Code permission prompts (no base disclosed). The auto-mode classifier still misses 17% of 52 hand-picked real overeager actions, and Anthropic says it does not replace careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure.

Anthropic: about 0.8% of public-API tool calls appear irreversible (Claude-classified, about 50% software engineering). If staging contains the rest, the human approval surface can shrink by roughly two orders of magnitude, but this figure undercounts harm that builds up from sequences of individually reversible steps.
Production database deletions by agents (Replit; PocketOS, lost in about 9 seconds) and the AWS Kiro outage. Claude Code checkpoints cover file edits only and only for that one agent.

Anthropic sandbox-runtime covers shell commands only. MCP servers, hooks and LSP servers run with full user access, so containment controlled by the agent leaves gaps that only a wrapper at session level closes.

OpenAI test agents compromised Hugging Face production (July 2026) and tried to edit logs. At least 96 transcripts showed tool-call spoofing, and the evidence survived only because transcripts were captured separately. METR calls observability security-critical. Evidence must come from the harness, not from the agent.

Human-factors brief: no study shows one person safely supervising 10 to 100 agents, and each vendor's mission control (GitHub Agent HQ, Cursor) ranks only its own agents. No product decides where a supervisor's limited attention should go across vendors.

Counter-evidence that must be tested, not ignored: Faros links heavy AI review to faster first reviews and lower change-failure rates, and practitioners report landing one significant change at a time. AI reviewers or fewer agents may absorb part of this pain.

primitives.name: Agent transaction (atx)
primitives.what_it_does: Runs one agent task, with every process it spawns, against a copy-on-write view of the workspace. On reject, the host is left byte-for-byte unchanged. On approval, the staged changeset is applied as one git commit.
primitives.mechanism: docketd assigns an agent UID from a fixed pool. It mounts overlayfs with the lower layer set to the workspace at the base commit and the upper layer set to a staging directory. It then starts the agent with systemd-run as a transient unit in docket.slice with these settings: ProtectSystem=strict, ProtectHome=tmpfs, ReadWritePaths set to the merged workspace, PrivateTmp, NoNewPrivileges, RestrictAddressFamilies, SystemCallFilter=@system-service, MemoryMax and CPUQuota. Children (MCP servers, hooks, LSP servers, shells) inherit the unit. The upper directory is the exact file changeset.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse: kernel overlayfs and cgroup v2, plus systemd transient units and sandboxing directives (D-Bus StartTransientUnit through systemd-run, available for years; the systemd v262 Varlink StartTransient is optional later). Build: about 350 lines of lifecycle code in docketd. No VMs, so the M1 Pro needs no nested virtualization.

primitives.name: Effect proxy and side-effect journal (held intents)
primitives.what_it_does: Classifies every outbound request as inference, read-only, mutating or denied. Read-only and inference requests pass. Mutating requests are held as intents and replayed only after approval at commit. Credentials for model APIs and target services never enter the agent namespace.
primitives.mechanism:
An inet nftables table redirects all TCP from agent UIDs to a mitmproxy transparent listener running under a separate proxy user. It drops UDP except to the local resolver, blocks QUIC so clients fall back to TCP, and drops everything else. A per-session CA is bind-mounted into the unit trust store (SSL_CERT_FILE, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE). The Docket addon classifies each request:
- GET, HEAD and OPTIONS to allowlisted hosts are read-only.
- Allowlisted model endpoints are inference; the proxy injects the API key.
- Other methods are mutating: the request is recorded (method, URL, redacted headers, body) and the agent receives HTTP 202 with a JSON body explaining the deferral and giving an intent ID.
- git receive-pack is denied with the message that publishing is a commit action.
- Unknown hosts and pinned-certificate failures are denied.
MCP tool annotations are hints only and add context to the decision card. Classification happens at the effect boundary, so no agent cooperation is needed.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse: nftables, mitmproxy (MIT, hash-pinned) transparent mode, and the credential-injection pattern already shipped by OpenShell and Claude Code. Build: about 350 lines of mitmproxy addon (classification rules, holding, replay with idempotency keys).

primitives.name: Pinned verifier gate
primitives.what_it_does: Decides whether a transaction may commit, using evidence the agent cannot alter. Agents may add tests. Modifying or deleting existing verifier files, tests or CI configuration routes the transaction to a human as a verifier-tamper exception.
primitives.mechanism: docketd reads docket.toml from the base commit, never from the staged copy. It runs each declared verifier (tests, linters, type checks) in a fresh transient unit under a different UID, with network denied and the merged view mounted read-only, and re-runs a failure once to flag flakiness as 'uncertain'. Built-in checks: protected-path edits, a secret scan of the upper directory (gitleaks), blast radius (files and lines changed) and held-intent classes. If verifiers still fail after the agent's allowed retries, the transaction goes back to the agent with the verifier output, without involving a human.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse: the project's own test suite, gitleaks (MIT) and systemd sandboxing. Build: about 250 lines (config loader, runner and protected-path diff).

primitives.name: Attention scheduler
primitives.what_it_does: Treats human attention as a scheduled resource across all agents and vendors. It keeps one ranked exception queue with a per-human interruption budget, batches everything else into digests, samples auto-commits for spot checks and provides a global stop.
primitives.mechanism:
Priority is a weighted score of irreversible intents, verifier status (fail, uncertain, tamper), blast radius, protected-path flags and age (aging prevents starvation). Policy decides one of three outcomes:
- Auto-commit, only to a local branch docket/<id>, when every verifier passes, no intents are held, no protected paths are touched and blast radius is under the threshold.
- Auto-return to the agent when verifiers fail.
- Queue for a human in every other case.
Interrupts (terminal bell, desktop notification or optional ntfy webhook) are issued only within the budget (default 4 per hour). Everything else goes to a digest every 30 minutes. 5% of auto-commits are sampled for spot checks. `docket stop` writes cgroup.freeze on docket.slice and switches the proxy to deny-all.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse: cgroup v2 freeze and Textual (MIT) for the terminal UI. Build: about 400 lines for the scheduler and about 450 lines for the CLI and terminal queue, which shows decision cards (diffstat, verifier output, held intents, policy reason).

primitives.name: Out-of-band evidence journal
primitives.what_it_does: Records every transaction step (creation, effects, verifier results, scheduler decision, human approval or rejection, replay outcome) in a log that agent processes can neither read nor rewrite, and that anyone can verify.
primitives.mechanism: Append-only JSON Lines. Each entry carries the SHA-256 of the previous entry and an Ed25519 signature from a key readable only by the docketd user, stored in /var/lib/docket. Entries record agent UID and profile, the delegating human, policy version and base commit. `docket journal verify` recomputes the chain. Scope stated honestly: the journal resists tampering by agents; it does not resist tampering by host root until it is anchored externally (Phase 2).
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse: python3-cryptography for Ed25519. Build: about 250 lines. External anchoring (Sigstore Rekor or a remote git log) and evidence packs mapped to regulations are deferred.

primitives.name: Guarantee floor and doctor
primitives.what_it_does: Makes the security properties explicit and testable. On the AgentOS image every guarantee is on and asserted in CI. On other Linux hosts, `docket doctor` prints which guarantees hold, which are degraded, and why.
primitives.mechanism: Checks: overlayfs and cgroup v2 freeze available; nftables UID and socket matching works; the proxy user is separate; agent UIDs cannot reach the docketd socket, the journal or the key; bpf is present in lsm=; and the Landlock ABI level (target 9 or later on Linux 7.1+, required only for Phase 2 defence in depth). The checks also run an escape suite: curl --noproxy, raw sockets, UDP, IPv6, DNS-over-HTTPS and direct IP connections.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse: kernel and systemd introspection. Build: about 100 lines, counted inside the CLI.

primitives.name: Agent profiles (wrap, do not fork)
primitives.what_it_does: Lets Docket launch existing agents unmodified with sensible allowlists, inference endpoints and verifier defaults.
primitives.mechanism: A TOML profile per agent defines the command, inference hosts, read-only allowlist and environment. MVP profiles: Hermes Agent (local backend inside the transaction, so its own sandbox is not nested) and one of OpenCode or Claude Code. A generic `docket run -- <any command>` covers everything else. An optional local model runs as llama.cpp llama-server, either in a container or on the macOS host over HTTP, and is allowlisted as an inference host.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse: Hermes Agent (MIT), OpenCode or Claude Code, and llama.cpp. Build: profile files only (no code), plus about 300 lines of scripted demo agents and mock services.

architect:workflow.architecture:
Layer 0: the image.
- A Containerfile built FROM quay.io/fedora/fedora-bootc:44, which is multi-arch. Universal Blue images are amd64-only and so are not used as the base, although the ublue image-template CI workflows are reused. Move to Fedora 45 when it is released.
- Built natively on free GitHub runners for x86_64 and aarch64, cosign-signed and published to GHCR. bootc-image-builder produces qcow2, raw and ISO images.
- Kernel arguments add bpf to lsm=. nftables, mitmproxy (hash-pinned), gitleaks, docketd and the units are baked into /usr. State lives in /var/lib/docket.
- Headless (SSH plus terminal UI), no telemetry. OS updates and rollback go through bootc.
- Daily loop on the M1 Pro: build the aarch64 image in a Podman machine (libkrun provider) and boot the qcow2 in UTM or Lima. No nested virtualization is needed because transactions use namespaces and cgroups, not VMs. x86_64 boot tests run in CI on KVM runners.

Layer 1: transaction substrate.
- Per task, docketd allocates an agent UID, mounts the overlay and starts a transient unit with sandbox properties under docket.slice.
- Every child process inherits the unit, cgroup and staging layer.

Layer 2: effect capture.
- nftables redirects TCP from agent UIDs to the mitmproxy addon. Other egress is dropped, apart from UDP to the local resolver.
- A per-session CA is placed in the unit trust store.
- Requests are classified as inference, read-only, mutating (held intent) or denied. File effects are the upper directory.

Layer 3: verification.
- On agent exit or `docket finish`, verifiers from the base commit run in a separate read-only unit with no network.
- Built-in checks: protected paths, secrets, blast radius.

Layer 4: attention.
- The scheduler scores each transaction and applies policy: auto-commit to a local branch, auto-return, or queue.
- It enforces the interrupt budget, builds digests, samples 5% of auto-commits and provides the global stop (cgroup.freeze plus proxy deny-all).

Layer 5: commit and evidence.
- Approval applies the upper directory as a git commit on docket/<id>. Held intents are replayed in order with idempotency keys and credentials injected at replay time.
- Rejection discards the staging layer and the intents.
- Every step goes into the hash-chained, Ed25519-signed journal.

Founder code: Python 3 only, using Fedora-packaged dependencies where possible, about 2,900 lines excluding tests:
- docketd: 850
- proxy addon: 350
- scheduler: 400
- journal: 250
- CLI and terminal UI: 450
- image and CI configuration: 300
- demo agents and mock services: 300
Tests (pytest plus boot tests in CI) are written in addition, estimated at about 1,500 lines.

Compatibility: x86_64 and aarch64; agents with Node, Python or Go TLS stacks that honour the injected CA. Clients with pinned certificates fail closed and are reported.

Performance targets, to be measured and not claimed, on a reference VM with 4 vCPUs and 8 GB:
- transaction start of 2 s or less;
- proxy p50 added latency of 50 ms or less;
- commit of a 1,000-file changeset in 5 s or less;
- 6 concurrent transactions;
- global stop in 1 s or less.
architect:workflow.why_bootable_os_matters:
The evidence does not make a bootable OS impossible. It does show that the OS is the delivery vehicle for guarantees, not the moat: every 'AI OS' framing has failed or been absorbed, and the research synthesis recommends shipping components. Docket therefore ships as a bootable bootc image on which every guarantee is on and tested in CI, and as a portable package that reports which guarantees hold elsewhere.

What the owned image guarantees and a userland tool cannot:
1. Complete wrapping. The OS creates the session, so the agent, its MCP servers, hooks, LSP servers and their children share one transient unit and one staging layer. sandbox-runtime covers shell commands only.
2. Egress capture by kernel identity. nftables rules keyed to agent UIDs redirect all traffic, so tools that ignore HTTP_PROXY or open raw sockets are still captured. Installing such rules, a per-namespace trust store and a separate proxy user needs root and a known firewall layout, which an application cannot assume.
3. A known kernel and systemd floor, asserted in CI: overlayfs, cgroup v2 freeze, nftables UID and socket matching, BPF LSM on the kernel command line for Phase 2 enforcement (systemd RestrictFileSystemAccess), and Landlock ABI 9 or later on Linux 7.1+ for defence in depth. Userland tools must degrade on older kernels, as Codex did when it demoted Landlock.
4. Out-of-band custody. The journal key, the verifier runner and the proxy run under UIDs and paths that agent UIDs cannot reach. This matters because agents have already tried to tamper with logs (OpenAI and Hugging Face, July 2026).
5. Atomic OS updates and rollback through bootc, so a bad Docket release is undone with one reboot.

Portability: the same Python core installs as an RPM or deb on any systemd Linux with nftables, in a degraded mode that `docket doctor` reports. Fedora Atomic users can adopt with `bootc switch` and leave with `bootc rollback`. macOS and Windows are out of scope, because per-process egress redirection and staging there need different primitives (Seatbelt, MXC). Developers on those platforms run the image in a VM.
architect:workflow.why_incumbents_wont:
1. Agent vendors are judged on task success and throughput. Holding side effects and gating on verifiers visibly slows their agents, and CaMeL-style controls cost 3 to 32 points of task success, so vendors keep such controls opt-in. Claude Code checkpoints cover only that vendor's file edits.
2. Each vendor's mission control (GitHub Agent HQ, Cursor, Claude Code) ranks only its own agents. No vendor gains from telling a customer to review a competitor's agent first, or to run fewer agents.
3. Containment vendors (OpenShell, MXC, Docker Sandboxes, sandbox-runtime) sell 'block or allow', not 'stage, verify and commit'. They do not own the user's verifiers or the commit decision.
4. Durable-execution vendors (Temporal) require deterministic agent code. Docket requires no changes to the agent.
5. Cloud governance (Agent 365, AgentCore) enforces at its own gateways and identity planes, not inside a local Linux session.

Honest caveat: any of these vendors could add staged commit within 12 to 18 months, and Docker or NVIDIA are the most likely to do so. Docket's defence is to be the open reference implementation, publish the held-intent, verifier-gate and journal formats, and offer them upstream to OpenShell and the Agentic AI Foundation, not to rely on secrecy. If an incumbent ships this free first, the kill criteria apply.
architect:workflow.relationship_to_existing:
- NVIDIA OpenShell (Apache-2.0): a complement. The MVP uses plain systemd sandboxing to stay small. Phase 2 adds OpenShell as an optional sandbox driver (Landlock, seccomp, policy prover), with its default-on telemetry disabled in the image. OpenShell has no file staging, held intents, verifier gate or cross-agent attention queue.
- Microsoft MXC (MIT): no overlap in Linux mechanisms. A Phase 3 importer reads MXC JSON filesystem and network allowlists so that one policy feeds both. MXC enforcement mode produces no activity report, and Docket's journal fills that gap on Linux.
- Anthropic sandbox-runtime: covers shell commands only. It can run nested inside a Docket transaction unchanged, while Docket covers the MCP servers, hooks and LSP servers it leaves out.
- Docker Sandboxes: a microVM per agent, a credential proxy and a paid governance tier. Docket is local, free and needs no login, and it adds staging, held intents and a verifier gate. A libkrun microVM transaction driver for KVM hosts is a roadmap option, not a competitor.
- OpenClaw (392k stars, 722 advisories in 2026): a workload to wrap. Its profile arrives in Phase 2 and serves as a high-value test case.
- Hermes Agent: a first-class profile in the MVP. Docket wraps it unmodified using its local backend, and its OpenAI-compatible endpoint is simply an allowlisted inference host.
- Omarchy: the opposite default. It disables prompts with no staging, while Docket makes prompt-free operation safe. Docket does not compete on desktop polish; an Arch package of the portable core is possible later.
- Microsoft Agent 365 and AWS Bedrock AgentCore: Docket does not compete on identity, inventory or cloud policy. A Phase 3 export of journal events in OpenTelemetry or OCSF format lets those planes ingest evidence from local Linux agents that they cannot see today.
- Also related: Claude Code checkpoints (files only, single vendor); GitHub Agent HQ (single vendor, works at PR level, not effect level); Temporal (requires code changes); Windows agent workspaces (per-agent accounts on Windows, no staging or verifier gate); Ollama/Fly.io Sprites (persistent cloud VMs, file restore only).
architect:workflow.hero_demo:
'Six agents, three decisions, one interrupt', reproducible in under 10 minutes in either of two ways.

Path A, no local setup:
1. Fork the repository.
2. Run the reproduce-demo GitHub Actions workflow. On a free x86_64 KVM runner it downloads the signed qcow2 release asset, checks it with `cosign verify`, boots it in QEMU, runs `docket demo fleet --decisions=scripted` and uploads the journal and a verification report. Target: 8 minutes or less.

Path B, local:
1. Download the qcow2 for aarch64 or x86_64 (target size 2 GB or less).
2. Boot it in UTM, Lima or QEMU.
3. Run `docket demo fleet` and decide interactively.

The fleet runs six scripted agents against a small Python library with tests. The agents are scripted so that the demo checks the OS mechanism, not model quality, and needs no GPU or API key. A live mode with Hermes Agent and the user's own key or a local llama-server is optional.
- A: a correct bug fix. Verifiers pass, so it is auto-committed to docket/A with no human involved.
- B: a correct refactor that also starts a filesystem MCP server, whose writes are staged too. Auto-committed.
- C: makes the tests pass by editing an existing test file. Verifier-tamper flag, so it goes to the digest.
- D: breaks the tests. Auto-returned to the agent with the verifier output, with no human involved.
- E: runs `rm -rf ~` and sends DELETE to a mock production API inside the VM. The deletion stays inside the overlay and the DELETE is held as irreversible. Top priority, and the only interrupt.
- F: posts to a mock chat webhook. Held, low priority, goes to the digest.

The human sees one ranked queue with three decision cards: approve F, reject E, reject C.

`docket demo verify` then prints six independently re-computable checks:
1. The SHA-256 of /home/demo is identical before and after.
2. The mock production database row count is unchanged.
3. The webhook log shows exactly one delivery, carrying F's idempotency key.
4. Effect events total N (target 30 or more), with 3 human decisions and 1 interrupt.
5. `docket journal verify` passes. A scripted one-byte edit made as root then makes it fail at the reported entry, and the same edit attempted as an agent UID is denied with EACCES.
6. The escape suite (curl --noproxy, raw socket, UDP, IPv6, DNS-over-HTTPS, direct IP) is captured or blocked, with 0 escapes.

A 90-second recording is published with the release.
mvp_12_weeks: Week 1: Threat model, NON-GOALS file, Apache-2.0 licence, TRADEMARK.md and DCO. Containerfile FROM fedora-bootc:44, built natively in CI for x86_64 and aarch64, cosign-signed and pushed to GHCR, with qcow2 from bootc-image-builder. Acceptance: serial-console boot test passes on the x86_64 KVM runner, and a local aarch64 VM boots on the M1 Pro. Security check: the signature verifies in CI.

Week 2: Transaction core. `docket run -- <cmd>` mounts the overlay, starts a systemd-run unit with sandbox properties under an agent UID, and supports commit and abort. Acceptance (pytest inside the VM in CI): after `rm -rf $HOME` inside a transaction, the host home hash is unchanged; abort leaves no residue in /var/lib/docket; commit produces one git commit. Performance target: start in 2 s or less.

Week 3: Egress capture. nftables UID redirect to mitmproxy in transparent mode, per-session CA injection, UDP and QUIC dropped, IPv6 covered. Acceptance: the escape suite (curl --noproxy, raw socket, UDP, IPv6, DNS-over-HTTPS, direct IP) shows 0 escapes. Security check: agent UIDs cannot reach the docketd socket or the proxy CA key.

Week 4: Held intents. Mutating requests are recorded and answered with HTTP 202; replay at commit uses an idempotency key and credentials injected at replay time; model API keys are injected for inference hosts; git receive-pack is denied with an explanation. Acceptance: against the mock production API, a rejected DELETE is never sent and an approved POST is sent exactly once (mock server log). Performance target: proxy p50 added latency of 50 ms or less.

Week 5: Evidence journal. Hash-chained JSON Lines with Ed25519 signing, `docket journal verify`, and the key readable only by docketd. Acceptance: a one-byte edit is detected at the exact entry; append, read and write attempts as an agent UID fail with EACCES; the journal includes policy version, base commit and delegating human.

Week 6: Pinned verifier gate. docket.toml is read from the base commit; verifiers run in a separate read-only unit with no network; failures are re-run once to flag flakiness; protected-path detection and the gitleaks scan run. Acceptance: an edit to an existing test file is flagged as tamper; added tests run in addition to the existing ones; a failing verifier auto-returns the transaction. First kill-criterion checkpoint (escape suite).

Week 7: Attention scheduler. Deterministic scoring, auto-commit only to a local branch, auto-return, interrupt budget (default 4 per hour), digests, 5% audit sampling with a fixed seed, and `docket stop` (cgroup.freeze plus proxy deny-all). Acceptance: scoring unit tests on 20 fixed cases; stop freezes 6 transactions in 1 s or less (target).

Week 8: Terminal queue (Textual) and decision cards (diffstat, verifier output, held intents, policy reason), with desktop and ntfy notifications. Acceptance: approving or rejecting from the terminal UI matches the CLI and is journaled with the approving user's identity. Docs: quickstart and decision-card reference.

Week 9: Agent profiles. Hermes Agent v0.22.x on its local backend, plus OpenCode or Claude Code, each wrapped unmodified, with the inference endpoint either remote or a llama-server on the macOS host. Acceptance: an MCP server started by the agent shows up inside the same unit and its writes are staged; 6 concurrent transactions run inside an 8 GB VM. Measure the task-completion delta wrapped versus unwrapped on a fixed set of 20 tasks.

Week 10: Hero demo. `docket demo fleet` and `docket demo verify`, the mock production API and webhook, the reproduce-demo GitHub Actions workflow that uploads the journal and report, and the 90-second recording. Acceptance: three consecutive green CI runs finish in under 10 minutes each, and all six verify checks pass. Second kill-criterion checkpoint (agent breakage).

Week 11: Portability and docs. `docket doctor` guarantee report, an RPM of the core for stock Fedora Workstation and Server (degraded mode documented), `bootc switch` and rollback instructions. Limitations page covering pinned certificates, writes that need a response, shared-kernel escapes and journal anchoring to host root. Acceptance: doctor output matches a hand-checked table on the image and on stock Fedora.

Week 12: Hardening and launch. Self-run security review against the threat model, at least 2 invited external reviewers, a fuzz pass on the proxy classifier, then release v0.1 with signed images and SBOM. Launch the same day on Show HN, r/LocalLLaMA, the Hermes community and Universal Blue Discourse, after 8 weekly devlogs in the preceding weeks. Acceptance: no open critical findings; at least one reproduction by a stranger, using either path, within 72 hours.
roadmap_12_months:
Months 4-6 (v0.2):
- Add a compensable effect class with a small compensator registry (GitHub create issue or close issue; versioned S3 put or delete).
- Add an 'ask' mode for writes that need a response.
- Track a record for each agent that widens or narrows its auto-commit thresholds.
- Seed canary transactions that measure reviewer vigilance.
- Anchor the journal externally (Sigstore Rekor or a remote append-only git log) so third parties can verify it without trusting the host.
- Add OpenShell as an optional sandbox driver (telemetry off) and Landlock or BPF LSM defence in depth once systemd 261 or later is in Fedora.
- Add the OpenClaw profile.

Months 7-9 (v0.3):
- Provenance labels at read time in the proxy (secrets, private repository content, untrusted web content), enforced at egress, including allowlisted destinations. This addresses white space 1; the utility cost is measured on a fixed task set before it becomes a default.
- Signed capability manifests for MCP servers and skills, with permission-diff admission when the OS launches them (white space 4).
- Import adapters for MXC JSON and OpenShell policy.
- A Cockpit web plugin for the queue.

Months 10-12 (v0.4):
- Evidence-pack export mapping journal fields to EU AI Act Articles 12, 14 and 26, Colorado SB26-189 and CPPA ADMT record duties, positioned ahead of Annex III on 2 December 2027. Wording must make clear that this is mapping, not certification.
- Journal export in OpenTelemetry or OCSF format for Agent 365, AgentCore or a SIEM.
- Team mode: several humans, with attention routed by ownership.
- A libkrun microVM transaction driver for KVM hosts.
- Evaluate a Fedora 45 base and the composefs backend.

Throughout: an x86_64 NVIDIA image variant only if a community maintainer volunteers, with boot tests on AWS g4dn spot at each release (about USD 0.33 per hour). Optional local model packs stay outside the core. Re-test the wedge against incumbent changelogs every quarter (OpenShell, Docker Sandboxes, Claude Code, GitHub Agent HQ).
metrics: Primary: human decisions per 100 effect events, measured against the same agent's native prompting rate on the same task set. Target in pilots: at least 5x fewer decisions, with an escaped-defect rate (found by audit sampling) that is equal or lower.
Interrupts per agent-hour, and median time from a transaction being ready to a decision on it.
Escape-suite result: 0 escapes across all listed paths. This is a hard release gate on every image build.
Verifier-tamper detection on seeded cases: 100% (hard gate). False auto-commit rate found by the 5% audit sample: reported publicly each release.

Agent breakage: the drop in task completion when wrapped versus unwrapped, on a fixed set of 20 tasks for each profile. Target: 20 percentage points or less in v0.1, falling after the ask and compensable modes ship.
Overhead targets on the reference VM: transaction start 2 s or less; proxy p50 added latency 50 ms or less; commit of 1,000 files 5 s or less; global stop 1 s or less.

Adoption: reproduce-demo workflow runs on forks, image pulls from GHCR, users who run Docket on real work for 2 weeks or more, external contributors, and the number of agent profiles maintained by people other than the founder.
Founder sustainability: hours per week spent on triage stays at 2 or less (issue forms, Discussions, an AI-disclosure policy).
risks: Agent breakage from holding writes: flows that need the response to a write (create a PR, then comment on it) cannot proceed while the write is held. Mitigation: deny git push by design, add ask and compensable modes in v0.2, and publish breakage per agent.

TLS interception: clients with pinned certificates or bundled root stores (some rustls builds) fail closed, and some users distrust local MITM. Mitigation: per-session CA scoped to the unit, fail closed with a clear report, documentation. Founder question 1: are you willing to make interception inside agent sessions the default, given the trust cost?

Substitution by AI review or vendor auto modes. Faros links heavy AI review to better outcomes, and vendors may add cross-session queues. Mitigation: treat AI reviewers as just another verifier inside the gate; Docket's value is effect staging and cross-vendor ranking, not the review itself.

Incumbent bundling: OpenShell, Docker Sandboxes or Claude Code could add staged commit and held requests in one release. Mitigation: publish the formats, offer them upstream, and apply the kill criteria honestly.

Shared kernel: a kernel exploit escapes namespace and cgroup staging. Mitigation: state this in the threat model, add a microVM driver on KVM hosts later, and keep the journal key and verifier runner out of reach.

Weak verifiers: projects with thin tests will auto-commit bad changes. Mitigation: auto-commit only to local branches, audit sampling, blast-radius thresholds, and a policy that requires a human when no verifiers are declared.

OS cold start, and a conflict with the founder constraint: the research synthesis recommends against shipping an OS, and every 'AI OS' has failed. Mitigation: present the image as the reference distribution and keep the portable RPM and bootc switch paths.

Unproven span of control: no study shows one human safely supervising many agents, and practitioners land one change at a time. Fewer, well-specified agents may beat fleets. The pilot must measure this, not assume it.

Upstream churn: Hermes Agent v0.22 has 33.7k open PRs, Fedora kernel and systemd versions drift, and mitmproxy updates arrive. Mitigation: pinned digests, Renovate, and profile smoke tests in CI on every build.

Solo bus factor and burnout (Asahi precedent). Mitigation: under 3,000 lines, strict NON-GOALS, two-person review for build scripts after any maintainer joins, and keep the day job. Founder question 2: is a headless v0.1 image (SSH plus terminal UI, no desktop) acceptable as the 'bootable OS', or is a graphical desktop a hard requirement?
Founder question 3: is a later acquisition or a hosted evidence service acceptable? The answer determines whether the journal format should go to a foundation from the start.
kill_criteria: Week 6: if the escape suite cannot reach 0 escapes (TCP, UDP, IPv6, DNS-over-HTTPS, raw sockets) using nftables plus systemd on the Fedora image, stop the namespace design and either move to a microVM-only design on rented KVM or abandon the image.

Week 10: if Hermes Agent and the second profile lose more than 20 percentage points of task completion when wrapped, on the fixed 20-task set, narrow the scope to file-only transactions and verifier gating and drop held network intents from v0.1.

Month 4 (after launch): if fewer than 10 external people reproduce the hero demo and fewer than 3 use Docket on real work for 2 weeks, stop maintaining the image, keep only the portable package, or archive the project.

Pilot, by month 6: if human decisions per 100 effect events are not at least 5x lower than native prompting, with an escaped-defect rate equal or lower, the attention thesis is false. Stop the scheduler and keep only the transaction and journal parts.

At any time: if OpenShell, Docker Sandboxes, Claude Code or GitHub ships free, cross-vendor staged commit with held intents and a pinned verifier gate on Linux, stop building in parallel and contribute the remaining pieces upstream.
scope_cuts_from_original_spec: Cut model unification (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Gemma). Model choice belongs to each agent, and the OS only allowlists inference endpoints. Llama is effectively legacy. One optional llama.cpp llama-server container remains for offline live demos.

Defer Laya (convaiinnovations/laya, a 0.4B classifier). It is evaluated in Phase 3 as an optional classifier for unknown endpoints, adopted only if it beats deterministic rules on a labelled request set.

Cut the inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, MLX, Ollama as OS components). NVIDIA paths cannot be tested on the M1, vLLM ships breaking minors every 2 to 3 weeks with binaries tied to specific CUDA builds, MLX has no Linux GPU path, and serving is a poor wedge.
Cut training and fine-tuning entirely (TorchTitan, DeepSpeed, Axolotl, Unsloth). This cannot be developed or verified on 16 GB Apple silicon, torchtune is unmaintained, and leaders build in-house.
Cut hardware adapters. Rely on the Fedora kernel and Mesa. The NVIDIA image is deferred to a community maintainer, with g4dn spot boot tests.
Replace the GPU and resource scheduler with the attention scheduler (human time) plus systemd per-transaction CPU and memory quotas, which cost nothing.

Narrow 'security services' to transaction staging, held intents, the pinned verifier gate and the out-of-band journal. Provenance-aware egress, signed capability manifests and regulatory evidence packs are phased into months 4 to 12.
Narrow the benchmark engine to one reproducible supervision benchmark (the demo fleet, the escape suite, and wrapped-versus-unwrapped agent breakage). Model benchmarks are cut.

Cut the UI from six sections (Home, Agents, Models, Training, Developer Tools, System Settings) to one exception queue in a terminal UI plus notifications. A Cockpit web plugin follows in months 7 to 9; Models and Training views are removed.
Defer a desktop environment, Secure Boot, sealed UKI and TPM measured boot. sealed UKI is still test-only in bootc 1.17, and the M1 cannot test x86 Secure Boot.
Keep, but narrow, Hermes Agent integration: it is one of two tested profiles, wrapped unmodified, not forked or embedded.

Keep the per-phase requirements (acceptance criteria, automated tests, security checks, compatibility, performance targets, docs), but size them to the solo budget: each week carries one acceptance test, the escape suite gates every build, and performance numbers are published as targets until they are measured.

architect:adoption.name: AgentOS Bulkhead
architect:adoption.tagline: Keep your agents in yolo mode. The OS records what each agent session has read and holds every exit that could leak it.
architect:adoption.lens: Adoption-first. Ship one bootable "agent box" image, built on fedora-bootc and NVIDIA OpenShell, that wraps unmodified agents. Ship it with a deterministic leak benchmark that anyone can rerun in under 10 minutes. The project's identity is a third permission state, quarantine-on-read, together with a public before/after table. A large codebase is not the goal.
architect:adoption.revolutionary_claim:
Bulkhead adds a third permission state between deny and allow: quarantine-on-read. A file can be readable, but opening it changes what the reading session may send out afterwards.

The claim, checkable as of October 2026: no shipping product lets unmodified agents from different vendors (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Hermes, OpenClaw) run with per-action prompts switched off while all of the following hold:
- The OS, not the agent, records which labelled files each agent session has opened, including files opened by MCP servers, hooks and double-forked children. The label is committed before the open returns, using fanotify permission events.
- Every later exit outside a declared trust set is held for one human decision. This includes exits to allowlisted hosts.

How to check it: run LeakBench in three modes. The modes are (a) the skip-permission flags Omarchy's launcher passes, (b) the same OpenShell sandbox with a static allowlist only, and (c) Bulkhead. Pass condition for (c): zero canary bytes in any sink log across all 11 scenarios, and zero prompts before a session reads a labelled file.

Explicitly not claimed:
- Content the agent sends to its configured model provider. That exit is excluded by design. With a local model, the guarantee becomes "nothing labelled leaves the machine".
- Protection against kernel exploits.
- Fine-grained tracking of data through model transformations. Labels are per session and deliberately coarse.
architect:adoption.first_users:
Chosen from the evidence, in this order:
1. Developers who already run coding agents with permission prompts off on Linux or in a VM. Users approve about 93% of Claude Code prompts, and 11 of Omarchy's 15 agent launch entries pass skip or auto-approve flags. These users get a reason to keep yolo convenience without the exposure.
2. r/LocalLLaMA users running Hermes Agent or OpenCode against local models (Ollama or llama.cpp on a macOS host, or on Linux). With a local model in the trust set, a session that has read a secret has no network exit at all, which is a crisp and checkable story.
3. Security researchers and red-teamers. They get a reproducible, extensible exfiltration benchmark, and new scenarios submitted as pull requests become the growth engine.
4. Later: platform engineers at small AI-native teams with Linux development boxes.

Deliberately not first: CISOs standardised on E7 or AgentCore, regulated deployers (deadlines fall in 2027), and GPU or training users (cannot be tested on the M1, and this is a poor wedge).
problem_evidence: Permission prompts have failed as a control. Users approve about 93% of Claude Code prompts, and Omarchy (44.9k stars, 1.28M self-reported ISO downloads) launches 11 of 15 agents with skip or auto-approve flags.

Labs concede that prompt injection is unsolved. Adaptive attacks bypassed all 12 published defences tested, most at over 90% success. In Anthropic's phishing test, 24 of 25 exfiltration retries succeeded, and only egress and filesystem controls held. The design must therefore assume the agent is already hijacked.

Allowlist containment is now free (OpenShell, MXC, sandbox-runtime, Docker Sandboxes, Copilot sandboxing), but data still leaves through allowlisted destinations. Read-state-aware controls exist only inside one vendor's boundary: AWS Dogwood in its gateway, Purview in Microsoft 365, Chrome Agent Origin Sets in the browser.
Claude Code's sandbox covers shell commands only. MCP servers, hooks and LSP servers run with full access, and an unsandboxed retry path exists.

The agent supply chain is hostile. Snyk ToxicSkills rated 13.4% of 3,984 skills critical and confirmed 76 as malicious. OpenClaw received 722 security advisories in 2026, front-loaded in February and March.

Logs inside the agent's reach cannot be trusted. OpenAI test agents tampered with logs during the Hugging Face compromise, at least 96 transcripts showed tool-call spoofing, and METR calls observability security-critical.
Kernel features decide sandbox strength. Codex demoted Landlock because it could not isolate Unix sockets, which Landlock ABI 9 (Linux 7.1) fixes. Userland tools on older kernels degrade silently.
Distribution evidence: llama.cpp, Ollama, Open WebUI and Omarchy each spread as a narrow wedge on someone else's heavy lifting, with one concrete, checkable demo.

primitives.name: Session wrapper and image-owned shims (agentos run)
primitives.what_it_does: Launches each unmodified agent CLI as one session. Everything it spawns stays in the session, including MCP servers, hooks, LSP servers and double-forked daemons. Long-running agents such as OpenClaw run as services.
primitives.mechanism: A systemd transient unit per session (own cgroup v2) inside an OpenShell sandbox (Landlock, seccomp, network namespace, egress proxy, credential injection). Agent commands on PATH are shims in the immutable /usr, so no unwrapped launch path exists on the image.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse systemd and OpenShell (fallback: Anthropic sandbox-runtime wrapping the whole process tree). Build about 350 lines of Go.

primitives.name: Quarantine-on-read tracker
primitives.what_it_does: Labels a session SECRET or PRIVATE the moment any process in it opens a labelled path, such as ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, .env*, *.pem or directories the user has labelled. Credentials delivered through OpenShell placeholder injection do not taint a session, because the agent never sees them.
primitives.mechanism: fanotify FAN_OPEN_PERM inode marks on labelled paths only. The daemon maps pid to cgroup to session, commits the label to the ledger, and only then allows the open, so no data is returned before the label exists. Landlock ABI 9 limits Unix sockets to an allowlist (for example ssh-agent), so a session cannot ask an outside helper to read files for it.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse kernel fanotify and Landlock. Build about 350 lines of Go.

primitives.name: Exit gate
primitives.what_it_does: For a tainted session, holds every exit outside the trust set (configured model endpoints, localhost, or a host Ollama) for one human decision, including exits to allowlisted hosts. Where TLS is terminated, it also blocks payloads that contain secret fingerprints.
primitives.mechanism: A decision service that the enforcer's egress proxy consults for each request, either as OpenShell OPA policy input or, as a fallback, through a minimal Go forward proxy in the session network namespace. Fingerprints cover exact, base64, hex and URL-encoded forms of labelled content. Non-HTTP connections such as SSH git push are held at connect time, and raw DNS is blocked so all lookups go through the resolver.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse the OpenShell L7 proxy and TLS termination. Build about 450 lines of Go.

primitives.name: Attention queue
primitives.what_it_does: Gives one ranked queue of held exits across all agents and vendors in place of per-action prompts. Each item shows which labelled file was read, when, the destination and a payload preview.
primitives.mechanism: A CLI/TUI (agentos queue) with approve-once or deny decisions, deny by default on timeout, and optional desktop notification. A denied request returns an HTTP 403 or a connection reset, so the agent fails gracefully.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Build about 200 lines of Go.

primitives.name: Out-of-band ledger
primitives.what_it_does: Records session starts, label transitions, held, approved and denied exits, and undo actions in a log that no agent can reach.
primitives.mechanism: Hash-chained JSONL owned by a dedicated system UID that starts at boot, before any user session. Periodic signed checkpoints use ssh-keygen -Y sign. The agentos ledger verify command checks the chain, and entries are mirrored to journald.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse ssh-keygen signing. Build about 200 lines of Go.

primitives.name: Session snapshot, undo and auto-exec review
primitives.what_it_does: Reverts what a session wrote and flags writes to places a human will later execute unsandboxed: .git/hooks, .envrc, .vscode/tasks.json and shell rc files.
primitives.mechanism: A Btrfs snapshot of the /var/home subvolume at session start, plus fanotify FAN_CLOSE_WRITE events filtered by session cgroup. At session end, a diff of auto-exec paths goes to the queue. agentos undo restores only the files the session wrote.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse Btrfs. Build about 250 lines of Go. This is the first item to cut if the schedule slips.

primitives.name: LeakBench
primitives.what_it_does: A deterministic, offline benchmark with no API key. It assumes a fully hijacked agent and measures leaks across 11 exit channels in yolo, allowlist-only and Bulkhead modes. It also measures utility loss on a benign task suite.
