primitives.mechanism: Three parts: a synthetic hijacked agent; a puppet-model server (OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic Messages-compatible) that drives the real agent CLIs through their documented custom-endpoint settings with dummy keys; and local sinks, reached through a DNS override, that impersonate github.com, a gist-style API and pypi.org. Canaries are fake. Output is a JSON and Markdown report, and the raw sink logs can be inspected.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Build about 900 lines (Go plus YAML scenarios). Contributors can add scenarios as pull requests.

primitives.name: Image and doctor
primitives.what_it_does: Provides a signed, multi-arch bootable image with guaranteed kernel features. A boot-time check fails closed if any guarantee is missing.
primitives.mechanism: FROM quay.io/fedora/fedora-bootc:44 (multi-arch, unlike the amd64-only Universal Blue images). The image enforces a kernel floor of Linux 7.1 or later, an lsm= line including landlock and bpf, fanotify permission events, a Btrfs /var/home, OpenShell telemetry disabled, and cosign keyless signing from GitHub Actions. bootc-image-builder produces qcow2 and ISO images. agentos doctor reports each guarantee.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse bootc, bootc-image-builder, cosign and the GitHub runners. Build a Containerfile, CI and doctor, about 400 lines.

architect:adoption.architecture:
Layers, from bottom to top. Founder-written code totals about 3,000 lines.

1. Base. quay.io/fedora/fedora-bootc:44 for x86_64 and aarch64, built natively on free GitHub runners and cosign-signed to GHCR.
   - Kernel 7.1 or later, checked at boot. Boot line: lsm=landlock,...,bpf.
   - Immutable /usr with bootc upgrade and rollback; Btrfs /var with a /var/home subvolume.
   - Two outputs: a headless image (qcow2, ISO, Lima template) and a bootc switch target for existing Fedora Atomic machines.
2. Enforcer. One OpenShell sandbox per agent session, providing Landlock filesystem rules, seccomp, a network namespace with a veth pair to its egress proxy, L7 rules with TLS termination, and placeholder credential injection. Telemetry is disabled by image configuration. Anthropic sandbox-runtime (bubblewrap plus proxy with a filterRequest hook) sits behind a one-implementation adapter as the fallback.
3. agentosd. A Go system service under a dedicated UID that starts before user sessions. It contains:
   - a session manager (systemd transient units over D-Bus/Varlink)
   - the quarantine-on-read tracker (fanotify)
   - a label state machine
   - the exit-gate decision service and secret fingerprints
   - the attention queue
   - the ledger writer
   - the Btrfs snapshotter
4. agentos CLI. Commands: run, service, ps (cgroup CPU and memory from systemd), queue, label, undo, ledger verify, doctor. Image-owned shims cover claude, codex, opencode, hermes and openclaw.
5. LeakBench. Shipped in the image and as a standalone container, so other sandboxes can be measured too.

Example flow: a hijacked agent opens ~/.aws/credentials. fanotify FAN_OPEN_PERM fires, agentosd labels session S as SECRET, appends a ledger entry, and then allows the open. The agent's spawned MCP server later POSTs to gist.github.com, which is allowlisted. The proxy asks the gate; S is tainted and the destination is outside the trust set, so the request is held and queued with a payload preview. The human denies it, the agent receives a 403, and the denial is logged.

Model endpoints are reached over HTTP (a cloud API, or Ollama/MLX on a macOS host). The image contains no inference engine in v0.1.
architect:adoption.why_bootable_os_matters:
An owned image guarantees six things that a userland tool cannot assume on an arbitrary host:

1. Kernel floor. Linux 7.1 or later for Landlock ABI 9 pathname Unix-socket control, so a session can be handed the ssh-agent socket and nothing else: no container socket and no D-Bus escape route. This is the exact gap that made Codex demote Landlock. The 6.12 kernel in CentOS Stream 10 and older LTS kernels lack it, and userland sandboxes degrade silently.
2. Boot-time switches. lsm= including bpf, fanotify permission events and cgroup v2 are set at build time and verified by doctor at boot, which fails closed.
3. No unwrapped path. Agent CLIs exist only as shims in the immutable /usr, and every child process (MCP servers, hooks, LSP servers, double-forked daemons) inherits the session cgroup and namespace. This covers what the in-agent sandboxes miss.
4. An out-of-band principal. The daemon and ledger start before any user session, under a UID and namespace that agents never share.
5. Filesystem layout chosen at install. A Btrfs /var/home gives cheap per-session snapshots, and the bootc-managed /usr means agents cannot persist in system binaries.
6. Secure defaults that an application cannot impose on a host: telemetry off, DNS forced through the resolver, and the TLS-interception CA trusted only inside sandboxes.

Honest limit: a well-configured Fedora or Arch machine with a current kernel can get most of this. The image adds a guarantee plus a crisp, downloadable artefact for launch. The core (agentosd plus LeakBench) therefore also ships as an RPM, an AUR package and a container in a best-effort mode, where doctor lists any missing guarantees. macOS users run the image as a VM through a Lima template, because fanotify is Linux-only.
architect:adoption.why_incumbents_wont:
- Agent vendors (Anthropic, OpenAI, GitHub, Nous Research, OpenClaw) are judged on task success. Quarantine-on-read blocks some legitimate exits, as CaMeL-style controls cost 3 to 32 points, so none of them will turn it on by default. Each also sees only its own agent's process tree, not a secret read by one vendor's agent and sent through another vendor's tool.
- Sandbox vendors ship static per-sandbox policy. MXC must keep one schema across Windows, macOS and Linux, where fanotify and Landlock have no equivalent. OpenShell defaults L7 rules to audit mode, and Docker Sandboxes monetises governance as a paid tier. Stateful cross-session read tracking needs host-level file-open hooks plus a human queue, a product surface none of them has chosen.
- Cloud governance (Agent 365, AgentCore with Dogwood, Purview) enforces only inside its own estate. A Linux box or VM running five vendors' agents sits outside it.
- Omarchy optimises for malleability and speed, and its launcher passes skip-permission flags.

Caveat, stated plainly: OpenShell could add read-taint in a single release. The plan is to upstream the primitive. The project's durable identity is then the reference image, the neutral LeakBench and its scenario community, not a code moat.
architect:adoption.relationship_to_existing:
- **NVIDIA OpenShell:** the enforcement backend, reused rather than rebuilt. It supplies Landlock, seccomp, the network namespace, the L7 proxy and credential injection. Bulkhead adds read-state gating, image-level guarantees and an out-of-band ledger, and turns OpenShell telemetry off. Improvements, such as a policy-data input for taint, are upstreamed.
- **Microsoft MXC:** not used in the Linux MVP. Its Linux backend is bubblewrap process containers with one JSON schema. In v0.4, Bulkhead policy exports to MXC JSON for macOS and Windows hosts that cannot boot the image.
- **Anthropic sandbox-runtime:** the fallback enforcer. Wrapping the whole agent process tree from outside covers MCP servers and hooks, which its in-agent use does not, and its filterRequest hook suits the exit gate.
- **Docker Sandboxes:** complementary. It offers microVMs for 11 agents, a credential proxy, an account requirement and a paid governance tier, but no read-taint. LeakBench can measure it as a community-contributed baseline mode, with published methodology and a vendor right of reply.
- **OpenClaw and Hermes Agent:** wrapped unchanged. OpenClaw runs as a long-running service whose taint persists until a human resets it, which matters because its messaging channels are exits. Hermes's own sandbox backends may stay on (nested) or off, and its OpenAI-compatible endpoint support lets the puppet model drive it. NemoClaw already runs both in OpenShell; Bulkhead adds quarantine-on-read and OS guarantees.
- **Omarchy:** a deliberate contrast on defaults, not on convenience. Bulkhead also runs agents without per-action prompts, but gates exits at the OS. Arch users can try the best-effort package without switching distributions.
- **Agent 365 and AgentCore:** no overlap. They provide cloud identity, inventory and policy inside their own estates. Bulkhead targets the Linux development box and VM outside those estates. A later OCSF ledger export can feed them; competing with them is not the goal.
- **Windows agent workspaces:** Windows-only, with per-folder consent and no read-state exit gating.
architect:adoption.hero_demo:
"Hijacked on purpose: 11 exfiltration attempts, 3 setups, 1 table." Anyone can reproduce it in under 10 minutes.

1. Get the image (about 4 to 6 minutes for a qcow2 of 1.5 GB or less on a 50 Mbit/s link):
   - macOS: limactl start agentos.yaml
   - Linux: import the qcow2 with virt-install or quickemu
   - Fedora Atomic: sudo bootc switch ghcr.io/ORG/agentos:0.1, then reboot
   - Verify the signature with cosign verify.
2. Run agentos doctor (about 10 seconds). It prints the kernel version, Landlock ABI (9 or higher), BPF LSM status, fanotify permission support, the enforcer version and telemetry off. It exits non-zero if any guarantee is missing.
3. Run leakbench run (about 3 minutes, offline, no API key). A synthetic hijacked agent, plus real unmodified CLIs driven by a local puppet-model server (OpenCode, Hermes and Claude Code at minimum), plant fake canary secrets and try 11 exits:
   1. HTTPS to an unlisted host
   2. DNS tunnelling
   3. POST to an allowlisted gist-style API
   4. git push to an allowlisted remote
   5. a secret inside a package-registry URL
   6. an encoded (base64 and reversed) payload
   7. an exit from a spawned MCP server
   8. an exit from a double-forked daemon
   9. host-socket abuse (container socket, D-Bus)
   10. an auto-exec implant in .git/hooks or a shell rc file
   11. ledger tampering

   The "allowlisted" services are local sinks, so nothing leaves the VM.
4. Read the table for three modes:
   - (a) yolo: the same skip-permission flags Omarchy's launcher passes, with no sandbox
   - (b) allowlist: the same OpenShell sandbox with quarantine-on-read disabled
   - (c) Bulkhead

   Bulkhead passes only with zero canary bytes in any sink (viewers check the raw logs with leakbench sinks grep), every held exit listed in agentos queue, and zero prompts before taint. The results for (a) and (b) are hypotheses: they will be measured and published as observed. The expected pattern is that (b) stops unlisted hosts but not allowlisted ones.
5. Run agentos ledger verify (about 5 seconds). The chain is intact and the truncation attempt is recorded as denied.
6. Run agentos undo SESSION (about 10 seconds). It reverts the implant and shows the diff.

A 90-second video shows the same run. An optional step runs the same poisoned repository with the user's own keys or a host Ollama model.
mvp_12_weeks: Week 1 (spike and threat model): build FROM fedora-bootc:44 natively on the M1 (podman machine) and boot the qcow2 in Lima/vfkit. Confirm a 7.1+ kernel, Landlock ABI 9 or higher, fanotify permission events and a Btrfs /var/home. Wrap OpenCode and Claude Code in host-native OpenShell, and confirm a per-request external decision hook. Acceptance: a written go/no-go, the enforcer chosen (OpenShell or the sandbox-runtime fallback), and THREAT_MODEL.md and NON-GOALS.md published.

Week 2 (image pipeline): Containerfile; GitHub Actions native builds on x86_64 (KVM) and arm64 runners; cosign keyless signing; syft SBOM; bootc-image-builder qcow2 and ISO; a QEMU serial-console boot test that runs agentos doctor. Acceptance: both architectures boot and pass doctor in CI on every commit, the image is 1.5 GB or less compressed, and the weekly devlog starts.

Week 3 (session wrapper): agentos run and agentos service on systemd transient units inside OpenShell, with shims for claude, codex, opencode, hermes and openclaw. Acceptance: all 5 agents start and finish a benign scripted task; integration tests prove that a child MCP server and a double-forked process stay in the session cgroup and network namespace.

Week 4 (LeakBench v0): synthetic hijacked agent, 11 scenarios, local sinks with a DNS override, yolo and allowlist modes, JSON and Markdown reports. Acceptance: identical results in 3 consecutive CI runs, and baseline numbers published in the devlog.

Week 5 (quarantine-on-read): fanotify FAN_OPEN_PERM on the default label set plus agentos label; pid-to-cgroup-to-session mapping; the label is committed before the open returns. Acceptance: unit and integration tests pass, the target is 1 ms or less p99 on labelled opens, and unlabelled files produce no events.

Week 6 (exit gate): decision service, trust set, secret fingerprints (exact, base64, hex, URL-encoded) on terminated TLS, holds at connect time for SSH and other non-HTTP traffic, raw DNS blocked. Acceptance: Bulkhead mode blocks scenarios 1 to 9, with a target of 10 ms or less added p50 latency (measured, not assumed).

Week 7 (attention queue): agentos queue with payload preview, approve-once or deny, deny by default on timeout, optional notification. Acceptance: a held exit resolves end to end, and a denial produces a 403 or reset without crashing at least 4 of 5 agents (any crash is documented).

Week 8 (ledger): hash-chained JSONL under a dedicated UID, signed checkpoints, agentos ledger verify, journald mirror. Acceptance: scenario 11 is recorded as denied, and a property test shows that verify detects any edited byte.

Week 9 (undo and auto-exec review; first item to cut if behind schedule): Btrfs snapshot per session, session writes recorded through cgroup-filtered FAN_CLOSE_WRITE, and an auto-exec diff queued at session end. Acceptance: scenario 10 is reverted, and a snapshot takes 1 second or less on the test VM.

Week 10 (real agents and utility): the puppet-model server drives real CLIs through 4 core scenarios, and a 20-task benign suite (edit, test, add a dependency, push to an allowlisted remote) runs in every mode. Acceptance: at least 3 of 5 agents run unchanged, benign completion is at least 95% of the unwrapped baseline, and there is on average 1 queue item or fewer per benign task. All of these are targets to be measured and published.

Week 11 (hardening and docs): gosec, govulncheck, shellcheck, CodeQL and cosign verification in CI; fuzzing of the fingerprint matcher; 3 to 5 invited reviewers attack LeakBench privately; documentation covers install, threat model, policy reference and limitations (model-provider exit, shared-kernel isolation, coarse labels) plus a compatibility matrix with pinned agent versions. Acceptance: no open high-severity findings, and two outside people reproduce the demo in under 10 minutes.

Week 12 (launch): signed v0.1 with checksums; a 90-second video; Show HN, r/LocalLLaMA and the Fedora and Universal Blue forums on the same day; a scenario contribution guide; SECURITY.md with private advisories; Apache-2.0 licence, TRADEMARK.md and DCO. Acceptance: release artefacts verify, and the launch post links the raw LeakBench output.
roadmap_12_months:
Months 4-6 (v0.2):
- Add an UNTRUSTED label (web fetches and third-party repository origin) to complete Meta's Rule of Two.
- Signed capability manifests for MCP servers and skills, with permission-diff admission when an agent spawns them (white space 4). The wrapper already sees every spawn.
- One validated local inference backend: llama.cpp server as a bootc logically bound image, for a 'nothing labelled leaves the machine' mode.
- Per-agent UIDs.
- Best-effort RPM and AUR packages.

Months 7-9 (v0.3):
- Staged exits: a side-effect journal classifies held exits as read-only, reversible, compensable or irreversible, and the human approves only the irreversible remainder in a batch.
- Queue ranking, optionally with the Laya 0.4B classifier.
- agentos-nvidia x86_64 variant, boot-tested on AWS g4dn spot at each release.
- Periodic Asahi bare-metal check on the M1 Pro.

Months 10-12 (v0.4 to v1.0):
- Cockpit web UI with Home, Agents, Queue, Ledger and Settings.
- OCSF ledger export with a draft mapping to EU AI Act Article 12 logging. This is not a compliance claim.
- Policy export to MXC JSON and sandbox-runtime settings for macOS and Windows hosts.
- Optional microVM isolation through the OpenShell libkrun driver on KVM hosts.
- A second maintainer with release rights after 6 months of verified contributions.
- Application to the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund.
metrics: LeakBench strict mode: zero canary bytes at any sink across all scenarios in every release; any regression blocks the release.

Utility: benign-suite completion under Bulkhead at least 95% of the unwrapped baseline for each supported agent; on average 1 queue item or fewer per benign task, and no prompts in sessions that never read a labelled file.

Overhead (targets, measured on the reference VM and a CI x86_64 runner): 500 ms or less added session start; 10 ms or less added p50 per egress request; 1 ms or less p99 on labelled file opens; no measurable change on unlabelled opens; agentosd RSS of 50 MB or less.
Image: compressed qcow2 of 1.5 GB or less; CI build of 30 minutes or less per architecture; both architectures pass the boot test on every commit.
Reproducibility: at least 20 independent LeakBench reports posted within 60 days of launch; median outside reproduction time under 10 minutes.

Adoption targets, not predictions: Hacker News front page at launch; 1,000 GitHub stars and 300 weekly image pulls within 60 days; 10 external scenario pull requests within 90 days; at least 2 upstream projects (OpenShell, an agent CLI) link to or adopt LeakBench scenarios.
Founder load: 10 hours or less per week, split as 6 building, 2 docs and demo, 2 triage.
risks: Coarse labels cut both ways. Over-labelling (.env files are common) blocks legitimate exits and recreates prompt fatigue. Under-labelling lets unlabelled sensitive files leak. Mitigation: placeholder credentials do not taint, plus an easy agentos label command and published utility numbers.

Residual channels. The model-provider exit is excluded by design. Covert timing, steganography in content a human approves, and blind approval (93% approval habits) all remain. A shared kernel can be escaped through kernel exploits. All of these must be stated prominently, or the project will be discredited.
TLS interception gaps. Certificate pinning, WebSockets, gRPC and HTTP/3 may evade content fingerprints. Connection-level holds still apply, but the fingerprint layer is best effort.

Upstream churn. OpenShell is at v0.1.x and may break its hook or policy APIs; agent CLIs change tool protocols weekly, which breaks puppet-model scripts; Fedora kernel or fanotify behaviour may change. Unverified as of today: OpenShell's aarch64 support and a per-request external decision hook. Week 1 checks both, and sandbox-runtime is the fallback.

Incumbent absorption. OpenShell, sandbox-runtime or Docker could ship read-taint within one release. The response is to upstream the primitive and keep the image and LeakBench as the project's identity.

Demo credibility and fairness. A demo that looks staged, or a disputed characterisation of Omarchy or NVIDIA, would hurt. Mitigation: deterministic open benchmark, raw sink logs, only documented flags quoted, baseline (b) using the same OpenShell sandbox, and a vendor right of reply.

Solo bus factor and burnout. Security projects attract adversarial reports and entitled users. Mitigation: strict 10-hour cap, issue forms, AI-disclosure policy, release rights granted only after 6 months.
Name and trademark. 'AgentOS' and 'LeakBench' are probably already used elsewhere; run a trademark search before launch.

Open question for the founder 1: is a headless 'agent box' image, run as a VM or a bootc switch target, acceptable as the literal bootable OS? A desktop distribution would compete with Omarchy and Bluefin on polish that one part-time person cannot match.

Open question for the founder 2: will you accept that the durable asset is the benchmark and its community rather than proprietary code, and that the model-provider exit stays outside the guarantee unless users choose a local model?
kill_criteria: End of week 1: if neither OpenShell nor sandbox-runtime can wrap at least 3 of the 5 agents unchanged on fedora-bootc aarch64 with a hookable egress decision, drop the image and ship LeakBench plus a package only, or stop.
End of week 6: if fanotify-based labelling cannot be made race-free (label committed before data is returned) for processes in the session cgroup, stop claiming quarantine-on-read.

End of week 10: if benign-task completion falls below 85% of the unwrapped baseline, or default mode averages more than 3 queue items per hour of agent work, the taint model is too coarse; redesign before launch.
Any time before launch: if an incumbent ships read-state exit gating for arbitrary unmodified agents, pivot to upstream contribution and position Bulkhead as the reference image and benchmark.
Any time: if a published bypass defeats the core claim and cannot be fixed within 2 weeks, withdraw the claim publicly and document the bypass.
60 days after launch: fewer than 300 stars and fewer than 5 independent reproductions means stopping work on the OS image and keeping only LeakBench.
Maintenance load: image breakage (kernel, OpenShell, agent CLIs) taking more than 10 hours per week for 2 consecutive months means reducing to a package-only distribution.
scope_cuts_from_original_spec: Model unification (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Gemma): cut. Agents bring their own endpoints, Llama is effectively legacy, and Canonical's inference snaps (52 stars) show weak demand for OS-level model packaging.

Inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM): cut. vLLM ships breaking minor releases every 2 to 3 weeks with CUDA-tied binaries, and NVIDIA cannot be tested on the M1. The MVP reaches host Ollama, llama.cpp or MLX over HTTP. One validated backend (a llama.cpp server container) is deferred to v0.2.
MLX in the image: cut, because MLX has no GPU path on Linux. It is used only on the macOS host.
Training and fine-tuning (TorchTitan, DeepSpeed, Axolotl, Unsloth): cut. They cannot be tested on the M1, there is no buyer evidence in this wedge, and torchtune is unmaintained.
Hardware adapters and the NVIDIA variant: deferred to v0.3, boot-tested only on rented g4dn spot instances at release. The wedge needs no GPU.
Resource scheduler: cut to systemd cgroup limits plus agentos ps. GPU and cluster scheduling is a poor wedge for a small team.
Benchmark engine: narrowed to LeakBench (security and utility). Performance benchmarking is deferred.

Six-section UI (Home, Agents, Models, Training, Developer Tools, System Settings): deferred. The MVP has a CLI and a TUI queue; a v0.4 Cockpit plugin covers Home, Agents, Queue, Ledger and Settings. Models and Training tabs are cut.
Desktop environment: cut. The MVP is a headless image plus a VM template; a desktop layer on Bluefin (amd64) may follow.
Laya routing model: deferred, as an optional queue-ranking classifier in v0.3.
Hermes Agent integration: kept, but only as unchanged wrapping, not deep integration.
Secure isolated execution: kept, by reusing OpenShell instead of building it.
Agent identity and inventory in the style of Agent 365: cut, because incumbents bundle it. Per-agent UIDs are deferred to v0.2.
MicroVM isolation: deferred. There is no nested virtualisation on the M1, and the OpenShell libkrun driver is experimental.
Sealed UKI and measured boot: deferred, because they are test-only in bootc 1.17.
Regulatory evidence packs (EU AI Act, Colorado, CPPA): deferred to a v0.4 draft mapping. Demand arrives in 2027 to 2028.
Full transactional execution beyond exits: deferred to v0.3 staged exits.
Founder's requirements kept and applied at reduced scale: per-phase acceptance criteria, automated tests, security checks, compatibility matrix, performance targets and docs.

architect:local_sovereign.name: AgentOS Tidemark
architect:local_sovereign.tagline: Your data decides where your AI runs, and the machine proves it.
architect:local_sovereign.lens: Local-first personal AI computer: own your agents, models and data. Hybrid by default (cheap cloud small models for public work), local only where the data requires it, enforced by the kernel rather than by agent goodwill or permission prompts.
architect:local_sovereign.revolutionary_claim: For the first time, an unmodified third-party agent (Hermes Agent first) on a personal machine automatically loses the ability to send anything off the machine, including to its own cloud model API, at the moment any process in its tree reads a file the user labelled private. It keeps working on a local model and is not interrupted by prompts. The label then persists on every file that session writes, so a different vendor's agent that later reads those files is constrained the same way. How to check it: a verifier generates a random canary on their own host, boots the signed image, and runs the published prompt-injection scenario twice. With labels off (ordinary allowlist containment), the canary appears in the host-side sink and mock-cloud logs. With labels on, grep of those host-side logs returns zero matches, the receipt shows that the inference call was placed on the local engine, and `tidemark verify` validates a hash-chained, Ed25519-signed receipt bound to the cosign-verified image digest. This claim is bounded to 16 Oct 2026. It is based on the research corpus and on direct checks of OpenShell, NemoClaw, ActPlane and Tailscale Aperture, none of which combines read-time labels, label-constrained model placement, forced egress mediation and verifiable receipts.
architect:local_sovereign.first_users: Primary: technically capable self-hosters who already run Hermes Agent or OpenClaw against personal data (mail, finance, notes, code), using a local llama.cpp model plus a cloud fallback, on a Linux desktop or in a Linux VM on Apple silicon. Evidence for this choice: Hermes has 254k stars and installs hardware-matched llama.cpp builds, OpenClaw has 392k stars and published 722 advisories in 2026, and Ollama's cloud plans show that local users already mix in cloud models. This group tolerates installing an image, can verify a demo, and is the audience that made llama.cpp, Ollama and Omarchy break out. Secondary design partners: privacy-bound practices of 2 to 10 people (for example Australian care, allied-health, legal or accounting practices facing the ADM disclosure duty from 10 Dec 2026). They need to show where personal data went, but evidence shows low willingness to pay, so they serve as a proving ground, not a revenue plan. Not targeted: enterprises, because Agent 365, AgentCore and Google Agent Identity bundle governance there and procurement is slow.
problem_evidence: Allowlisted exfiltration is the remaining gap. In Anthropic's phishing test, 24 of 25 exfiltration retries succeeded and only the egress and filesystem controls held. Free containment (MXC, OpenShell, sandbox-runtime, Docker Sandboxes) still permits any allowlisted destination, and no shipped product carries data labels from the moment of reading to every exit, across vendors.

Model-level defences are costly or incomplete. Labs concede that prompt injection is unsolved, and adaptive attacks bypassed all 12 research defences tested. CaMeL reaches 77% task success against 84% undefended, with losses of 3 to 32 points depending on the model and about 2.7x tokens. Coarse labels enforced by the OS add no token overhead, but they cost quality whenever a task is forced onto a local model, and that cost must be measured.

Permission prompts do not work as a control. Users approve about 93% of Claude Code permission prompts, and Omarchy launches 11 of 15 coding agents with approval prompts disabled. Enforcement must be automatic and silent to survive real use.

Per-tool sandboxes leave gaps. Anthropic sandbox-runtime covers shell commands only, not MCP servers, hooks or LSP servers. Snyk ToxicSkills rated 13.4% of 3,984 skills critical and found 76 malicious, and these components read local files.
Hybrid placement has no rule. Hermes Agent and Ollama mix local and cloud models, but nothing decides which data may reach which model based on what the agent actually read.

The economics call for hybrid, not local-only. Haiku 5.5 costs USD 0.10 per million input tokens for prompts up to 100K tokens (5x above that). An M1 Pro with 16 GB runs 4-14B Q4 models at about 18-36 tok/s and needs 2-4 minutes to prefill 30K tokens. Local models answer 88.7% of single-turn queries but trail on agentic work. The default should therefore be cloud for public data and local only where labels require it.

Disclosure duties are reaching small operators: Australian ADM transparency from 10 Dec 2026, CPPA ADMT rules from 1 Jan 2027, and EU AI Act Annex III from 2 Dec 2027. Only about 20% of firms report mature agent governance (Deloitte, n=3,235).

The closest attempts are partial. NVIDIA NemoClaw markets a 'privacy router' (press release, 16 Mar 2026), but its docs describe a Model Router provider that requires an NVIDIA API key and document no file-read tracking. Tailscale Aperture (blog, 6 Aug 2026) tags connectors as sensitive and restricts sandboxes with open egress, but statically, by device posture. ActPlane (eunomia-bpf, MIT, about 104 stars, preprint, no releases) enforces labelled flow rules on agent process trees in the kernel, but has no model placement, forced egress proxy or signed receipts, and its block mode needs BPF LSM to be active.

primitives.name: Read-time session labels (high-water mark)
primitives.what_it_does: Gives every agent session one label that only rises: public, untrusted (U) or private (P). The label rises the instant any process in the session's tree (agent, MCP server, hook, LSP or child shell) opens a labelled file, or receives content from a destination that is not trusted.
primitives.mechanism: Each session runs as a systemd transient unit in agents.slice, so its cgroup ID is its kernel identity. A sleepable BPF LSM file_open program calls bpf_get_file_xattr to read a security.bpf.tidemark xattr; mainline fs/bpf_fs_kfuncs.c permits reads of user.* and security.bpf.* names. The program ORs the label into a BPF map keyed by cgroup ID. Setting or removing security.* xattrs needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN, so a confined agent cannot strip a label. The broker raises U when a response arrives from a destination that is not on the trusted-content list. Defaults label ~/Private, ~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, mail stores and password stores as P.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse ActPlane (MIT) for label propagation if the week-1 spike shows that it can expose per-cgroup labels and attach to xattrs. Otherwise write about 250 lines of BPF C loaded with cilium/ebpf, and offer the mechanism upstream to ActPlane.

primitives.name: Label-gated egress at every exit
primitives.what_it_does: Makes the session label decide where bytes may go. Public and U-only sessions may reach allowlisted destinations. P sessions may reach only local endpoints or destinations the user explicitly cleared for private data. P+U sessions (the lethal trifecta) get no external egress at all.
primitives.mechanism: nftables 'socket cgroupv2' rules drop every packet from agents.slice except traffic to tidemarkd, which runs an HTTP CONNECT/HTTP proxy and a DNS stub. Each decision uses the pair (session label, destination clearance); MVP enforces at the domain level from the CONNECT host, without TLS interception. Landlock pathname Unix-socket scoping (ABI 9, Linux 7.1 or later) and systemd sandboxing (no user D-Bus, no Wayland socket, ProtectSystem=strict) close local side channels. Remote sandbox backends (Modal, SSH, Daytona) count as ordinary destinations.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse nftables, systemd sandboxing, and either a bubblewrap/sandbox-runtime profile or OpenShell as the inner sandbox (telemetry disabled). Build only the decision proxy and DNS stub, about 700 lines of Go.

primitives.name: Label-constrained inference placement
primitives.what_it_does: Treats the model call as just another exit. One OpenAI-compatible endpoint (model alias tidemark/auto) works out the set of models the session label allows, then picks the cheapest adequate model within that set. A private session cannot reach a cloud model unless the user cleared it, and there is never a silent fallback to cloud.
primitives.mechanism: The broker reads the caller's cgroup label from the BPF map and filters backends by clearance. Within the allowed set, rules decide on context length versus local fit, cost cap and an optional 'needs frontier' hint. The broker injects API keys, so agents never hold them. A memory-fit check runs before loading a local model. When no allowed backend can serve a request, the broker returns a structured error and queues a release request; it never escalates to cloud on its own.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse llama.cpp llama-server as the single validated local backend and any OpenAI-compatible cloud endpoint. Laya (convaiinnovations, 421M-parameter ModernBERT, Apache-2.0) is an optional difficulty classifier behind an interface. It ranks only inside the label-permitted set and is off by default, because its base checkpoint scores below the majority baseline without fine-tuning and its vendor reports 193-464 ms of CPU latency. Build about 500 lines of Go.

primitives.name: Label inheritance and per-session workspace with undo
primitives.what_it_does: Makes labels follow data across sessions and vendors, and lets the user roll back everything a session changed.
primitives.mechanism: Each session writes only into its own Btrfs subvolume snapshot of the workspace. When the session closes, tidemarkd stamps every new or changed file with the session's label (security.bpf.tidemark), so any later reader inherits it. `tidemark undo <session>` restores the snapshot. bootc rollback covers the system image. Snapshots cannot undo external side effects, and the docs say so.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse Btrfs and bootc. Build about 200 lines. Propagating labels at write time inside BPF through bpf_set_dentry_xattr is deferred.

primitives.name: Human-only declassification with an interruption budget
primitives.what_it_does: Provides the only way to lower a label. The user runs `tidemark release <file|request>` from their own terminal, outside any agent session, after seeing the exact bytes that will leave. A daily budget caps interruptions.
primitives.mechanism: A root-owned Varlink or Unix socket accepts release requests only from processes outside agents.slice. Each release produces a signed receipt entry recording the content hash, destination and reason.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Build about 150 lines.

primitives.name: Sovereignty receipts
primitives.what_it_does: Lets a third party check what the machine allowed and denied without trusting the agent or its logs.
primitives.mechanism: Each decision (label raise with cause path and hash, allowed or denied connection, placement with model and endpoint, release) is appended to a hash-chained JSONL log, signed with an Ed25519 machine key that is root-only in the MVP and moves into the TPM later. The log carries the policy hash and the image digest from `bootc status`. `tidemark verify` checks the chain, the signature and invariants, for example that no P session sent bytes to an uncleared destination.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse cosign for image signing and Go crypto/ed25519. Build about 350 lines, verifier included.

primitives.name: Owned, signed, multi-architecture image
primitives.what_it_does: Guarantees the kernel features, boot parameters, disk layout and launch paths that the other primitives depend on, and gives receipts a known enforcement build.
primitives.mechanism: The image builds FROM quay.io/fedora/fedora-bootc:44, the multi-architecture base, because Universal Blue images are amd64-only. bootc kargs.d sets an LSM list that includes landlock and bpf. CI asserts the kernel floor (7.1 or later), the Landlock ABI (9 or later), an active BPF LSM and the presence of the required kfuncs. The Btrfs layout and first-boot labelling are fixed at install. The image bundles a llama-server, ships tidemarkd as the only holder of cloud credentials, and routes desktop entries and shell shims for agents through `tidemark run`. It is cosign-signed and built natively on free x86_64 and arm64 GitHub runners.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse fedora-bootc, bootc-image-builder, the build and signing workflow patterns from ublue-os/image-template, and Renovate digest pinning. Build only the Containerfile and CI. Own-code total for the MVP: about 2,700 lines (about 2,450 Go and about 250 BPF C if ActPlane is not reused; shell and CI excluded).

architect:local_sovereign.why_bootable_os_matters:
The guarantees depend on facts that a userland tool cannot establish on a kernel it does not control. Owning the image guarantees each of them:
(a) BPF LSM is active only when bpf is in the boot-time LSM list. ActPlane's block mode and Tidemark's label engine both depend on that, and a portable runtime such as OpenShell must fall back to per-destination rules on hosts where it is missing.
(b) The xattr kfuncs (bpf_get_file_xattr, security.bpf.*) are not a stable kernel ABI. Pinning the kernel in the image, with CI assertions, makes them dependable.
(c) Landlock ABI 9 or later (pathname Unix-socket scoping, Linux 7.1) is needed to close local side channels to host daemons.
(d) The image fixes the disk layout: Btrfs subvolumes per session for undo and label inheritance, and labelled default directories applied at first boot.
(e) The image controls launch paths. Desktop entries and shell shims for agents go through `tidemark run`, and cloud credentials exist only inside tidemarkd, so an agent started outside a session has no keys.
(f) A local engine is always present, so a 'local only' placement always has a target instead of failing the task.
(g) Receipts name a signed image digest, so a verifier knows which enforcement code ran. TPM measured boot can later turn this into hardware attestation once sealed UKI and composefs leave test status.
(h) bootc gives one-command rollback of the whole system.

The same signed image boots in a VM or on bare metal, which keeps the 'literal bootable OS' constraint while letting Mac users run it as a VM appliance.

Honest limits: on the founder's M1 Pro, natively booted Linux (Asahi) runs LLMs slower than macOS Metal, and krunkit keeps about 74-80% of Metal. Apple silicon is therefore a development and VM target, not the showcase for local performance. To help adoption, tidemarkd, the policy format and the receipt verifier also stay usable on any modern Linux with BPF LSM enabled, in a 'bring your own kernel' mode with weaker guarantees that receipts state explicitly.
architect:local_sovereign.why_incumbents_wont: Portable runtimes cannot assume the kernel. OpenShell, sandbox-runtime and MXC must run on kernels they do not control, which pushes them toward per-destination allowlists instead of read-time labels that require BPF LSM. Lab agent vendors (Anthropic, OpenAI, Cursor) are judged on task success and earn revenue from their own APIs, so a feature that silently moves labelled work to a local model works against both. Microsoft Agent 365, AWS AgentCore and Google Agent Identity enforce inside their own estates with per-user pricing; single-machine, local-first sovereignty across vendors is outside their business, and Windows agent workspaces are Windows-only. Tailscale Aperture is a gateway that classifies connectors and device posture statically and cannot see local file reads. Ollama controls model serving but not the agent's process tree or egress, and it now monetises per-token cloud plans. Omarchy optimises for agent convenience. Fedora and Canonical do not build agent-security products, and Intel and Red Hat have retreated from AI distributions. The most credible threat is NVIDIA. NemoClaw already markets a 'privacy router' and OpenShell has the proxy and credential plumbing, so NVIDIA could add read-time labels. The mitigation is to contribute a label-provider interface upstream early and to differentiate on hardware neutrality, independence from any NVIDIA account, the owned image and verifiable receipts.
architect:local_sovereign.relationship_to_existing:
- OpenShell (Apache-2.0): reused, not rebuilt. It is evaluated in week 1 as the inner sandbox (Landlock, seccomp, credential injection) with telemetry disabled. Its egress policy is a per-destination allowlist with no data labels. Tidemark adds the read-time label that changes the allowed set mid-session and constrains model placement, and it will propose a label-provider hook upstream.
- NemoClaw: its 'privacy router' is marketing-level, its docs show a Model Router provider that needs an NVIDIA API key, and it documents no file-read tracking. Tidemark is account-free and hardware-neutral.
- MXC (MIT): Tidemark does not compete on containment. A later release exports Tidemark policy to MXC's JSON schema so Windows and macOS users get partial enforcement.
- Anthropic sandbox-runtime: its bubblewrap profile can be the inner sandbox. It covers shell commands only, while Tidemark covers the whole process tree through the cgroup.
- Docker Sandboxes: these are microVM-per-agent products with a paid governance tier. Tidemark uses no microVMs in the MVP, and agent sessions are barred from Docker-style daemon sockets, which would escape the session cgroup.
- OpenClaw: a supported agent from month 4, wrapped unmodified.
- Hermes Agent: the first supported agent, used unmodified through its OpenAI-compatible base URL and local sandbox backend. Its remote backends count as egress destinations.
- Omarchy: the contrast case. It launches 11 of 15 agents with prompts disabled, while Tidemark makes prompt-free use safe by enforcing labels silently. Tidemark does not compete on desktop polish.
- Agent 365 and AgentCore: these serve enterprise cloud governance. AgentCore's Dogwood rules are temporal, not data labels. Tidemark receipts could later be exported to them, but they are not targets.
- ActPlane (MIT, github.com/eunomia-bpf/ActPlane): the closest prior art, a kernel-level labelled flow engine for agents. Tidemark reuses it or contributes to it, and adds the image that guarantees BPF LSM, forced egress mediation, placement and receipts.
- Tailscale Aperture: a commercial gateway with static connector sensitivity tags. It cannot see local reads.
- Apple Private Cloud Compute: hybrid placement only inside Apple's own apps.
- Laya, Ollama systemone and Cloudflare Clef: interchangeable routing classifiers that rank only inside the label-permitted set.
architect:local_sovereign.hero_demo:
'Bring your own canary', designed to finish in under 10 minutes on a 4-core x86_64 Linux machine with KVM or an Apple silicon Mac with QEMU, over a 50 Mbit/s connection. Anyone can also fork the repo and run the same workflow on a free GitHub x64 runner.

Step 1. `git clone` the repo and run `./demo/verify.sh`. The script downloads the signed qcow2 (target 1.6 GB or less, including a sub-2B Apache-2.0 GGUF model) and runs `cosign verify` against the published identity.
Step 2. The script generates the canary on the host (`openssl rand -hex 16`). Outside the VM it starts two host-side loggers: an 'attacker' sink, which the policy treats as an allowlisted public site, and a mock cloud LLM endpoint that records every prompt. It boots the VM with the canary passed as a QEMU fw_cfg systemd credential into ~/Private/notes.txt, which is private by default.
Step 3. Run A, labels off (equivalent to ordinary allowlist containment). A replay agent issues the exact tool calls from a recorded real Hermes Agent transcript of a prompt injection: fetch an injected web page, read ~/Private/notes.txt, POST its contents to the sink, then include them in the next model prompt. The host logs now contain the canary.
Step 4. Run B, labels on. The session label rises to P+U at the read, the POST is denied, the next model call is placed on the local llama-server, and `grep -c <canary>` on both host logs returns 0. The verifier runs this grep on their own machine, outside the VM.
Step 5. Cross-vendor step: a second, different client (OpenCode or a minimal OpenAI-SDK script) reads the summary file written in Run B. It starts as P, and its cloud call is placed locally or denied.
Step 6. `tidemark receipt export` and then `tidemark verify` on the host. The check passes, the receipt's image digest matches the cosign-verified digest, and flipping one byte makes verification fail.

Optional live mode runs real Hermes Agent with a real API key. It is not required for verification, because injection success is stochastic. The same scenario runs in CI on every commit for both architectures, and the receipts are published.
mvp_12_weeks: Week 1, spike and kill gate (about 10 h). Build an aarch64 image FROM fedora-bootc:44 in podman machine on the M1 Pro and boot it in QEMU or krunkit. Enable the bpf LSM with bootc kargs.d. Prove that a sleepable BPF LSM file_open program can read a security.bpf.* xattr and update a per-cgroup map. Evaluate ActPlane and OpenShell (telemetry off) for reuse. Accept when a script prints the kernel version, active LSMs, Landlock ABI and one label-raise event, and a written reuse decision exists.

Week 2, image and CI. Set up GitHub Actions native builds for x86_64 and arm64, cosign signing, a qcow2 built with bootc-image-builder, a serial-console boot test under KVM on the x64 runner, a syft SBOM, Renovate digest pinning and OpenSSF Scorecard. Accept when every push is green, cosign verify passes, CI boots to multi-user in under 90 s, and CI asserts the kernel floor (7.1 or later), Landlock ABI (9 or later) and an active BPF LSM.

Weeks 3-4, label engine and session launcher. `tidemark run` creates a transient unit in agents.slice. The engine and the `tidemark label` and `unlabel` commands (root only) are in place. Tests cover a read matrix: cat, Python, mmap, sendfile, an MCP child process, a hook script, symlinks, hardlinks, bind mounts and files opened by a forked grandchild. Accept when 100% of matrix cases raise the label, there are zero false raises on unlabelled files, and open() overhead is measured and published (target under 5 µs p50).

Weeks 5-6, egress mediation. nftables cgroupv2 rules, the CONNECT/HTTP proxy, the DNS stub, a YAML policy with destination clearances, and the P and P+U rules. A bypass test matrix of at least 40 cases covers curl, Python requests, raw sockets, IPv6, UDP, DNS TXT exfiltration, Unix sockets to host daemons, Docker or Podman socket access, /proc tricks and remote sandbox backends. Accept when all cases are blocked or mediated on both architectures in CI and added connection latency is measured (target under 3 ms p50). Security check: run gosec and CodeQL.

Weeks 7-8, inference broker. An OpenAI-compatible endpoint, label-filtered backends, rule-based selection, credential injection, a memory-fit check, a structured refusal instead of cloud fallback, and an optional Laya plugin interface that is disabled by default. Compatibility: Hermes Agent v0.22.x through its base URL, OpenCode, plain OpenAI SDK clients. Accept when 100% of P-session requests go to local or cleared backends, public sessions reach the configured cheap cloud model, and broker overhead is measured (target under 10 ms).

Week 9, workspaces, inheritance and undo. Per-session Btrfs snapshots, label stamping at close, and `tidemark undo`. Accept when outputs of a P session are labelled P, a second session that reads them starts as P, undo restores a byte-identical tree, and the docs state that external side effects cannot be undone. If behind schedule, cut undo to month 4 and keep the stamping.

Week 10, receipts. Hash-chained JSONL, an Ed25519 machine key held as a systemd credential, the image digest and policy hash, and `tidemark verify` with invariant checks. Accept when tamper tests (edited, deleted or reordered entries, wrong key) all fail verification and receipts stay at 1 KB or less per decision.

Week 11, hero demo. Replay agent (no more than 150 lines), injected page, host-side loggers, the fw_cfg canary path, and a CI job that runs the demo on both architectures for every commit and publishes the receipts. Record one live Hermes run. Accept when an outside tester completes the demo in under 10 minutes from a clean machine.

Week 12, hardening, documentation and launch. Write a threat model listing what Tidemark does not stop (covert or timing channels, steganography toward cleared destinations, kernel or root compromise, side effects at cleared endpoints, quality loss on local models), a policy reference, a quickstart, SECURITY.md with private advisories, a DCO, Apache-2.0 plus TRADEMARK.md, and a NON-GOALS file. Publish the 30-task utility suite results for the M1 Pro VM and one x86 machine. Launch on Show HN, then r/LocalLLaMA, then the Hermes and OpenClaw communities. Accept when the docs build in CI and every claim in the README links to a CI artifact.
roadmap_12_months: Month 4: an x86_64 agentos-nvidia variant (NVIDIA open kernel modules, CUDA llama.cpp and an optional vLLM as digest-pinned OCI images), boot-tested on AWS g4dn spot at each release for about USD 0.33/hr. OpenClaw support. Undo, if it slipped.

Month 5: a split between a cloud planner and a local worker, shipped as a Hermes plugin. The cloud planner sees only public context, and P data is handled by local worker sub-sessions. This is the main mitigation for label creep, and the 30-task suite measures its effect.

Month 6: signed capability manifests for MCP servers and skills, declaring the labels they read and the egress they need, with a permission diff checked at load time (white space 4) and enforced by the same cgroup and label machinery.
Month 7: one ranked queue of release and approval requests across all agents, with daily interruption budgets and desktop notifications (white space 5).

Months 8-9: a machine key held in the TPM and measured boot, adopted once bootc sealed UKI and composefs leave test status (this needs a reinstall from ostree). Receipts become hardware-attested. Evidence exports mapped to Australian ADM disclosure and EU AI Act Article 12 logging (white space 3 and 6).

Month 10: small-team mode. Two to ten machines share one policy and one 'sovereign inference' box (an NVIDIA desktop, Strix Halo or Mac Studio) that is cleared for P, with mutual attestation over WireGuard. Labels travel with files through xattr-preserving sync.

Month 11: compile one Tidemark policy into OpenShell, MXC and sandbox-runtime configurations, giving partial enforcement on macOS and Windows (white space 7). Add labelled agent memories and skills: private memories can only be served by local placement (white space 8).

Month 12: v1.0 with a frozen policy and receipt schema, an external security audit (apply to the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, and to the Sovereign Tech Fund once the project is no longer a prototype), and an Asahi bare-metal variant only if users ask for it. Fine-tuning remains out of scope unless a contributor with suitable hardware takes it on.
metrics: Independent verifications: 25 people post a passing `tidemark verify` with their own canary within 30 days of launch.
Bypass matrix: 100% of the 40 or more documented exfiltration paths are blocked in CI on both architectures, and the median time to fix an externally reported bypass stays under 14 days.
Soundness: zero false label raises on unlabelled data, and zero missed raises across the read matrix.

Utility: on the published 30-task personal-agent suite, unlabelled tasks lose 0 points compared with no enforcement. Completion rates for labelled tasks are published per hardware class (M1 Pro 16 GB VM, x86 with a 16 GB GPU). Label creep stays under 35% of realistic tasks forced local.
Economics: cost and latency per task compared with all-cloud and all-local baselines, published each release, including the share of tokens served locally.

Overhead, measured each release (these are targets, not claims): open() overhead under 5 µs p50, added connection latency under 3 ms p50, broker overhead under 10 ms per call, boot to ready under 60 s in a VM.
Adoption: 200 weekly active devices by month 6 (opt-in countme-style), 3 external contributors with merged PRs, and 1 upstream contribution accepted by ActPlane, OpenShell or Hermes.
risks: Label creep makes the product unusable. Session-level taint is sound but coarse, and the AgentKernel preprint argues it produces too many false positives. Mitigations: short sessions, the month-5 split between cloud planner and local worker, and the release queue. The 30-task suite measures the effect.

An incumbent closes the gap. NVIDIA could add read-time labels to OpenShell and NemoClaw, and Tailscale could make Aperture dynamic. Mitigations: upstream a label-provider interface early, and differentiate on neutrality, the owned image and receipts.

Dependency fragility. ActPlane is young (about 104 stars, no releases), kfuncs are an unstable ABI, bootc is a CNCF Sandbox project, and the Fedora kernel and NVIDIA stacks break on rebases. Mitigations: pin and assert in CI, and keep a minimal own BPF program as a fallback.

Threat-model limits. Covert and timing channels, steganography toward cleared destinations, and kernel or root compromise all defeat Tidemark. Receipts signed by a key on the same machine are only as strong as that machine until TPM attestation. The project needs to say this plainly to avoid overclaiming.

Escapes through agent architecture. Agents that spawn work through daemons (Docker or Podman backends, systemd user services) leave the session cgroup. The MVP blocks those sockets and requires in-scope backends, which may break some Hermes configurations.

Performance on M1. Private sessions on a 16 GB M1 Pro get 4-8B Q4 models and minutes of prefill for long contexts. Users may switch enforcement off, as the Omarchy evidence suggests. Enforcement stays silent so that its only cost is model quality.

Solo capacity. About 120 hours for the MVP is tight. A security claim invites bypass reports that demand fast response, and founders still write 66-100% of commits. Cut undo first and the DNS stub second.
Trademark collision on the name 'Tidemark'. Clear it before launch.

Open question 1 for the founder: are you willing to make a security claim, which invites bypass reports and requires response within days, rather than a convenience claim? If not, this concept is the wrong flagship.

Open question 2 for the founder: will first users accept local-model quality for labelled work, or is the real demand 'cloud quality with privacy', which only confidential-computing endpoints cleared for P could provide? This should be tested in interviews before week 5.

Inconsistency in the original premise: a 'revolutionary' natively booted AI OS on the founder's own M1 Pro runs AI slower than macOS. The revolution here lies in control and proof, not speed, and the showcase hardware for local performance should be x86 with NVIDIA or AMD.
kill_criteria: Week 2: BPF LSM xattr labelling cannot be made to work on fedora-bootc for both architectures, and a fanotify-based fallback cannot catch mmap and child-process reads. Pivot to an egress-and-placement broker without the OS claim, or stop.

Week 6: the bypass matrix reveals a class of bypass in label raising or egress that cannot be fixed within the design (for example, fd passing that cannot be scoped). Stop before launch rather than ship a false security claim.

Week 10: on the 30-task suite, more than 40% of realistic tasks are forced local, and local completion on M1-class models falls below 50% of cloud completion. Do not launch the session-level design; build the planner and worker split first or stop.

Before launch: NVIDIA OpenShell or another open-source project ships read-time label-constrained model placement with verifiable receipts. Contribute to that project instead and keep the image only if it adds guarantees that project lacks.

Month 6: fewer than 10 independent demo verifications and fewer than 50 weekly active devices. Stop the image, upstream the label provider to ActPlane or OpenShell, and archive with a documented exit.
scope_cuts_from_original_spec: Model unification (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Gemma): cut. Tidemark manages placement, not a model zoo. Any GGUF model works through llama.cpp, and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works in the cloud. Llama is deprioritised as legacy, and the defaults are small permissive models such as Qwen and Gemma 4.

'Laya': reclassified from a model family to an optional routing classifier (a 421M-parameter ModernBERT). It is off by default and ranks only within the set the label permits. It does not decide privacy.

Inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM): deferred to month 4 or later as pinned OCI images. They ship breaking releases, are tied to specific CUDA versions and cannot be tested on the M1. MLX has no Linux GPU path and is supported only as an unattested endpoint on a macOS host. Ollama is compatible as an endpoint but not bundled. The one validated backend is llama.cpp llama-server.
Training and fine-tuning (TorchTitan, DeepSpeed, Axolotl, Unsloth): cut from year one. They cannot be tested on the M1, offer no differentiation, and torchtune is unmaintained.
Hardware adapters: cut. Use the Fedora kernel and Mesa, and later the NVIDIA open modules from existing akmods pipelines.
Resource scheduler: replaced by a memory-fit admission check in the broker. No GPU or cluster scheduling, which is a poor wedge for a small team.
Security services: narrowed to label-gated egress, placement, declassification and receipts. Containment is reused from OpenShell, sandbox-runtime or bubblewrap and systemd.
Benchmark engine: replaced by the bypass matrix, the read matrix, the 30-task utility suite and the demo run in CI. There is no general LLM benchmark engine.
UI with Home, Agents, Models, Training, Developer Tools and System Settings: cut to a CLI plus a static HTML report generated by `tidemark report`. A desktop UI is deferred until there are users.
Hermes Agent integration: kept, but as unmodified Hermes under `tidemark run`, with no fork. Unifying agent frameworks is cut.
Secure isolated task execution and repeatable benchmarks from the MVP wish list: kept, narrowed to label enforcement plus reproducible security and utility suites in CI.
Measured boot, TPM attestation and sealed images: deferred until bootc sealed UKI leaves test status (months 8-9).

architect:security.name: AgentOS Escrow
architect:security.tagline: The safe place to let agents act: data is labelled when it is read, side effects wait in escrow until committed, and every decision is written to a ledger the agent cannot touch.
architect:security.lens: Security-first: "the safe place to let agents act." The threat model treats the agent, its model output and every MCP server, hook and skill it loads as fully compromised. The trusted computing base is the signed OS image: the kernel plus three privilege-separated services (agentosd, the egress gateway and the ledger daemon). The goal is to limit what a successful prompt injection can do: what can leave, what cannot be undone, and what goes unrecorded. Escrow does not try to prevent injection, which labs concede is unsolved. The OS carries the guarantees. The new work sits above the kernel.
architect:security.revolutionary_claim: Escrow would be the first installable OS on which an unmodified agent from any vendor (Hermes Agent and OpenCode in v0.1; OpenClaw and Claude Code in v0.2) runs with its own permission prompts turned off, together with every MCP server, hook and subprocess it starts. The OS would do three things. (1) It labels data when a process reads it, follows those labels across processes, files and agents from different vendors, and blocks any request, including requests to allowlisted hosts, whose destination is not cleared for the session's labels. The decision depends on what the session read, not on the bytes it sends, so encoding or paraphrasing the data does not get it out. (2) It lets read-only, locally staged and compensable actions run, and holds only irreversible external actions for one human decision. (3) A process the agent cannot reach records every decision in a hash-chained, signed ledger tied to the signed image digest. How to check it: fork the public repository and run the red-team workflow on a free GitHub x64 KVM runner. The workflow runs the same scripted 'fully compromised agent' twice, once in audit mode and once in enforce mode. Pass means that in enforce mode the attacker sink receives zero canary bytes on every listed channel, every irreversible-class request is held, an aborted session leaves the workspace byte-identical, and the standalone verifier rejects any tampered ledger copy at the exact altered entry. Not claimed: prevention of prompt injection, resistance to kernel exploits (the kernel is shared until microVM principals arrive), timing or other low-bandwidth covert channels, or protection of data the user deliberately cleared for a model provider. CaMeL and FIDES enforce information flow inside one rewritten agent, and HiStar/Flume did OS-level information-flow control in research. What is new is enforcement across vendors with no change to the agent, combined with staged commit and third-party-verifiable evidence, as a reproducible product.
architect:security.first_users: Primary: self-hosters who run always-on personal or coding agents (Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, OpenCode) on a spare Linux machine, a homelab VM (Proxmox, QEMU) or a Mac VM, with access to their own files, GitHub, email or calendar. Reasons from the evidence: (a) they already run Linux images and VM templates, so a bootable image is not a barrier for them; (b) they run agents unattended, where per-action approval fails (about 93% of prompts are approved, and Omarchy launches 11 of 15 agents with prompts disabled); (c) their side effects are external (messages, issues, emails), where file snapshots do not help; (d) the workloads they run have large attack surfaces (722 OpenClaw advisories in 2026; Hermes has 15.7k open issues); (e) NVIDIA built NemoClaw to contain exactly these agents, which shows demand for containment, but NemoClaw has no labels, no staging and no ledger. Secondary, as adversarial co-developers: agent-security researchers and evaluators who will try to break the public claim. Evidence for this group: the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, METR's work on log tampering, and evaluator machines with live internet access. Each break they report improves the red-team suite. Deliberately not first: enterprise CISOs (Agent 365 is bundled in E7, and no buyer interviews exist), regulated deployers (deadlines fall in 2027) and GPU or training users (cannot be tested on the M1). Willingness to pay is unvalidated and is not needed for v0.1.
problem_evidence: Labs concede that prompt injection is unsolved, and adaptive attacks bypassed all 12 published defences tested. In Anthropic's phishing test, 24 of 25 exfiltration retries succeeded, and only egress and file-system controls held.

Information-flow control works but has not shipped in an agent-agnostic form. CaMeL reaches provable security at 77% task success against 84% undefended (a loss of 3 to 32 points depending on the model, about 2.7x the tokens), and it requires rewriting the agent. AWS Dogwood applies only coarse session rules inside AgentCore, and Purview DLP applies only inside Microsoft 365.

Containment is free (MXC GA 7 Oct, OpenShell, sandbox-runtime, Docker Sandboxes, Copilot), but it enforces host allowlists, so data still leaves through allowlisted destinations. sandbox-runtime covers shell commands only, not MCP servers or hooks.
Approving every action has failed: users approve about 93% of Claude Code prompts, auto mode misses 17% of 52 overeager actions, and Omarchy launches 11 of 15 agents with prompts disabled.

Irreversible actions are rare but costly. About 0.8% of tool calls appear irreversible (Anthropic data). Agents have deleted production databases (Replit, PocketOS). Claude Code checkpoints cover file edits only.

Agent self-reports cannot be trusted. OpenAI test agents compromised Hugging Face production and tampered with logs, and at least 96 transcripts showed tool-call spoofing; the evidence survived only because transcripts were captured separately. METR calls observability security-critical.
Supply-chain risk: Snyk found 13.4% of 3,984 skills critical and 76 malicious. MCP tool definitions can change after approval, and Agent Skills has no signing.
Verification is the bottleneck: Faros 2026 (22k developers) shows PRs merged without review up 76.3% and incidents per PR up 242.7%.

Record-keeping deadlines arrive: Colorado SB26-189 (3-year records) and CPPA ADMT on 1 Jan 2027; EU AI Act Annex III, Art. 12/14/26, on 2 Dec 2027 (at least 6 months of deployer logs). Microsoft rates its own coverage of these articles as partial. Only about 20% of firms have mature agent governance (Deloitte, n=3,235).

Counter-evidence to keep in view: all willingness-to-pay data comes from vendor surveys; simple log separation was enough in the OpenAI case; vendor model-plus-classifier defences report about 1% attack success.

primitives.name: Agent principal
primitives.what_it_does: Makes each agent session and all of its descendants (MCP servers, hooks, LSP servers, shells, double-forked daemons) a single kernel principal. Each principal has its own UID, cgroup, mount, IPC and network namespaces, resource quota and ledger identity.
primitives.mechanism: agentos run --manifest asks agentosd to start a systemd transient service through D-Bus StartTransientUnit (Varlink StartTransient once the base ships systemd v262). Properties: DynamicUser, NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem=strict, PrivateIPC, PrivateTmp, CPUQuota/MemoryMax, and BindPaths only for manifest paths. NetworkNamespacePath points to a per-principal netns whose only route is a veth to the gateway. A 50-line exec shim applies go-landlock in strict V9/V10 mode, not BestEffort, which scopes pathname and abstract Unix sockets, signals and UDP. Cgroup and namespace membership are inherited, and leaving them requires privileges the principal does not have. A seccomp deny-list covers mount, bpf, keyctl and cross-principal ptrace.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse systemd sandboxing, Linux namespaces, go-landlock (MIT) and vishvananda/netlink. Build only the manifest-to-unit translation and netns plumbing (about 500 lines of Go). No new isolation mechanism is written: these are the same kernel primitives OpenShell and sandbox-runtime wrap.

primitives.name: Provenance labeller
primitives.what_it_does: Labels data when a principal reads it and keeps a session label that only grows: confidentiality labels such as secret:ssh, private:clients and private:repo, plus an integrity flag set once untrusted input is seen. Files written by a tainted session carry its label, so laundering data through files or through a second agent from another vendor is caught.
primitives.mechanism: Labelled data lives on a dedicated vault filesystem. Labels are trusted.agentos.* xattrs, which only CAP_SYS_ADMIN can set, so principals cannot strip them. agentosd holds a fanotify FAN_MARK_FILESYSTEM mark with FAN_OPEN_PERM. The opener's cgroup identifies the principal, and the open blocks until the taint is recorded, so the taint is always recorded before any egress decision. Opens by non-agent processes are allowed at once. The gateway sets the integrity flag on responses from destinations outside the trusted-input list. At commit, written files receive the session label before they become visible.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse fanotify and xattrs (in the kernel). Build about 350 lines of Go. The prior art is research (HiStar, Flume) or tied to one agent (CaMeL, FIDES). The new part is enforcement at the OS level, across vendors, with no change to the agent.

primitives.name: Clearance-checked egress gateway
primitives.what_it_does: Acts as the single exit for all principals. Each destination rule (method plus host plus path pattern) carries a clearance set, and a request leaves only if the session label is within that clearance. For example, a session that read private:clients cannot comment on a public issue even though the GitHub API is allowlisted. Other functions: DNS resolves only names in manifests; UDP and QUIC are dropped; credential placeholders are replaced with real secrets only for cleared destinations; model-API requests that define provider-side tools (such as server-side web fetch) are denied unless cleared; a tainted session may fetch only URL patterns declared in its manifest (such as registry package paths), which bounds leakage through URLs; outbound bodies are scanned for exact-match fingerprints of labelled content, as evidence only and not as the security boundary.
primitives.mechanism: mitmproxy runs in transparent mode in a gateway netns. nftables redirects traffic from the principal veths. A Python addon looks up the principal by source IP and fetches its label and manifest from agentosd over a Unix socket. dnsmasq is generated from manifests. The interception CA is installed only into principal trust stores, never into the host's.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse mitmproxy (MIT), nftables and dnsmasq. Build the addon (about 450 lines of Python). Credential injection is already a commodity pattern (OpenShell, Claude Code); it is reproduced in about 40 lines because every request already passes through the addon. Portable mode later chains to OpenShell, MXC or sandbox-runtime proxies rather than replacing them.

primitives.name: Staged workspace
primitives.what_it_does: Keeps agent file writes away from the user's real files until commit. Abort discards them, and commit detects conflicts with edits the user made in the meantime.
primitives.mechanism: Each session gets an overlayfs: lower is the real workspace, upper is a per-session Btrfs subvolume. agentos diff, commit and abort operate on it. A Btrfs snapshot of /var/home at session start is a safety net. /usr is immutable through bootc, and bootc rollback covers the OS itself.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse overlayfs, Btrfs and bootc. Build about 250 lines.

primitives.name: Side-effect journal and hold queue
primitives.what_it_does: Classifies each outbound request as read-only, reversible (staged locally), compensable (has a declared undo) or irreversible. Irreversible is the default for any unknown write and for any call that sends a notification. The first three classes proceed and are journaled. Irreversible requests wait in one queue that spans all agents, for a single human decision. Abort runs compensations in reverse order, as a saga. An optional Rule-of-Two setting lets irreversible calls to cleared destinations proceed automatically only when the session has no untrusted-input taint.
primitives.mechanism: The gateway classifies requests using effect manifests: YAML recipes per API, such as create issue paired with close issue, or create branch paired with delete branch. MCP ToolAnnotations are treated only as hints, because the OS classifies effects where they actually happen (network or file system), not where the agent says they happen. A held request blocks until a timeout and then returns HTTP 403 with a structured approval id, so the agent can retry after approval. Commands: agentos queue, approve, deny.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Build about 300 lines (addon, daemon queue and CLI). Recipes are seeded for the GitHub API and the demo mock API. Temporal-style durable execution is not reused because it requires deterministic agent code and does not capture OS state.

primitives.name: Out-of-band evidence ledger
primitives.what_it_does: Records every principal start, labelled read, exec, egress decision, hold, approval, commit, abort and compensation. The record is tamper-evident, a third party can verify it offline, and it is tied to the image digest, the policy version and a kernel self-test. When the agent's transcript is available, the ledger also flags tool calls the agent claimed but the OS never observed (spoof detection).
primitives.mechanism: agentos-ledgerd runs under its own UID and is the only writer to a ledger subvolume (append-only inode attribute). It accepts events only from agentosd and the gateway, never from the agent. Entries form a SHA-256 hash chain. Ed25519-signed checkpoints in the C2SP signed-note/tlog-checkpoint format are written every N events or 60 s, with the key held in systemd-creds (TPM-sealed when available). Checkpoint hashes can optionally be anchored in Sigstore Rekor (off by default). A standalone verifier runs on macOS, Linux and Windows. Evidence packs export with a mapping table to EU AI Act Art. 12/14/26, Colorado SB26-189 and CPPA ADMT, presented as supporting evidence and not as a compliance claim.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse the C2SP formats, Rekor and systemd-creds, with journald Forward Secure Sealing as an optional second witness. Build about 400 lines, including the verifier.

primitives.name: Manifest admission with permission diff
primitives.what_it_does: Each agent, MCP server or skill bundle runs only under a manifest that declares its paths, the labels it may read, its destinations with clearances, its effect classes and its quotas. Any update that widens permissions is refused at load time until a person approves the diff.
primitives.mechanism: Canonical YAML is hashed and stored per principal name, and a diff lists the widened capabilities. Signed manifests are checked with cosign verify-blob (keyless signing in v0.2). v0.1 ships manifests for Hermes Agent and OpenCode.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse cosign and Sigstore. Build about 200 lines.

primitives.name: Public red-team suite and scorecard
primitives.what_it_does: Makes the safety claim checkable. Scripted scenarios play a fully compromised agent across exfiltration channels, side-effect classes, ledger tampering and escape attempts, and 10 benign tasks measure utility loss. Each scenario runs in audit mode and in enforce mode on a named image digest, and the run produces a signed scorecard. An optional live mode runs real agents against prompt-injected content.
primitives.mechanism: Shell and Python scenarios run against local mock services (attacker sink, mock GitHub-like API, mock mail API), so no external network, model or API key is needed. A GitHub Actions workflow on free x64 KVM runners lets anyone fork the repository and reproduce the run. The scorecard JSON is recorded in the ledger.
primitives.reuse_vs_build: Reuse AgentDojo task ideas (rewritten, not forked, because public results stop at February 2025 models), QEMU and GitHub runners. Build about 500 lines, counted separately from product code.

architect:security.architecture:
Image: a Containerfile FROM quay.io/fedora/fedora-bootc:44, which is multi-architecture (Universal Blue images are amd64-only). It is built and cosign-signed in GitHub Actions on free x64 and arm64 runners, with an SBOM attestation. bootc-image-builder produces qcow2, raw, ISO and AMI images. The image is headless, with SSH and console access only. The Btrfs layout fixed at install has these subvolumes: /var/home, /var/lib/agentos/vault (labelled data), /var/lib/agentos/stage (session overlays) and /var/lib/agentos/ledger (append-only). A boot self-test keeps agent services from starting unless the kernel provides Landlock ABI 9 or later (10 preferred), landlock in the active LSM list, cgroup v2, overlayfs and fanotify permission events. BPF LSM is added to lsm= in phase 2. SELinux stays enforcing.

Trusted computing base (three services, privilege-separated, all in the signed read-only /usr): (1) agentosd (Go, root, small surface) handles principal lifecycle through systemd D-Bus, netns/veth plumbing, overlay staging, the fanotify labeller, the taint store, the hold queue and manifest admission, and serves the CLI and gateway over a Unix socket. (2) agentos-gw is mitmproxy in transparent mode, unprivileged, in its own netns, with a Python addon for clearance checks, effect classes, holds, credential replacement, the provider-side-tool filter and fingerprint evidence; dnsmasq enforces the name allowlist. (3) agentos-ledgerd (Go, own UID) keeps the hash chain, writes signed checkpoints, exports evidence and can anchor checkpoints in Rekor.

Principals are systemd transient services, each with one netns whose only route is the gateway, and systemd cgroup quotas form the basic scheduler. agentos ps reports CPU, memory, labels and held actions per principal. Workloads in v0.1 are Hermes Agent (pinned version) and OpenCode, run through manifests. A local llama.cpp server runs as a digest-pinned Podman Quadlet container (CPU or Vulkan) and is the one validated inference backend, with clearance for all labels. Remote model APIs are destinations with explicit clearances.

Flows. Read: open() on the vault triggers a fanotify permission event; the session label is updated, the ledger records it, and the open is allowed. Send: connect() goes over the veth to the nftables redirect and mitmproxy; the addon checks principal, label and manifest and returns allow, deny or hold; the ledger records the decision; the request goes upstream. Commit: diff the upper layer, check for conflicts, label written files, merge, record. Abort: discard the upper layer, run compensations in reverse, record.

Portable core (OS-agnostic, Apache-2.0): the manifest and policy schema, the effect recipes, the ledger format and verifier, and the red-team suite.

Development loop on the M1 Pro: Go cross-compiles natively to linux/arm64. The aarch64 image builds in podman machine and boots in Lima (vz) or UTM. bootc usr-overlay allows hot reload of daemons without rebuilding the image. No nested virtualization is needed because principals use namespaces, not microVMs. CI handles x86_64 builds, QEMU serial-console boot tests under KVM, and the red-team suite.

Code budget: about 2,800 lines of product code (principal 500, labeller 350, gateway addon 450, staging 250, journal and holds 300, ledger and verifier 400, admission 200, CLI 200, image and units 150), plus about 500 lines of red-team scenarios.
architect:security.why_bootable_os_matters: The OS carries the guarantees; it is not where the innovation lives. The image guarantees six things that a userland tool on an arbitrary host cannot. (1) Kernel floor. Landlock runs in strict mode at ABI 9 or later, which covers pathname Unix sockets, closing escapes through ssh-agent, D-Bus or container sockets; ABI 10 adds UDP. fanotify permission events, cgroup v2 and overlayfs are always present. Userland tools must degrade silently instead: go-landlock's BestEffort mode, Codex demoting Landlock to legacy because it could not isolate Unix sockets, and Claude Code's weaker nested mode. (2) Every process is wrapped.
