- Boot self-test: agent sessions refuse to start unless the kernel has Landlock ABI 9 or later, bpf and landlock in the active LSM list, the xattr kfuncs, cgroup v2, overlayfs and a Btrfs /var.
- Image-owned agent shims and the llama-server Quadlet.
- Headless (SSH and serial console). No telemetry.
architecture_layers.tech_choices: bootc and bootc-image-builder (qcow2, raw, ISO, AMI); cosign keyless signing through GitHub OIDC; syft SBOM; trivy; Renovate digest pinning; native builds on free GitHub x86_64 and arm64 runners. fedora-bootc:45 was verified on 16 Oct 2026 as a manifest list containing amd64 and arm64, updated 15 Oct 2026.

architecture_layers.components: Sleepable BPF LSM file_open program and a pinned per-cgroup label map; Landlock in strict mode; seccomp; mount, network and IPC namespaces; the cgroup v2 freezer and quotas; overlayfs.
architecture_layers.tech_choices: BPF C compiled with clang and loaded through cilium/ebpf (bpf2go); go-landlock; systemd unit properties.
architecture_layers.rationale: Only kernel primitives that already exist are reused. The single new kernel-side code is a small BPF program, and the Phase 0 gate tests it before any other work.

architecture_layers.tech_choices: Go, statically linked. No dependency on systemd 261 or 262 features: D-Bus transient units work on the base's systemd.
architecture_layers.rationale: tidemarkd is the only component that needs root, so it is kept small and its root operations are listed and reviewed. Everything that parses untrusted input runs unprivileged.

architecture_layers.components:
- tidemark-gw: egress, with one Unix socket per session.
- tidemark-broker: model calls. Accepts OpenAI Chat Completions, Responses and Anthropic Messages; enforces placement, strips provider-side tools and injects credentials.
- Release queue.
architecture_layers.tech_choices: Go, unprivileged, each under its own UID and systemd sandboxing. Domain-level CONNECT decisions with no TLS interception in v0.1. Labels are read synchronously from the pinned BPF map.
architecture_layers.rationale: Identifying the session by its socket removes the attribution gap in the original Tidemark design. Avoiding TLS interception avoids mitmproxy (not packaged by Fedora) and breakage from certificate pinning. The broker sees model request bodies in plaintext on the local link, which closes the provider-side tool channel without any interception.

architecture_layers.components: tidemark-ledgerd (its own UID, append-only subvolume, Ed25519 key in systemd-creds) and tidemark-verify (macOS, Linux, Windows).
architecture_layers.tech_choices: in-toto Statement v1 inside DSSE (go-securesystemslib), a SHA-256 hash chain, crypto/ed25519. Rekor anchoring is optional from Phase 6.
architecture_layers.rationale: Agents have tampered with logs before (OpenAI and Hugging Face, July 2026). Standard formats let existing tools verify the evidence, and the verifier runs outside the VM.

architecture_layers.components:
- llama-server as a Podman Quadlet pinned by digest: CPU by default, Vulkan optional.
- Model store in /var/lib/tidemark/models, pulled by digest.
- Backend registry with clearances.
- Host endpoint registration for macOS Metal llama.cpp or Ollama, recorded as unattested local.
- Cloud providers as destinations.
- Optional ranker plugin interface (Laya adapter), off by default.
architecture_layers.tech_choices: ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp server image, pinned by digest; arm64 availability is confirmed in Phase 0 or the image is built in CI. One default small, permissively licensed GGUF model. The demo uses a model under 2B parameters.
architecture_layers.rationale: This meets the spec's minimal model layer with one validated backend. Placement is a clearance decision, which turns local inference into an enforced privacy control without forcing every private task onto a weak model.

architecture_layers.components:
- Profiles for Hermes Agent v0.22.x (local sandbox backend, base URL set to the broker, its own llama.cpp auto-install disabled), OpenCode and Claude Code.
- Generic `tidemark run -- <cmd>`.
- Agents installed on demand into /var/lib/tidemark/agents, pinned by version and hash.
architecture_layers.tech_choices: YAML profiles. Agents are never redistributed inside the image, because Claude Code is proprietary and Hermes Agent changes too often.
architecture_layers.rationale: Agents are wrapped, not forked. Hermes Agent is one profile among several. Its remote sandbox backends count as ordinary destinations, and its Docker backend is unavailable because the session cannot reach the socket.

architecture_layers.components:
- CLI: tidemark run | ps | stop | resume | label | audit-labels | diff | commit | abort | queue | release | receipt | doctor | demo.
- Read-only local web dashboard on 127.0.0.1:9470 inside the VM, reached through an SSH port forward. Pages: Home (doctor, image digest), Sessions (labels, CPU and memory, placement), Models (backends, clearances, queue), Receipts, System.
architecture_layers.tech_choices: Go html/template with no JavaScript framework, no CDN, a strict CSP and no mutating routes. In v0.1 approvals happen only in the CLI. A Cockpit plugin, which reuses Cockpit's PAM authentication, adds approvals in Phase 6.
architecture_layers.rationale: This is the cheapest credible interface that still covers the spec's Home, Agents, Models and System Settings. A read-only dashboard has no authentication or CSRF surface. The Training and Developer Tools pages are cut.

architecture_layers.components:
- tidemark-bench, a standalone OCI container: adversarial and benign scenarios, a puppet-model server that drives real CLIs, host-side sinks, and adapters for the Omarchy launcher flags, Fedora with sandbox-runtime, OpenShell and Tidemark.
- GitHub workflows: build, boot test, integration, bench, reproduce (fork and run), release, nightly live mode.
architecture_layers.tech_choices: Go plus YAML scenarios; QEMU under KVM on free x64 runners; native builds on arm64 runners, with a CI step that records whether /dev/kvm exists there.
architecture_layers.rationale: The benchmark is the unit of adoption that spreads even when people never boot the image, and it survives if an incumbent bundles enforcement.

architecture_layers.components: tidemark-lite RPM (Fedora), DEB (Ubuntu) and AUR packages, with doctor guarantee levels written into every receipt. The specification files (policy, receipt predicate) are published separately under Apache-2.0.
architecture_layers.tech_choices: The same Go binaries. Hosts with BPF LSM enabled, as stock Fedora has, get labels. Other hosts run in audit-only mode and say so.
architecture_layers.rationale: This lowers the barrier for people who will not boot an image, while staying honest about weaker guarantees.

Code budget for v0.1: about 2,900 lines of product code:
- session and shim: 450
- labels: 200 BPF C plus 200 Go
- gateway: 450
- broker: 500
- staging: 250
- ledger and verifier: 350
- queue and stop: 150
- CLI and doctor: 200
- dashboard: 150

On top of that: about 700 lines of benchmark and demo code, plus tests.
stack: Go (version pinned in Phase 0) for every daemon, the CLI, the verifier and the benchmark. Rust (aya, the landlock crate) was considered. Go wins for five reasons: cilium/ebpf is more mature, go-landlock is maintained, DSSE and in-toto libraries exist, cross-compiling to linux/arm64 from macOS with CGO_ENABLED=0 is trivial, and one part-time founder writes it faster. Both languages are memory-safe, and the BPF program is written in C either way.
BPF C, compiled with clang/LLVM inside a Fedora toolbox container and loaded through cilium/ebpf with bpf2go.
go-landlock in strict mode (never BestEffort); godbus/dbus and coreos/go-systemd for transient units.
secure-systems-lab/go-securesystemslib (DSSE), the in-toto attestation Go bindings, and crypto/ed25519.
Base image: quay.io/fedora/fedora-bootc:45, pinned by digest. It was verified on 16 Oct 2026 as a manifest list with amd64 and arm64 children. :44 stays as a fallback build.
bootc, bootc-image-builder, cosign keyless signing (GitHub OIDC), syft, trivy, Renovate and the OpenSSF Scorecard workflow.
Podman Quadlet running the ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp server image, pinned by digest, as the one validated inference backend.
Btrfs, overlayfs and systemd-creds.
Dashboard built with Go html/template and served without any CDN or JavaScript framework. A Cockpit plugin follows in Phase 6.
Testing: go test with native fuzzing, a QEMU/KVM boot harness on GitHub Actions, gosec, govulncheck, staticcheck, CodeQL and shellcheck.
Added in Phase 5: elazarl/goproxy (BSD-3) for opt-in TLS termination on declared APIs only, and cosign verify-blob for effect manifests.
Development tools on the M1 Pro: podman machine (libkrun or applehv provider), Lima (vz), UTM or QEMU with HVF, and VS Code Remote-SSH.

assets: User secrets: SSH and GPG keys, cloud credentials, password stores and tokens in their usual locations.
Private data: notes, mail, and client or financial files in labelled folders.
Model API keys, and later forge credentials, held only by the broker and gateway.
Integrity of the workspace and host: files, auto-exec paths, and the immutable /usr.
External accounts reachable through cleared destinations, and the integrity of side effects on them. v0.1 does not hold these effects; v0.2 holds irreversible ones for declared APIs.
Integrity of the evidence: the ledger, receipts and the signing key.
The human's attention: release requests and the interruption budget.
adversaries: A prompt injector who controls content agents read, such as web pages, issues, READMEs, emails and documents.
A malicious or compromised skill, MCP server, plugin, hook or agent package running inside the session (supply chain).
The agent or model acting deceptively: spoofing tool calls, tampering with logs, trying to persist.
A second agent, possibly from another vendor, used to launder data through files.
trust_boundaries: Session to kernel: namespaces, cgroup, Landlock, seccomp and BPF LSM. The shared kernel is trusted.
Session to Tidemark services: exactly two per-session Unix sockets (egress and models). The socket identifies the session, and the control socket is unreachable from sessions.
Session to network: no interface except loopback. Every exit passes through tidemark-gw or tidemark-broker.
Session to filesystem: read-only /usr, a staged overlay workspace and bind paths limited to the profile. Changing a label requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN.
Exit plane to ledger: an append-only event socket that accepts only known peer UIDs.
Human to machine: release, commit and stop are accepted only from processes outside the agents slice.
Machine to verifier: receipts and host-side sink logs are checked outside the VM. The verifier trusts only the published cosign identity and its own canary.
Machine to cleared destinations: clearing a destination is the user's trust decision, and Tidemark does not police what that destination does.
Build pipeline to image: keyless signing in GitHub Actions, an SBOM and pinned digests. Users verify the image with cosign.
guarantees: These hold on the signed image when `tidemark doctor` passes and the kernel is not compromised.

G1 Containment. Every process descended from a session (MCP servers, hooks, LSP servers, double-forked daemons) stays in the session's cgroup, network namespace and mount view, and is killed when the session stops.
G2 Single exit. A session has no network path except tidemark-gw and tidemark-broker. DNS, UDP, QUIC, IP literals and host Unix sockets (D-Bus, Podman, ssh-agent) are unavailable.
G3 Label before read. When any session process opens a labelled file, the session label is raised before open() returns. A session cannot remove or change file labels, or its own label.

G4 Clearance rule. A connection or model request leaves only if the session's labels are a subset of the destination's clearance. The decision does not depend on the request bytes, so encodings and paraphrase cannot bypass it.

G5 Model channel. A labelled session is never placed on a backend outside its clearance, and nothing falls back to the cloud silently. Undeclared provider-side tools are stripped or refused for tainted sessions, and model API keys never enter a session.

G6 Staging. A session's file writes are invisible to the host and to other sessions until commit. Abort restores a byte-identical workspace, committed files carry the session label, and writes to auto-exec locations need explicit acceptance.

G7 Evidence. A process the session cannot reach records every decision. Any edit, deletion, insertion or reordering of a receipt is detected offline, and each receipt names the image digest, the policy hash and the doctor result.
G8 Stop. `tidemark stop` freezes every session and denies every exit, with a target of 1 s or less.
G9 Declassification. Only a human can lower a label, and each release is recorded with the content hash and the destination.
non_guarantees: Tidemark does not prevent prompt injection and does not make the agent's output correct.
A kernel exploit or root compromise defeats every guarantee. The kernel stays shared until the optional microVM principals arrive in Phase 7.

Covert and timing channels toward cleared destinations remain: request counts, timing, choice of URL, and CDN domain fronting through a cleared domain. Careful clearance choices bound them but do not eliminate them.
Data sent to a destination the user cleared, including a cleared cloud model provider, is outside Tidemark's control.
Unlabelled data is unprotected. `tidemark audit-labels` only reports unlabelled files that look sensitive.
In v0.1, external side effects at cleared destinations are neither held nor undone. Snapshots never undo sent emails or API calls; holds for irreversible effects on declared APIs arrive in v0.2.
v0.1 does not inspect content: decisions are per destination domain. Clearances by method and path arrive in v0.2 with opt-in TLS termination.
Receipts signed by a key on the machine are only as trustworthy as that machine until TPM sealing or external anchoring is added.
Hosts running tidemark-lite get only the guarantees `tidemark doctor` reports, and macOS host endpoints are recorded as unattested.
Availability is not guaranteed: an agent can deny service to itself, and quotas limit resource abuse without eliminating it.
Enforcement may move work to weaker local models. That quality cost is measured and published, not hidden.

phases.phase: Phase 0: Specification, threat model, benchmark methodology, repository skeleton, kernel kill gate

benchmark_methodology: Threat assumption: the agent is fully compromised. The adversary is a set of scripted tool-call sequences delivered by a puppet-model server, which speaks the OpenAI and Anthropic Messages APIs and accepts dummy keys, to real, unmodified agent CLIs (Hermes Agent, OpenCode, Claude Code). A synthetic agent covers the channels that CLIs cannot express. The gating suite needs no live model and no API key.

Canary handling: the host running the benchmark generates a random canary for each run and injects it into the VM, through a QEMU fw_cfg systemd credential or a file copy on Lima. Sinks run on the host, outside the VM. Pass or fail is the grep count on host logs. No canary ever appears in scenario source.

Live mode, which does not gate releases: real Hermes Agent with a local llama-server or the tester's own key faces injected content. The report gives injection success and leak rates over at least 10 runs, with confidence intervals.
Model placement cost, reported separately: completion of labelled tasks on the local model against a cloud model, for each hardware class. The quality cost of privacy is shown, not hidden.

Extensibility: scenarios are YAML plus a script, and community pull requests are welcome. A new scenario counts only if it leaks in audit mode. Bypasses are credited in a hall of fame and become regression tests.
Reporting rules: every number in the README links to a CI artifact, each report lists its known gaps, and no claim goes beyond what the scenarios measure.
non_goals: Preventing prompt injection or judging whether agent output is correct.
Building a new kernel or a new distribution, or shipping a desktop environment in the first year.
Per-token information-flow tracking inside the model, as in CaMeL. Labels are per session by design.
Eliminating covert or timing channels to destinations the user has cleared.
Inference serving performance, multi-engine auto-tuning, or GPU and cluster scheduling.
Training and fine-tuning.
Agent identity, inventory or governance dashboards; Agent 365, AgentCore and Okta already cover these.
Rebuilding containment that OpenShell, MXC or sandbox-runtime already provide on other operating systems.
Compliance certification. Evidence mapping is supporting material only.
Any telemetry. The image sends nothing home.
Redistributing proprietary agents inside the image.
Windows or macOS enforcement in the MVP. Only the verifier runs there.

dev_environment: Host: M1 Pro with 16 GB, running macOS 27. Install through Homebrew, pinned where possible: Go, podman, lima, qemu, cosign, syft, gh and shellcheck. Edit code in VS Code with Remote-SSH into the development VM.

Native aarch64 image builds: run a rootful podman machine (libkrun or applehv provider, 4 vCPU, 4 GB) and stop it when not building. Use `podman build`, then run bootc-image-builder inside the podman machine to produce a qcow2.
Boot: use a Lima (vz) template that points at the qcow2 (4 vCPU, 6 GB, 40 GB disk) for the daily loop. Use UTM or QEMU with HVF for ISO installs and for testing the fw_cfg canary path.
Memory budget: the 6 GB dev VM, the 4 GB podman machine and about 5 GB for macOS do not fit at full size together. Run them one at a time.

Code loop: cross-compile with CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64. Compile the BPF program with clang in a Fedora toolbox container through bpf2go. Run `bootc usr-overlay` in the dev VM, copy the binary with scp and restart it with systemctl for hot reload. Rebuild the image only when image files change.

Local model: run a small GGUF model on CPU in the VM, or register the host's llama.cpp Metal server as an unattested local endpoint through host.lima.internal. Testing krunkit with Vulkan is optional.

x86_64 runs only in CI, on free GitHub x64 runners with KVM enabled through a udev rule; the MVP needs no x86 machine. arm64 runners do native builds, and a CI step records whether /dev/kvm is present.
No nested virtualization is required, because sessions use namespaces rather than microVMs. MicroVM work waits for Phase 7 on KVM hosts.
Weekly cadence: 6 hours building, 2 hours on docs, demo and devlog, and 2 hours on triage. CI must be green every Friday.
Optional: if the founder builds with AI coding agents, run them inside Tidemark sessions from Phase 2 onward as daily dogfooding.
synthesize.budget:
Cash: about USD 15 to 40 per month in total.
- Free for a public repository: GitHub Actions (x64 and arm64 runners), GHCR and Sigstore.
- Domain: about USD 15 per year, bought only after the trademark check.
- Model API for the nightly live-mode runs: USD 0 to 15 per month, using a cheap small model (for example Claude Haiku 5.5 at USD 0.10 per million input tokens) or the local model only.
- AWS g4dn spot for NVIDIA boot tests, from Phase 6: about USD 0.33 per hour; 10 to 20 hours per month comes to about USD 3 to 7 plus storage.
- Optional before v1.0: one-off professional trademark clearance, roughly USD 300 to 1,500 (an unverified estimate). Self-search the USPTO, EUIPO and IP Australia databases first.

Hardware: no purchase is needed for the MVP. Consider an x86 test machine with an NVIDIA GPU only if the NVIDIA variant gains a maintainer, and get quotes first.

Time:
- Phase 0: 20 hours.
- MVP: 120 hours. The realistic range is 120 to 170 hours, managed through a cut order agreed in advance.
- Post-MVP: about 380 hours (38 weeks at 10 hours).
- Every week keeps the 6 / 2 / 2 split between building, docs and triage.

Cut order if the week-9 checkpoint shows more than one week of slippage:
1. Replace the dashboard with a static HTML report.
2. Drop the Btrfs workspace safety snapshot.
3. Drop the Claude Code profile and keep Hermes Agent and OpenCode.
4. Move the OpenShell baseline to v0.2 if setting it up costs more than 4 hours.
5. Run the aarch64 demo locally only, not in CI.

risks.risk: Label creep. Session-level taint is coarse, and normal sessions may become useless.
risks.mitigation:
- Clearances are set per destination, and users may clear a specific provider for private data.
- Placeholder credentials do not taint a session.
- Repository files are unlabelled by default.
- Sessions are kept short.
- A planner/worker split is tested in v0.2.
- The utility suite measures creep, and kill criterion 3 applies.

risks.risk: Local models on the M1 are slow and weak at agentic work: 4-8B models in 16 GB, and minutes to prefill 30K tokens.
risks.mitigation:
- Placement is a clearance decision, not a forced move to local.
- A Metal endpoint on the host is supported.
- The x86 GPU variant in Phase 6 is the showcase for local performance.
- Completion is published for each hardware class.
- The founder is told plainly that the revolution is control and proof, not speed.

risks.risk: Kernel-level fragility: the xattr kfuncs are not a stable ABI, overlayfs may interact badly, and the BPF verifier may behave differently across architectures.
risks.mitigation:
- The kernel is pinned through the image digest, with assertions in CI.
- A Phase 0 kill gate tests this first.
- A fanotify vault fallback exists.
- Renovate digest bumps merge only after the boot test and the read matrix pass.

risks.risk: Scope versus solo capacity: about 2,900 lines of security code, with estimates of 120 to 170 hours.
risks.mitigation:
- A Phase 0 gate and a cut order agreed in advance.
- A schedule checkpoint at week 9.
- No dependency on OpenShell or ActPlane.
- A single language (Go).
- A hard 6/2/2 weekly time cap.

risks.risk: Agents break: clients that ignore proxy settings, no DNS inside the session, SSH git denied, Node proxy environment variables.
risks.mitigation:
- Profiles set the proxy variables, such as NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY.
- Structured 403 messages explain each denial.
- Clients fail closed rather than leak.
- A compatibility matrix is published for every release.

risks.risk: Domain-level clearance is coarse: one host may serve both public and private APIs, and CDN domain fronting is possible.
risks.mitigation:
- Documented as a non-guarantee.
- Guidance to clear only suitable destinations.
- Clearances by method and path arrive in v0.2, with opt-in TLS termination for declared APIs.

risks.risk: Incumbents bundle the idea: NVIDIA adds labels to OpenShell, AWS adds labels to Dogwood, or Anthropic extends its sandbox to MCP servers.
risks.mitigation:
- Open specifications and an upstream label-provider interface.
- A neutral benchmark that keeps its value either way.
- Incumbent changelogs reviewed every quarter.
- Kill criterion 5 applies.

risks.risk: Credibility: critics will say the authors scripted the attacker.
risks.mitigation:
- The puppet model drives real, unmodified CLIs.
- The canary is generated on the tester's host, and the grep runs on the host.
- Community scenarios are counted only if they leak in audit mode.
- Live-mode results are reported separately.

risks.risk: Disputes over benchmark fairness with Omarchy, OpenShell or sandbox-runtime.
risks.mitigation:
- Baselines are labelled precisely, for example 'Omarchy launcher flags'.
- Each tool runs in its strongest documented configuration, and all configurations are published.
- Each project gets a right of reply 7 days before publication.
- Results are reported only as measured.

risks.risk: Adoption: people may not boot an image, and Omarchy already owns the 'agentic distro' label.
risks.mitigation:
- The benchmark container and the verifier are useful on their own.
- tidemark-lite ships in v0.2.
- A Lima template starts it with one command, and Fedora Atomic users can run `bootc switch`.
- Positioning is a safe home for the agents people already run, not a distro.

risks.risk: Upstream churn: Hermes Agent has 15.7k open issues and 33.7k open PRs, Fedora releases every six months, bootc is a CNCF Sandbox project, and llama.cpp changes often.
risks.mitigation:
- Digests are pinned.
- Profile smoke tests run nightly.
- Agents are installed in /var, outside the image.
- Rebases happen every six months, only after full CI passes.

risks.risk: Base image is new: fedora-bootc:45 was published on 15 Oct 2026 and may have early regressions.
risks.mitigation:
- Pin by digest.
- Keep the :44 fallback build in CI until launch.
- The design does not depend on systemd 261 or 262 features.

risks.risk: Root code in the trusted computing base (tidemarkd).
risks.mitigation:
- The gateway, broker and ledger daemon run unprivileged under separate UIDs.
- The list of root operations is short and reviewed.
- Fuzzing in CI.
- The daemons are themselves sandboxed by systemd.

risks.risk: Burnout from security reports (the Asahi precedent).
risks.mitigation:
- Triage capped at 2 hours per week, with issue forms and SECURITY.md.
- A hall of fame credits reporters.
- A 14-day target for fixes.
- A second maintainer after 6 months.

risks.risk: Receipts could expose sensitive file paths or request bodies.
risks.mitigation:
- Paths and bodies are hashed by default.
- Redaction is documented.
- Receipts are never forwarded off the machine.

risks.risk: Overclaiming compliance.
risks.mitigation:
- Evidence mapping waits until Phase 6.
- It is labelled as supporting evidence, not certification.

kill_criteria: End of Phase 0 (week 2). Trigger: BPF LSM label raising cannot be made reliable on fedora-bootc for both architectures, and the fanotify vault fallback misses reads by child processes or through mmap. Action: drop the claim of kernel-recorded labels and ship the gateway, broker and receipts as an audit tool, or stop.

Week 6. Trigger: at least 4 of the 5 self-hosters interviewed would neither label their data nor accept local placement or provider clearances. Action: re-scope to a benchmark-first project for security researchers before building further.
End of Phase 2 (week 9). Trigger: the bypass matrix reveals a class of bypass that the design cannot fix. Action: do not launch the enforcement claim, and narrow it publicly.

Launch gate (week 14). Trigger: with the default policy, benign completion in enforce mode is below 80% of audit mode; or more than 35% of realistic tasks are forced onto a local model and local completion is below 50% of cloud completion on the reference hardware. Action: ship audit mode and receipts only, and build the planner/worker split before enforcement becomes the default.

Any time. Trigger: an incumbent ships free, cross-vendor exit control driven by read-time labels, with label-constrained model placement and verifiable receipts. Action: contribute upstream, keep the benchmark and the specifications, and keep the image only for guarantees the incumbent lacks.
Any time. Trigger: a published bypass of a core guarantee is not fixed within 14 days. Action: withdraw that guarantee publicly and document the bypass.

Month 6. Trigger: fewer than 10 independent BYOC verifications, and fewer than 3 users running real work for 2 weeks or more. Action: stop maintaining the image and keep tidemark-lite, the benchmark and the specifications.

Month 6 (v0.2). Trigger: holds on irreversible effects make more than 30% of real-agent tasks fail, and retries after a structured 403 cannot bring failures below 15%. Action: drop remote-effect holds and keep labels, staging and receipts.
Maintenance. Trigger: image breakage takes more than 4 of the 10 weekly hours for 2 consecutive months. Action: ship only a guest image plus tidemark-lite.
Founder capacity. Trigger: available time stays below 6 hours a week for 4 consecutive weeks. Action: freeze scope at the benchmark and receipts.
open_questions_for_founder: Is a headless VM appliance (SSH, CLI and a read-only local web dashboard, with no desktop) acceptable as the 'literal bootable OS'? The evidence argues against building a desktop.

The realistic estimate for Phase 0 plus the MVP is 140 hours, with a range of 120 to 170. Do you accept the cut order agreed in advance, or would you rather have a 16 to 18 week MVP than stretch your weekly hours?

Will you make and defend a public security claim? That means handling bypass reports and meeting a 14-day fix target within 2 triage hours a week. If not, the launch should be audit-and-benchmark only.

Should the default policy let users clear a cloud provider for private data (better utility, a weaker sovereignty story), or should private data stay local-only by default? The answer decides the hero message.
Do you accept that, if kill criteria trigger, the durable asset may be the benchmark and the open policy and receipt specifications rather than the OS?
'AgentOS' is a crowded name (the AIOS research kernel among others), and 'Tidemark' needs a trademark search. Will you choose and clear a name before Phase 4?

DCO or CLA? A DCO keeps Apache-2.0 contributions simple and rules out relicensing. A CLA keeps a future hosted service under other terms possible. This must be decided before the first outside contribution.
For your first users, which data matters more: code and secrets, or mail and personal files? The answer sets the default labels and which effect manifests come first in v0.2.
Will you build Tidemark with AI coding agents? The hour estimates assume some assistance. If yes, dogfood those agents inside Tidemark from Phase 2.
changes_from_red_team: Aggregation check (challenge to the inputs). The aggregate totals split identical concepts across different names. Summed per concept across all three judges, Escrow (security-first) scores 122, Tidemark 116, Escrow (radical) 113, Docket 109 and Bulkhead 106, and two of the three judges ranked Escrow first. As instructed, the final concept keeps Tidemark's identity, kernel mechanism and host-verifiable canary, but adopts Escrow's clearance rule as its enforcement law, so neither ranking is discarded.

Fixed Tidemark's fatal flaw of forcing private work onto local models. The old rules ('private means local only'; 'private plus untrusted means no egress') are replaced by one: a session's labels must be a subset of the destination's clearance. Model providers count as destinations, the user may clear a provider for private data, and secret data is cleared only to the local engine by default. The untrusted flag no longer cuts egress; in v0.2 it gates whether irreversible effects are approved automatically (Rule of Two).

Fixed Tidemark's missing link between a connection and its session. Each session gets its own Unix sockets, bind-mounted into a PrivateNetwork namespace, and the socket is the identity. The gateway and broker read the pinned BPF map synchronously, so the ring-buffer race found in Escrow (radical) cannot occur.

Corrected the case for owning the OS image. Stock Fedora already lists bpf and landlock in CONFIG_LSM, so enabling them is no argument. The image is justified instead by: a pinned kernel, with CI assertions, for the xattr kfuncs (not a stable ABI); a Landlock ABI 9 floor; launch shims owned by the image; credentials held only by daemons; a disk layout fixed at install; receipts bound to the image digest; and bootc rollback.

Base image: fedora-bootc:45 pinned by digest instead of :44. On 16 Oct 2026 the :45 tag was verified as a manifest list with amd64 and arm64 children, updated 15 Oct. Fedora 44 reaches end of life in mid-2027. Nothing depends on systemd 261 or 262, and :44 stays as a fallback build until launch.

Fixed Escrow's scope flaw. Eight primitives become seven small ones in a single language. mitmproxy (not packaged by Fedora) and TLS interception are removed from the MVP. Compensations, effect manifests, capability admission and the verifier gate are assigned to v0.2 and v0.3 from day one. An explicit cut order and a week-9 checkpoint are added.

Fixed Escrow's 'vault only' adoption flaw. Labels attach by xattr to default sensitive paths at first boot (~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, keyrings, cloud credential files, ~/Private, mail stores). The fanotify vault remains only as the Phase 0 fallback.

Closed the model-provider and provider-side-tool channel, the fatal flaw shared by Bulkhead and Docket. The broker is the only path to model providers. It reads request bodies in plaintext on the local link, strips undeclared server-side tools for tainted sessions and holds every model key.

Fixed Docket's GET-leak flaw. Decisions never depend on the HTTP method or the bytes sent, so a labelled session cannot reach uncleared public hosts at all, and leaks through query strings or GET requests are closed.
Fixed the fingerprint flaw of Escrow (radical). Content fingerprints are never a security boundary. They are at most evidence, and are deferred.

Removed the synthetic 202 responses from Docket and Escrow (radical). v0.1 denials and v0.2 holds return a structured 403 carrying a release or approval id, so agents get an honest failure they can retry.
Fixed Bulkhead's prompt-fatigue flaw. Only exits outside clearance are denied, and nothing prompts per action. Placeholder credentials do not taint, and repository files are unlabelled by default.

Removed dependencies on undocumented or immature upstream code: OpenShell's undocumented external decision hook and ActPlane, which has no releases. OpenShell becomes a benchmark baseline and a later export target; ActPlane becomes a place to contribute upstream.
Graft from Tidemark: bring-your-own-canary, delivered as a QEMU fw_cfg systemd credential, with the grep run on the host outside the VM.

Grafts from Bulkhead: the benchmark as a standalone container that measures other sandboxes; a puppet-model server that drives real CLIs; review of auto-exec writes; placeholder credentials that do not taint.
Grafts from Docket: a global stop (cgroup.freeze plus deny-all); a doctor report of which guarantees hold; the pinned verifier gate in v0.2.

Grafts from Escrow (radical): receipts as in-toto Statements in DSSE envelopes; Forgejo and Mailpit Quadlets for the v0.2 demo extension; annotations that may raise an effect class but never lower it; any effect that notifies a person counts as irreversible.

Grafts from Escrow (security-first): audit-versus-enforce runs in a fork-and-run workflow; strict Landlock at ABI 9 or later; a ledger daemon under its own UID; holds on irreversible effects only, answered with a structured 403 (v0.2).

Addressed the third judge's cross-cutting challenge. Useful pieces spread without anyone booting the image: the benchmark container and the cross-platform verifier at launch, and tidemark-lite in v0.2.
Privilege separation answers the root-daemon concern raised against Escrow. tidemarkd keeps a small root surface, while the gateway, broker and ledger daemon run unprivileged.
Addressed the 'model under 2B parameters proves routing, not usefulness' criticism. The demo model only proves placement, and the utility suite reports usefulness separately for each hardware class.
Made Docket's unproven span-of-control thesis something to measure. Attention scheduling is deferred to Phase 6 and must be measured there, not claimed.

Surfaced an inconsistency in the founder's premise. Natively booted Linux on the M1 runs AI slower than macOS Metal, so the project's revolution is control and proof, not speed. The local-performance showcase moves to x86 GPU hardware in Phase 6.

redteam:scope.lens: Scope, solo-maintainer capacity and adoption realism (adversarial). Executive summary: the strategy can survive, but the schedule cannot. Phase 0 plus the MVP is roughly 2 to 3 times larger than the stated 140 hours, and the 6/2/2 split leaves only 84 hours for building. The hero demo contains a determinism contradiction. Hermes Agent's self-written memory is an unaddressed laundering channel. The named first users (users of $5 VPS hosts and always-on messaging gateways whose private data comes through APIs) mostly fall outside what v0.1 protects. Clarifying questions for the founder: (1) What hands-on experience do you have with BPF LSM, the systemd D-Bus APIs, overlayfs and Go? The estimates assume an expert. (2) Will AI coding agents write most of the code, and who reviews security-critical diffs? (3) Will you accept a product delivered as an RPM daemon, with the bootable image as a thin layer that installs it? (4) Where does your target users' private data actually live: local files, or APIs such as Gmail, IMAP and Notion? Evidence files: /Users/mac/.claude/projects/-Users-mac-Desktop-AI-Operating-System/0d2e94e4-925c-41b7-98f4-90ee4854045b/tool-results/bn2heqr9p.txt (lines 38, 55, 170, 186, 221), /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-mac-Desktop-AI-Operating-System/0d2e94e4-925c-41b7-98f4-90ee4854045b/scratchpad/dims.txt

critical_issues.issue: The MVP cannot ship in about 12 weeks at 10 hours a week. Build capacity is overstated by a factor of 2 to 3.
critical_issues.evidence: The plan's own 6/2/2 split leaves 14 x 6 = 84 build hours for Phase 0 plus the MVP. In that time it must deliver about 2,900 lines of product code, about 700 lines of bench and demo code, tests for more than 100 matrix cases with property tests, fuzzers and contract tests, 8 CI workflows, image builds for 2 architectures in 4 formats, 4 demo paths and about 25 documents. That is roughly 6,000 to 8,000 lines, or 70 to 95 tested lines per build hour, of kernel and systemd integration code. The prior feasibility brief (bn2heqr9p.txt line 186) advised holding v0.1 to under 1,000 lines of the founder's own code. Line 55 notes that even Universal Blue's small team had to cut image variants. Reviewer estimate: 250 to 400 hours at the full scope, which is 40 to 65 weeks at 6 build hours a week.
critical_issues.fix: Re-baseline publicly. Either keep this scope with a target of April to May 2027, or apply the default cuts below (not contingent ones) to fit 14 weeks. Make the cut order the default plan rather than a week-9 fallback. Add a checkpoint at week 5, not only week 9.

critical_issues.issue: Several components are underestimated by factors of 3 to 5.
critical_issues.evidence: The broker is budgeted at 500 lines for OpenAI Chat Completions, Responses and Anthropic Messages with SSE streaming, per-protocol stripping of provider-side tools, model aliasing, credential injection, placement, memory-fit admission and FIFO fairness. Proxies that do this run to thousands of lines. Staging is budgeted at 250 lines, yet it must handle overlay whiteouts, opaque directories, renames, xattr stamping and conflict detection, and pass a property test requiring parity with an unwrapped run over 1,000 operations. The bench and puppet code is budgeted at 700 lines, but every agent has different tool schemas (Hermes terminal, OpenCode bash, Claude Code Bash), so transcripts are needed per agent and per scenario. The session principal is budgeted at 450 lines, but a per-session UID pool conflicts with persistent agent state: ~/.hermes written by one UID cannot be written by the next session's UID, so idmapped mounts or a fixed per-agent UID are needed.
critical_issues.fix: Re-estimate with these ranges: broker 1,500 to 2,500 lines, staging 800 to 1,200, bench and puppet at least 2,000, session at least 800. Accept only OpenAI Chat Completions in v0.1, since Hermes Agent and OpenCode both speak it. Drop memory-fit admission, the cost cap and the ranker stub. Use one fixed UID per agent profile with per-session cgroups.

critical_issues.issue: Hermes Agent's persistent memory launders labelled data across sessions. This breaks G3 and G4, the cross-vendor claim and the demo.
critical_issues.evidence: The Hermes documentation says the agent writes to ~/.hermes/memories/MEMORY.md and USER.md itself ('The agent saves automatically'), and that this content loads into the system prompt at the next session start. In the plan, labels are stamped only when the workspace is committed. Profile BindPaths (agent state directories) are neither staged nor labelled. A private session can therefore write the canary into MEMORY.md, and the next, unlabelled session sends it to an uncleared cloud model or a public host. OpenCode and Claude Code keep state of the same kind.
critical_issues.fix: Stamp the session label on every file a labelled session creates or modifies on any writable path, not only on commit. Two options: a write-side BPF hook using the security.bpf xattr setter kfunc, or a stamping pass at session end before the unit is released. Add 'agent-memory laundering' to the bypass matrix and to the hero demo. Budget 15 to 25 extra hours.

critical_issues.issue: The hero demo contradicts itself: once the label rises, the puppet stops driving the agent.
critical_issues.evidence: After the read, the broker must send the private session's model calls to the local llama-server. The real, unmodified Hermes Agent then gets its next responses from a model under 2B parameters, not from the scripted puppet. The remaining exit attempts become stochastic, which conflicts with the gate of 3 identical runs, and a CPU prefill of agent system prompts on a 4 vCPU runner would take tens of seconds per call. Step 6, where OpenCode's call is placed locally, has the same problem.
critical_issues.fix: In the gating suite, register two puppet backends: a local puppet cleared for all labels, and a cloud puppet whose log is the sink. Placement is then proven by which log receives the request. Show real llama-server inference only in a separate, non-gating placement smoke test, and say so in the demo text.

critical_issues.issue: A stranger cannot reproduce the demo in under 10 minutes as specified.
critical_issues.evidence: The stated 1.6 GB download leaves out the separate model (about 1 GB), agent installs from PyPI and npm, the sink and bench containers, and the baseline tools. Step 10 reruns steps 4 and 5 under three baselines, which is the whole benchmark run with its own 10-minute target, so the demo takes at least 20 minutes. There are four host paths (GitHub workflow, Linux QEMU, Mac QEMU with HVF, Lima), each injecting the canary differently. Lima provisions guests through a cloud-init NoCloud 'cidata' path, and the plan does not check whether the bootc image supports it. Many Macs have 8 GB of RAM but the VM needs 4 to 6 GB. On Path A the fork runs the project's own workflow YAML, so it is weak evidence of independence, and Actions are disabled on forks by default.
critical_issues.fix: Run v0.1's demo on one primary path: x86_64 Linux with KVM, plus the fork workflow. Show 6 to 8 headline channels and run no baselines in the demo; move them to a separate `tidemark-bench compare`. State the total download size honestly. Gate the release on a measured wall-clock run on a clean runner that includes every download. Document the Mac and Lima paths as best effort, and check cidata support in Phase 0.

critical_issues.issue: Releasing a request 'after seeing the exact bytes' is impossible for HTTPS in v0.1.
critical_issues.evidence: v0.1 has no TLS interception: the gateway passes CONNECT tunnels through opaquely. Yet the release primitive and G9 promise that the human sees the exact bytes and that each release records a content hash. For a CONNECT, a release can only grant the whole tunnel, with unbounded content.
critical_issues.fix: In v0.1, allow content-hashed releases only for broker requests (plaintext on the local link) and plain HTTP. Record a CONNECT release as a per-session destination grant without a content hash, and rewrite G9 to match. Alternatively, cut releases entirely and keep only stop and re-run.

critical_issues.issue: The tagline promises more than v0.1 delivers.
critical_issues.evidence: 'Agents run without prompts' paired with v0.1's non-guarantee that external side effects are neither held nor undone means an unlabelled session with prompts off can still delete a production database or a repository at a cleared destination: the Replit and PocketOS pattern the plan cites as pain. Holds arrive only in v0.2.
critical_issues.fix: Limit the v0.1 tagline to confidentiality, for example 'what a session has read decides where it may send'. Recommend keeping agent prompts on for tools with side effects until v0.2 holds ship, and say so in the release notes.

critical_issues.issue: The first-user choice does not match where those users run agents or where their private data lives.
critical_issues.evidence: Hermes' README says 'Run it on a $5 VPS'. Such a host cannot run llama-server and rarely accepts custom images. Its main mode is an always-on gateway to Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp and Signal. With domain-level clearance, clearing api.telegram.org for private data also permits sending to any chat, so the guarantee becomes hollow for this mode. Private mail, calendar and notes mostly arrive through APIs or IMAP, which the gateway marks as untrusted but never labels as confidential. Mac users would have to move their data into the VM, and security.* xattrs on virtiofs shared folders are unverified. The OpenClaw profile is deferred to v0.2, yet OpenClaw users are named as primary users.
critical_issues.fix: Narrow the first users to homelab and Proxmox users who run coding or research agents in a dedicated VM over local files. Add destination source labels to the MVP (about 50 to 100 lines): reading from imap.gmail.com, for example, raises the session to private. Exclude VPS hosts, always-on messaging gateways and OpenClaw from the v0.1 claims. Test labels and staging on virtiofs or 9p in Phase 0.

critical_issues.issue: The user validation comes too late and asks leading questions.
critical_issues.evidence: The five interviews finish at week 6, after Phase 1 (weeks 3 to 5) is built. 'Will you label your secrets?' invites polite yes answers. The plan also concedes that willingness-to-pay evidence across the research is vendor-survey based.
critical_issues.fix: Hold 8 to 10 observational interviews in weeks 1 and 2. Ask participants to show their agent configuration, data sources, cleared destinations and hosting. Move kill criterion 2 to week 3.

critical_issues.issue: The open-source sustainability plan is not credible for a project that makes a public security claim.
critical_issues.evidence: Triage is capped at 2 hours a week, yet the launch invites 'break it' reports, promises a 14-day fix target and a 7-day right of reply to NVIDIA, Anthropic and Omarchy, and withdraws a guarantee if a fix misses 14 days. Reproducing a bypass needs the VM loop on a 16 GB M1, which cannot run the podman machine and the dev VM together. Founders write 66 to 100% of commits even in breakout projects (bn2heqr9p.txt line 170), so 'a second maintainer after 6 months' is unlikely. The distribution advantage of Omarchy-style projects came from an existing audience (line 221). STF excludes prototypes and NLnet excludes AI projects, and no audit is funded before v1.0.
critical_issues.fix: Launch enforce mode as a 'preview', with a 90-day coordinated disclosure window instead of 14 days. Assume a bus factor of 1 through month 12, and treat a second maintainer as a bonus, not a deliverable. Before launch, verify one audit-funding path whose eligibility rules fit the project, and recruit the two or three pre-launch reviewers by name in Phase 0.

critical_issues.issue: The post-MVP phases are overloaded by a factor of 3 or more.
critical_issues.evidence: Phase 6 packs capability manifests, an attention queue, a Cockpit plugin, evidence mapping for four jurisdictions, OTel and OCSF export, Rekor anchoring, a policy compiler for two targets, an NVIDIA variant, the Laya evaluation and new BPF hooks into about 130 hours, which is about 78 build hours. Phases 5 and 7 are similar.
critical_issues.fix: Plan one theme per quarter, chosen by user evidence at each milestone. Move the regulatory mapping, Cockpit, the NVIDIA variant, the policy compiler, the attention queue and microVMs into a backlog, each with an explicit trigger.

critical_issues.issue: Phase 0 is overloaded, and the kernel gate depends on image work that has not yet been done.
critical_issues.evidence: In about 12 build hours, Phase 0 must deliver a BPF LSM spike on two architectures including overlayfs, a dual-architecture bootc pipeline with cosign, an SBOM and a QEMU smoke test, four ADRs, five documents, two specifications and six governance files. The aarch64 spike runs in Lima on the bootc image, which first needs Lima provisioning to work.
critical_issues.fix: Run the spike on a stock Fedora 45 Cloud VM in Lima (same kernel package, cloud-init included) and on a stock x86 runner. Build the image pipeline for x86_64 only at first. Merge the threat model, non-goals and guarantees into one document v0.

critical_issues.issue: The benchmark and CI targets do not fit the free runners.
critical_issues.evidence: The full benchmark must finish in 10 minutes or less across 5 configurations x (20 adversarial + 20 benign) scenarios, about 200 runs at roughly 2.4 s each, including VM boot and agent installs. Standard runners have a 14 GB SSD, and Bluefin reported that they lacked space for its image (bn2heqr9p.txt line 38). The plan builds qcow2, raw, ISO and AMI images for 2 architectures and also needs room for a model and agents.
critical_issues.fix: Run the full benchmark nightly with a 30 to 45 minute budget, and keep a 5-minute subset on pull requests. Ship only qcow2 and OCI images (OCI for `bootc switch`) in v0.1, and defer ISO, raw and AMI.

critical_issues.issue: The Omarchy baseline adds controversy but no information.
critical_issues.evidence: Baseline (a), the launcher flags with no sandbox, measures the same thing as (d), Tidemark in audit mode: an unenforced agent. Publishing 'Omarchy leaks everything' invites a dispute with a large audience that a solo founder cannot absorb within 2 triage hours a week. OpenShell needs Docker, Podman or host virtualization plus a local gateway, and its default sandbox has 'no agent installed', so the 4-hour cap will likely be exceeded.
critical_issues.fix: In v0.1, compare only Tidemark audit and enforce against sandbox-runtime. Move OpenShell to v0.2. Drop the Omarchy comparison or describe it neutrally as 'unsandboxed'.

incumbent_overlap.overlap: These already run Hermes Agent and OpenClaw, the exact first-user audience, inside policy sandboxes with credential injection. Installation needs only Docker, Podman or host virtualization plus a local gateway, which is far less friction than booting a new OS image.

Hermes Agent ships seven terminal backends (local, Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal, Daytona, Vercel Sandbox) and a memory write_approval option. Users can get containment without leaving the agent, and Nous could add label-like gating upstream.
Persistent hosted agent VMs offer always-on users an alternative to self-hosting a VM appliance, which competes for the same homelab and VPS users.

redteam:technical.lens: Adversarial technical-soundness and security review: do the kernel, egress, staging, and evidence mechanisms actually deliver the stated guarantees (G1-G9), and can the system be built and tested on an M1 Pro without nested virtualization. Reviewed against the plan JSON; prior-art and incumbent comparisons added from domain knowledge.

critical_issues.issue: Egress guarantee G4 has a connect-then-taint-then-send TOCTOU: a session that is clean when it opens an HTTPS CONNECT tunnel keeps that tunnel usable after the session is later tainted, so labelled data exits through an already-authorised opaque tunnel.
critical_issues.evidence: The gateway 'implements HTTP CONNECT and plain HTTP forwarding' and reads the label 'synchronously at every decision', but a CONNECT tunnel is decided once at connect time and is thereafter an opaque TLS pipe the gateway cannot re-evaluate. The high-water mark rises only when open() is called, which can happen after the tunnel is established. Nearly all real destinations are HTTPS, so this is the common case. The scripted heist reads the canary before attempting exits, so the demo never exercises this ordering.
critical_issues.fix: Make the gateway event-driven on label rise: subscribe to a teardown-only BPF ring buffer (fail-safe direction, so the map-update race they already avoided does not reappear) and immediately reset every live connection whose destination clearance no longer dominates the new session label. Re-evaluate plain HTTP per request. Add a benchmark scenario that opens the tunnel BEFORE the labelled read.

critical_issues.issue: Taint is incomplete because file_open is the only taint point: file descriptors inherited across the shim's exec (systemd credentials, pre-opened files) or received via SCM_RIGHTS let a session read labelled data without ever triggering the hook.
critical_issues.evidence: G3 asserts the label rises 'when any session process opens a labelled file', but inherited and passed fds are read via read()/mmap() on an already-open fd and never call security_file_open in the agent. The shim 'execs the agent', and systemd credentials are delivered as files/fds. The read matrix lists /proc/self/fd reopen but not exec-inherited fds or SCM_RIGHTS fds.
critical_issues.fix: The shim must close_range() all non-essential fds before exec; any inherited or credential fd pointing at a labelled inode must raise the session label at session start; add exec-inherited-fd and SCM_RIGHTS cases to the read matrix.

critical_issues.issue: The per-cgroup label map keyed by the immediate cgroup id breaks taint and quota enforcement if a session can create or be placed in a child cgroup.
critical_issues.evidence: Primitive 2 states a 'pinned map keyed by cgroup' and the hook 'exits unless the current cgroup belongs to a session'. If a profile sets Delegate=yes, or the agent creates a sub-cgroup, descendants run under a different cgroup id that the map does not recognise, so their reads are treated as non-session (no taint) and they escape CPUQuota/MemoryMax.
critical_issues.fix: Key the map by the session's ancestor cgroup id (bpf_get_current_ancestor_cgroup_id at the slice-relative level) rather than the exact cgroup id; set Delegate=no explicitly in every profile unless delegation is strictly required; add a sub-cgroup-spawning agent to the containment and read matrices.

critical_issues.issue: The whole product rests on the label hook reading security.bpf.tidemark through overlayfs, which may not surface the lower inode's xattr; reads through the staged workspace could therefore go untainted.
critical_issues.evidence: The plan itself lists this as a Phase 0 risk ('overlayfs may interact badly') and bpf_get_file_xattr operates on the opened dentry, which under overlayfs is an overlay inode, not the labelled lower inode. The read matrix includes 'an overlay path', but the fanotify fallback is only defined for a dedicated vault subvolume, not for overlay-mediated reads by children or via mmap.
critical_issues.fix: The Phase 0 kill gate must prove read-through-overlay tainting before any other code; resolve and consult the real underlying inode/path rather than the overlay dentry; and define, before committing to the fallback, how fanotify FAN_OPEN_PERM covers mmap and grandchild reads, since fanotify permission events have known gaps there.

critical_issues.issue: The cross-vendor claim 'labels travel with files' is fragile because security.* xattrs are not preserved by ordinary tools, so a committed labelled file loses its label as soon as it is rewritten, and the next agent reads it untainted.
critical_issues.evidence: G6 and the hero demo depend on a committed file carrying the private label to a second vendor's session. Editors (write-temp-then-rename), cp, git checkout, tar, and rsync drop security.* xattrs by default. The scripted demo commits once and reads immediately, so it passes while realistic rewrite workflows silently launder the label away.
critical_issues.fix: Do not rely on per-inode xattrs for travelling labels: maintain a side index keyed by content hash and/or confine labelled data to a dedicated labelled subtree whose whole-tree membership drives taint; narrow the public claim to files Tidemark itself controls; add a rewrite-then-reread laundering scenario to the benchmark.

critical_issues.issue: Authority for commit and auto-exec acceptance is unspecified, so a compromised in-session agent may be able to stamp labels, merge into the real workspace, or accept its own auto-exec implant; and writes to any writable bind path not covered by the overlay bypass staging entirely.
critical_issues.evidence: release and stop are explicitly 'refused from inside the agents slice' via SO_PEERCRED, but tidemark diff|commit|abort and the 'explicit acceptance flag' for auto-exec paths carry no such restriction. G6 claims writes are 'invisible to the host until commit', yet only the overlay-covered workspace is staged; a writable profile bind path outside the overlay is a direct, unstaged, unabortable write.
critical_issues.fix: Restrict commit and auto-exec acceptance to processes outside the agents slice (SO_PEERCRED plus cgroup check, as for release); require that every writable path be overlay-staged, and have doctor fail if a profile declares a writable non-overlaid path.

critical_issues.issue: Per-open xattr lookups will be costly for open-heavy workloads, and the 'first installable OS' claim does not address mature in-kernel incumbents.
critical_issues.evidence: A sleepable file_open hook doing an xattr syscall on every open inside a session pays that cost 10^5+ times for npm installs or compilers; the 10us p50 / 50us p99 targets assume a warm cache, while a sleepable hook can fault in the xattr. Separately, positioning omits Qubes OS (owned OS with kernel-enforced per-domain isolation and per-domain network control) and SELinux MLS/MCS (in-kernel label-based MAC with SECMARK network control already shipping on Fedora).
critical_issues.fix: Add a mount/path prefilter or a cached 'inode is unlabelled' decision so only files under labelled trees pay the xattr cost; benchmark a real npm/compile workload inside a session. In docs, differentiate explicitly from Qubes and SELinux and give the one-line justification for a bespoke BPF high-water mark (SELinux MLS has no dynamic float, which is a real and statable reason).

critical_issues.issue: Receipt wording overclaims for v0.1: 'tamper-evident, third-party-verifiable' and 'append-only' rest on an on-machine signing key and daemon-enforced (not kernel-enforced) append-only storage.
critical_issues.evidence: The Ed25519 key lives in systemd-creds readable by the ledger UID, and Btrfs offers no owner-proof WORM mode, so a compromise of the ledger daemon (which parses structured events) forges a self-consistent chain that the offline verifier accepts. The plan acknowledges this as a non-guarantee, but the revolutionary_claim and guarantees text still present receipts as externally verifiable evidence.
critical_issues.fix: Present the bring-your-own-canary host-side grep as the primary external check and the receipt as secondary until TPM sealing or Rekor anchoring lands; soften the public 'tamper-evident, third-party-verifiable' wording for v0.1.

critical_issues.issue: Testability gaps: x86 enforcement is only ever exercised in CI, and arm64 GitHub runners may lack /dev/kvm.
critical_issues.evidence: The founder develops on M1 and runs aarch64 under vz, with x86 'only in CI'. BPF verifier and kernel-config differences can produce x86-only bypasses the founder cannot reproduce interactively, slowing the 14-day fix target. The plan adds a step to 'record whether /dev/kvm exists' on arm64 runners, conceding it is uncertain; without KVM, TCG emulation can exceed the 90s boot target.
critical_issues.fix: Budget occasional rented x86 KVM time (consistent with the stated USD 15-40/month) for interactive x86 bypass triage; define a slower boot-time target or a KVM-required gate for the arm64 CI path.

critical_issues.issue: Session units do not explicitly deny user-namespace creation, which widens the single in-scope-excluded risk (kernel LPE).
critical_issues.evidence: The session properties list RestrictNamespaces and a SystemCallFilter but do not state that CLONE_NEWUSER is denied. Unprivileged user namespaces are the dominant Linux local-privilege-escalation vector, and the threat model treats kernel compromise as out of scope, so leaving user-ns open makes that excluded risk materially easier to reach from inside a session.
critical_issues.fix: Set RestrictNamespaces to deny user namespace creation (and all namespaces the agent does not need) in session units; assert this in the containment matrix.

incumbent_overlap.overlap: Uses the same kernel primitives (Landlock, seccomp, network namespace, credential injection) plus allowlisted egress and runtime access approval; the plan concedes NVIDIA could add read-time labels in one release (kill criterion 5), which would erase the core differentiator.
incumbent_overlap.source: Plan positioning section and OpenShell README (research facts, Oct 2026)

incumbent_overlap.overlap: An owned OS providing kernel-enforced per-domain isolation and per-domain network/firewall control; the closest existing 'owned OS plus controlled egress' prior art, and it is entirely unaddressed in the plan's positioning.

In-kernel label-based mandatory access control with file categories and SECMARK/peer network labelling, already shipping on Fedora; overlaps the labelling primitive and must be justified against rather than ignored.
incumbent_overlap.source: SELinux and Fedora documentation (reviewer domain knowledge)

incumbent_overlap.overlap: Process containment via bubblewrap/Seatbelt for agent shell commands; overlaps the containment layer, though it does not wrap MCP servers/hooks or the model channel.
incumbent_overlap.source: Plan positioning section and research facts (Oct 2026)

incumbent_overlap.overlap: Information-flow control for agents; the same confidentiality-IFC concept Tidemark applies at session granularity, so the novelty is the packaging and model-placement combination, not the IFC idea.
incumbent_overlap.source: Plan prior-art section and research facts (Oct 2026)

incumbent_overlap.product: Microsoft Agent 365 / AWS Bedrock AgentCore (Cedar, Dogwood) / Google Agent Identity
incumbent_overlap.overlap: Agent identity and policy governance; different layer today, but each is positioned to extend policy toward data-flow control and is bundled or cloud-native, pressuring the governance edge of the claim.

recommended_changes: Treat the CONNECT-tunnel TOCTOU as the launch blocker: implement event-driven teardown of live connections on label rise and add a connect-before-read benchmark scenario; the week-9 bypass matrix must include it.
Close taint-completeness holes before claiming G3: close_range() in the shim, taint on inherited/credential/SCM_RIGHTS fds, key the label map by the session's ancestor cgroup id, and set Delegate=no.
Prove read-through-overlay xattr tainting in Phase 0 as the first gate, and fully specify fanotify fallback coverage for mmap and grandchild reads before relying on it.

Re-scope the 'labels travel with files' claim: use a content-hash side index or a dedicated labelled subtree rather than per-inode security.* xattrs, and add a rewrite-then-reread laundering scenario.
Restrict commit and auto-exec acceptance to outside the agents slice (as release/stop already are), and require every writable path to be overlay-staged with a doctor check.
Add a mount/path prefilter so only labelled trees pay the per-open xattr cost, and benchmark a real npm/compile workload inside a session rather than only synthetic opens.
Add Qubes OS and SELinux MLS/MCS to positioning with explicit differentiation, and state why a bespoke BPF high-water mark is needed (SELinux lacks dynamic float).
Soften v0.1 receipt wording to 'append-only by the daemon' and 'offline-verifiable given key secrecy', and present the host-side canary grep as the primary external proof until TPM/Rekor land.
Deny user-namespace creation in session units and assert it in the containment matrix, since it is the main route to the otherwise-excluded kernel-LPE risk.
Budget occasional rented x86 KVM time for interactive x86 bypass triage, and define a KVM-required gate or a slower boot target for arm64 CI where /dev/kvm may be absent.

redteam:incumbent.lens: Incumbent overlap and novelty attack, as of 16 Oct 2026. Every primitive was checked against public repositories and official docs. Verdict in brief: only one claim is really new. That claim is that kernel-observed read history decides both egress and model placement for unmodified agents from different vendors. Sessions, egress proxying, credential placeholders, staging, rollback, audit chains, the kill switch and signed skill files are all integration work. Several of those pieces already ship elsewhere, and some ship in stronger form. White spaces 3 and 4 are already partly shipped.

critical_issues.issue: G4 can be bypassed with a tunnel opened before the label rises. The gateway decides once, when a CONNECT arrives, and v0.1 has no TLS interception. A session can open a CONNECT, keep-alive or WebSocket tunnel to an allowlisted public host while it is still unlabelled, then read the secret, then stream the secret through the tunnel that is already open.
critical_issues.evidence: The plan reads the BPF map synchronously at each decision, but decisions happen only per connection, at the domain level. None of the 40-case bypass matrix or the 14 channel classes covers a tunnel that already exists when the label is raised.
critical_issues.fix: On every forwarded chunk from the client, check the session's current label against the tunnel's clearance, or subscribe to label-raise events and close every tunnel whose clearance no longer covers the label. Add 'pre-opened tunnel', 'HTTP/2 connection reuse' and 'WebSocket opened before the read' to the bypass matrix and the benchmark.

critical_issues.issue: Data can be laundered through persistent agent state, or labels creep for good, and either outcome hits exactly the first-user segment. Hermes Agent memory and skills and OpenClaw state live in profile bind paths. Those paths are not the staged workspace, so writes to them are never stamped with a label. A later session, from any vendor, reads that memory unlabelled and can send it out. If the state directories are labelled instead, every always-on session becomes private permanently.
critical_issues.evidence: G6 stamps labels only when the staged workspace is committed. Profiles bind-mount the agent's own state paths. The first users are defined as people running always-on Hermes or OpenClaw against personal data. ActPlane already propagates labels along file write edges.
critical_issues.fix: Propagate labels in the kernel when a labelled session writes to any persistent path. Use bpf_set_dentry_xattr, which can write security.bpf.* only, from a sleepable LSM hook on file open with write mode and on file permission with MAY_WRITE. Run each user task as a short sub-session with its own label, and treat the agent's long-lived memory as a labelled store. In Phase 1, measure label creep on a real Hermes setup with memory turned on, before building Phase 2.

critical_issues.issue: Personal data that arrives over the network never raises a label. Labels rise only when a file is opened. For the target users, mail, notes and finance usually come through APIs (Gmail or IMAP, Notion, banking connectors reached through MCP), not local files.
critical_issues.evidence: The label raise is the file_open BPF hook. The gateway sets only the 'untrusted' integrity flag on content it receives. No destination carries a 'source label'.
critical_issues.fix: Add source labels to destinations. The gateway raises the session label as soon as a CONNECT is allowed to a domain tagged private-source. The broker does the same when a cleared tool or MCP result comes from a labelled source. Add 'read inbox through an API, then exfiltrate' to the hero demo and the benchmark.

critical_issues.issue: The receipts are oversold as proof that 'anyone can check from outside'. The signing key sits on the machine, and the image digest in each receipt is a value the machine reports about itself. The machine owner and root are out of scope as adversaries, yet either can sign whatever they like. Microsoft AGT already ships a Merkle audit log, and nono already ships append-only integrity hashing.
critical_issues.evidence: The plan's non-guarantees list already says receipts are 'only as trustworthy as that machine until TPM sealing or external anchoring' is added. The tagline and revolutionary_claim still promise third-party proof.
critical_issues.fix: For v0.1, describe receipts as 'tamper-evident against the agent'. Make the BYOC host-side grep the public proof. Add a TPM2-backed key early: swtpm in QEMU plus systemd-creds --with-key=tpm2. Add TPM quotes or Keylime-style remote attestation before claiming third-party verifiability.

critical_issues.issue: The novelty wording is wrong. Shipped operating systems have enforced kernel confidentiality labels on network exits for decades: SELinux MLS (Fedora ships selinux-policy-mls; RHEL earned LSPP certification) and Solaris Trusted Extensions, with labelled networking. The high-water mark itself goes back to ADEPT-50 in 1969. ActPlane hooks connect and can block through BPF-LSM.
critical_issues.evidence: ActPlane's README lists the hooks 'fork / exec / exit / open / unlink / rename / connect', says labels propagate along 'file read/write edges', and says BPF-LSM lets rules 'block before they commit'. The plan says ActPlane has 'no forced exit mediation' and cites only research systems as prior art.
critical_issues.fix: Narrow the claim to: high-water-mark labels on whole process trees of unmodified AI agents from different vendors, with the model API handled as a labelled exit and placement constrained by the label. Cite SELinux MLS, ADEPT-50 and ActPlane's connect hook as prior art.

critical_issues.issue: Several direct competitors are missing from the positioning, and the plan treats as unshipped some features that already ship.
critical_issues.evidence: nono (Apache-2.0, about 4.5k stars) ships Landlock/Seatbelt sandboxing, a credential proxy with phantom tokens, allowlist filtering by host and endpoint, 'Content-addressable rollback with SHA-256 dedup and Merkle tree integrity', append-only integrity hashing, and Sigstore-signed instruction files. AgentFS ships copy-on-write isolation and a SQLite audit log. agentsh ships an LLM proxy with DLP, approvals, soft_delete and checkpoints. container-use gives each agent a branch that can be discarded. Rubrik Agent Rewind (August 2025) rolls back files, databases and repositories. Invariant Guardrails ships data-flow rules across tool calls through an MCP or LLM proxy.
critical_issues.fix: Add all of these to the positioning. Add nono as a benchmark baseline. Reframe white space 4 as 'permission-diff admission' only, since signed instruction files already ship. Describe staging and receipts as integration, not novelty.

critical_issues.issue: The plan mischaracterises Anthropic's sandbox-runtime and NVIDIA's NemoClaw.
critical_issues.evidence: The srt README says it sandboxes 'the entire process tree', including local MCP servers, and has credential masking and a filterRequest hook. Only Claude Code's built-in sandbox is limited to shell commands. NemoClaw needs no NVIDIA account for local Ollama or vLLM and runs on Linux with rootless Podman and on Windows through WSL, so 'no account, hardware-neutral' does not set Tidemark apart.
critical_issues.fix: Base the differentiation only on label-driven exits, model placement and evidence. Treat NemoClaw as the main competitor in the self-hoster segment.

critical_issues.issue: OpenShell now documents an extension point that both threatens Tidemark and duplicates its gateway. Supervisor middleware 'inspects, transforms, or denies allowed HTTP and WebSocket traffic'. NVIDIA could therefore add a taint check as middleware in one release. Meanwhile, building tidemark-gw contradicts Tidemark's own non-goal of not rebuilding containment. OpenShell already has credential placeholders, request-level read/write limits and OCSF events, so Tidemark v0.1 is weaker on L7 rules and credentials.
critical_issues.evidence: docs.nvidia.com/openshell/extensibility/overview and /observability. The plan dropped OpenShell as 'undocumented'.
critical_issues.fix: Build the label engine and the clearance evaluator as a library with two front ends: the gateway inside the image, and an OpenShell supervisor-middleware adapter in v0.2. The incumbent then becomes a distribution channel rather than a kill criterion.

critical_issues.issue: v0.1 has a credential paradox. A git push to a cleared remote is in the benign suite, but without TLS termination the token has to live inside the session. If the token is labelled, it taints the session and the push is denied. If it is not labelled, an injected agent can exfiltrate it. OpenShell, srt, nono, Docker and Sprites already keep credentials out of the session.
critical_issues.evidence: Credential placeholder substitution is deferred to v0.2, together with goproxy.
critical_issues.fix: Move minimal credential injection into the MVP: TLS termination for git smart-HTTP and two declared APIs. Otherwise, remove the push task from the benign suite and document the limitation.

critical_issues.issue: Phase 5 holds desynchronise the agent from reality. An irreversible request is held, the agent receives a 403, and the request is replayed after a human approves it. The agent believes the action failed, so it may retry by another route and duplicate the effect. Temporal's sagas and agentsh's soft_delete or approve decisions are prior art for this pattern.
critical_issues.evidence: Phase 5 replays approved requests with an idempotency key after a timeout.
critical_issues.fix: Hold the request synchronously with a bounded wait. Alternatively, define an explicit 'queued' response contract in the profiles. Present the effect journal as integration on top of saga patterns.

critical_issues.issue: The benchmark is built around the one property only Tidemark has. OpenShell and srt allow allowlisted hosts by design, so the leak table is predetermined.
critical_issues.evidence: Of the 14 channel classes, 4 (upload, query string, push, model prompt) are leaks only under label semantics. The suite has no channels where the incumbents should win.
critical_issues.fix: Pre-register the methodology. Add channels where incumbents lead (L7 method and path rules, credential exfiltration, completion rate). Report benign completion for every baseline next to its leak count.

critical_issues.issue: The claim that 'model calls move, not fail' is overclaimed.
critical_issues.evidence: When no cleared backend fits the context or the memory limit (on the M1, prefilling 30K tokens takes 2 to 4 minutes), the request fails.
critical_issues.fix: Reword as 'never silently placed outside clearance; fails closed with a structured reason'.

critical_issues.issue: The calendar does not hold. The 6/2/2 weekly split gives 72 build hours in the 12-week MVP, not 120. Those hours must cover about 3,600 lines of product and benchmark code plus security tests.
critical_issues.evidence: Budget section and weekly cadence.
critical_issues.fix: Budget the MVP in build hours, or cut it to labels, the gateway with tunnel revocation, the broker and the BYOC demo, moving staging and the dashboard to v0.2.

incumbent_overlap.overlap: Landlock, seccomp and network-namespace sandboxing; default-deny egress with rules scoped to binaries and limited to read or write requests; credential placeholders resolved only at authorised endpoints; a policy prover; supervisor middleware that can deny allowed HTTP and WebSocket traffic; OCSF NET, HTTP and CONFIG events (unsigned, may drop events under load, not durable). Its managed inference router has been removed: 'Native requests are no longer filtered or rewritten'. No labels, no staging, no signing.

Runs OpenClaw and Hermes Agent inside OpenShell, with local Ollama or vLLM, or hosted providers. No NVIDIA account is needed for local models. Runs on Linux with rootless Podman and on Windows through WSL. Its 'Model Router' does not document any routing criteria.

Kernel sandbox on macOS, Linux and WSL2; credential proxy with phantom tokens; filtering by host and endpoint; Merkle-verified rollback; append-only audit hashing; Sigstore-signed instruction files. Overlaps primitives 1, 4 (credentials), 5 and 6, and white space 4.

Kernel labels propagate along fork/exec and file read/write edges. Hooks open, unlink, rename and connect. Can block through BPF-LSM. Supports Claude Code and Codex, plus any command through `actplane run`. Overlaps primitives 2 and 5 at the mechanism level.

Sandboxes the entire process tree, including local MCP servers. HTTP and SOCKS proxies reached over Unix sockets, a domain allowlist, credential masking with sentinels, a filterRequest hook and tlsTerminate. Windows support is in alpha. A label-aware filter could be built on it.

The sandbox covers shell commands only. Checkpoints cover only edits made by the file tools, not Bash changes or external effects. The plan describes both correctly, but wrongly extends the shell-only limit to srt.

incumbent_overlap.product: Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit (MIT, 6.4k stars, public preview)
incumbent_overlap.overlap: Merkle audit, EU AI Act mapping, a kill switch, execution rings, and OPA or Cedar policy. Partly covers white space 3 and the global stop (G8).
Copy-on-write file isolation and a SQLite audit of every file operation and tool call. Snapshots work by copying the database. Overlaps primitives 5 and 6.
